In curing the centurion's servant, Christ took notice of it as an instance of <hi type="italic">his faith,</hi> that he did not bring him to Christ, but believed he could cure him at a distance; here he commended <hi type="italic">their faith,</hi> because they did bring their friend through so much difficulty. Note, True faith and strong faith may work variously, conquering sometimes the objections of reason, sometimes those of sense; but, however manifested, it shall be accepted and approved by Jesus Christ. Christ said, <hi type="italic">Son, thy sins be forgiven thee.</hi> The <hi type="italic">compellation</hi> is very <hi type="italic">tender-Son;</hi> intimating a fatherly <hi type="italic">care</hi> of him and <hi type="italic">concern</hi> for him. Christ owns true believers as his sons: <hi type="italic">a son,</hi> and yet sick of the palsy. Herein God <hi type="italic">deals with you as with sons.</hi> The <hi type="italic">cordial</hi> is very rich; <hi type="italic">Thy sins are forgiven thee.</hi> Note, 1. Sin is the procuring cause of all our pains and sicknesses. The word of Christ was to take his thoughts off from the disease, which was the effect, and to lead them to the sin, the cause, that he might be more concerned about that, to get that pardoned. 2. God doth <hi type="italic">then</hi> graciously take away the sting and malignity of sickness, when he forgives sin; recovery from sickness is <hi type="italic">then</hi> a mercy indeed, when way is made for it by the pardon of sin. See <reference osisRef="Isa.38.17">Isa. xxxviii. 17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.103.3">Ps. ciii. 3</reference>. The way to remove the effect, is, to take away the cause. Pardon of sin strikes at the root of all diseases, and either cures them, or alters their property. <div eID="gen24362" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24363" type="x-p"/> V. The cavil of the scribes at that which Christ said, and a demonstration of the unreasonableness of their cavil. They were expositors of the law, and their doctrine was <hi type="italic">true</hi>—that it is blasphemy for any creature to undertake the pardon of sin, and that it is God's prerogative, <reference osisRef="Isa.43.25">Isa. xliii. 25</reference>. But, as is usual with such teachers, their application was <hi type="italic">false,</hi> and was the effect of their ignorance and enmity to Christ. It is <hi type="italic">true, None can forgive sins but God only;</hi> but it is false that therefore Christ cannot, who had abundantly proved himself to have a divine power. But Christ <hi type="italic">perceived in his spirit that they so reasoned within themselves;</hi> this proves him to be God, and therefore confirmed what was to be proved, that he had authority to <hi type="italic">forgive sins;</hi> for he <hi type="italic">searched</hi> the heart, and knew <hi type="italic">what was in man,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.2.23">Rev. ii. 23</reference>. God's royalties are inseparable, and he that could <hi type="italic">know thoughts,</hi> could <hi type="italic">forgive sins.</hi> This magnifies the grace of Christ, in <hi type="italic">pardoning sin,</hi> that he knew men's thoughts, and therefore knows more than any other can know, both of the sinfulness of their sins and the particulars of them, and yet is ready to pardon. Now he proves his power to <hi type="italic">forgive sin,</hi> by demonstrating his power to cure the <hi type="italic">man sick of the palsy,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.2.9-Mark.2.11">v. 9-11</reference>. He would not have pretended to do <hi type="italic">the one,</hi> if he could not have done <hi type="italic">the other; that ye may know that the Son of man,</hi> the Messiah, <hi type="italic">has power on earth to forgive sin,</hi> that I have that power, <hi type="italic">Thou that art</hi> sick of the palsy, <hi type="italic">arise, take up thy bed.</hi> Now, 1. This was a <hi type="italic">suitable</hi> argument in itself. He could not have cured the disease, which was the effect, if he could not have taken away the sin, which was the cause. And besides, his curing diseases was a figure of his pardoning sin, for sin is the disease of the soul; when it is pardoned, it is healed. He that could by a word accomplish the sign, could doubtless perform the thing signified, 2. It was suited to them. These carnal scribes would be more affected with such a suitable effect of a pardon as the cure of the disease, and be sooner convinced by it, than by any other more spiritual consequences; therefore it was proper enough to appeal, whether it is easier to say, <hi type="italic">Thy sins are forgiven thee,</hi> or to say, <hi type="italic">Arise, and walk?</hi> The removing of the punishment as such, was the remitting of the sin; he that could go so far in the cure, no doubt could perfect it. See <reference osisRef="Isa.33.24">Isa. xxxiii. 24</reference>. <div eID="gen24363" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24364" type="x-p"/> VI. The cure of the sick man, and the impression it made upon the people, <reference osisRef="Mark.2.12">v. 12</reference>. He not only <hi type="italic">arise</hi> out of his bed, perfectly well, but, to show that he had perfect strength restored to him, <hi type="italic">he took up his bed,</hi> because it lay in the way, <hi type="italic">and went forth before them all;</hi> and <hi type="italic">they were all amazed,</hi> as well they might, and <hi type="italic">glorified God,</hi> as indeed they ought; saying, "<hi type="italic">We never saw it on this fashion;</hi> never were such wonders as these done before in our time." Note, Christ's works were without precedent. When we see what he does in healing souls, we must own that we <hi type="italic">never saw the like.</hi>

<div eID="gen24364" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Christ among Publicans and Sinners.</title> <div sID="gen24365" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">13</hi> And he went forth again by the sea side; and all the multitude resorted unto him, and he taught them. <hi type="super">14</hi> And as he passed by, he saw Levi the <hi type="italic">son</hi> of Alphæus sitting at the receipt of custom, and said unto him, Follow me. And he arose and followed him. <hi type="super">15</hi> And it came to pass, that, as Jesus sat at meat in his house, many publicans and sinners sat also together with Jesus and his disciples: for there were many, and they followed him. <hi type="super">16</hi> And when the scribes and Pharisees saw him eat with publicans and sinners, they said unto his disciples, How is it that he eateth and drinketh with publicans and sinners? 17 When Jesus heard <hi type="italic">it,</hi> he saith unto them, They that are whole have no need of the physician, but they that are sick: I came not to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance. <div eID="gen24365" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24366" type="x-p"/> Here is, <div eID="gen24366" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24367" type="x-p"/> I. Christ preaching by the <hi type="italic">sea-side</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mark.2.13">v. 13</reference>), whither he went <hi type="italic">for room,</hi> because he found, upon second trial, no house or street large enough to contain his auditory; but upon the strand there might come as many as would. It should seem by this, that our Lord Jesus had a strong voice, and could and did speak loud; for <hi type="italic">wisdom crieth without</hi> in the <hi type="italic">places of concourse.</hi> Wherever he goes, though it be to the sea-side, <hi type="italic">multitudes resort to him.</hi> Wherever the doctrine of Christ is faithfully preached, though it be driven into corners or into deserts, we must follow it. <div eID="gen24367" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24368" type="x-p"/> II. His calling Levi; the same with Matthew, who had a place in the custom-house at Capernaum, from which he was denominated a <hi type="italic">publican;</hi> his place fixed him by the water-side, and thither Christ went to meet with him, and to give him an effectual call. This Levi is here said to be <hi type="italic">the son of Alpheus</hi> or <hi type="italic">Cleophas,</hi> husband to that Mary who was sister or near kinswoman to the virgin Mary and if so, he was own brother to James the less, and Jude, and Simon the Canaanite, so that there were four brothers of them apostles, It is probable that Matthew was but a loose extravagant young man, or else, being a Jew, he would never have been a publican. However, Christ called him to <hi type="italic">follow him.</hi> Paul, though a Pharisee, had been one of the chief of sinners, and yet was called to be an apostle. With God, through Christ, there is mercy to pardon the greatest sins, and grace to sanctify the greatest sinners. Matthew, that had been a publican, became an evangelist, the <hi type="italic">first</hi> that put pen to paper, and the <hi type="italic">fullest</hi> in writing the life of Christ. Great sin and scandal before conversion, are no bar to great gifts, graces, and advancements, after; nay, God may be the more glorified. Christ prevented him with this call; in bodily cures, ordinarily, he was <hi type="italic">sought unto,</hi> but in these spiritual cures, he was <hi type="italic">found of them that sought him not.</hi> For this is the great evil and peril of the disease of sin, that those who are under it, desire not to be <hi type="italic">made whole.</hi> <div eID="gen24368" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24369" type="x-p"/> III. His familiar converse with <hi type="italic">publicans and sinners,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.2.15">v. 15</reference>. We are here told, 1. That Christ <hi type="italic">sat at meat in Levi's house,</hi> who invited <hi type="italic">him and his disciples</hi> to the farewell-feast he made to his friends, when he left all to attend on Christ: such a feast he made, as Elisha did (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.19.21">1 Kings xix. 21</reference>), to show, not only with what cheerfulness in himself, but with what thankfulness to God, he quitted all, in compliance with Christ's call. Fitly did he make the <hi type="italic">day of his espousals</hi> to Christ a festival day. This was also to testify his respect to Christ, and the grateful sense he had of his kindness, in snatching him from the receipt of custom as a brand out of the burning. 2. That <hi type="italic">many publicans and sinners</hi> sat with Christ in Levi's house (for <hi type="italic">there were many</hi> belonging to that custom-house); and <hi type="italic">they followed him.</hi> They followed Levi; so some understand it, supposing that, like Zaccheus, he was <hi type="italic">chief among the publicans,</hi> and was <hi type="italic">rich;</hi> and for that reason, the inferior sort of them attended him for what they could get. I rather take it, that they <hi type="italic">followed Jesus</hi> because of the report they had heard of him. They did not <hi type="italic">for conscience-sake</hi> leave all to follow him, but <hi type="italic">for curiosity-sake</hi> they came to Levi's feast, to see him; whatever brought them thither, they were sitting with <hi type="italic">Jesus and his disciples.</hi> The publicans are here and elsewhere ranked with <hi type="italic">sinners,</hi> the worst of <hi type="italic">sinners.</hi> (1.) Because commonly they <hi type="italic">were such;</hi> so general were the corruptions in the execution of that office, oppressing, exacting, and taking bribes or fees to extortion, and <hi type="italic">accusing falsely,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.3.13-Luke.3.14">Luke iii. 13, 14</reference>. A faithful fair-dealing publican was so rare, even at Rome, that one Sabinus, who kept a clean reputation in that office, was, after his death, honoured with this inscription, <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">Kalos telonesanti</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">Here lies an honest publican.</hi> (2.) Because the Jews had a particular antipathy to them and their office, as an affront to the liberty of their nation and a badge of their slavery, and therefore put them into an ill name, and thought it scandalous to be seen in their company. Such as these our blessed Lord was pleased to converse with, when he appeared <hi type="italic">in the likeness of sinful flesh.</hi> <div eID="gen24369" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24370" type="x-p"/> IV. The <hi type="italic">offence</hi> which the scribes and Pharisees took at this, <reference osisRef="Mark.2.16">v. 16</reference>. They would not come to hear him preach, which they might have been convinced the edified by; but they would come themselves to <hi type="italic">see him</hi> sit with publicans and sinners, which they would be provoked by. They endeavoured to put the disciples out of conceit with their Master, as a man not of such sanctity and severe morals as became his character; and therefore put the question to them. <hi type="italic">How is it, that he eateth and drinketh with publicans and sinners?</hi> Note, It is no new thing for that which is both well-<hi type="italic">done,</hi> and well-<hi type="italic">designed,</hi> to be misrepresented, and turned to the reproach of the wisest and best of men. <div eID="gen24370" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24371" type="x-p"/> V. Christ's justification of himself in it, <reference osisRef="Mark.2.17">v. 17</reference>. He stood to what he did, and would not withdraw, though the Pharisees were offended, as Peter afterwards did, <reference osisRef="Gal.2.12">Gal. ii. 12</reference>. Note, Those are too tender of their own <hi type="italic">good name,</hi> who, to preserve it with some nice people, will decline a <hi type="italic">good work.</hi> Christ would not do so. They thought the publicans were to be <hi type="italic">hated.</hi> "No," saith Christ, "they are to be <hi type="italic">pitied,</hi> they are <hi type="italic">sick</hi> and <hi type="italic">need a physician;</hi> they are sinners, and need a Saviour." They thought Christ's character should separate him from them; "No," saith Christ, "my commission directs me to them; <hi type="italic">I came not to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance.</hi> If the world had been <hi type="italic">righteous,</hi> there had been no occasion for my coming, either to <hi type="italic">preach</hi> repentance, or to <hi type="italic">purchase</hi> remission. It is to a <hi type="italic">sinful world</hi> that I am sent, and therefore my business lies most with those that are the greatest sinners in it." Or thus; "<hi type="italic">I am not come to call the righteous,</hi> the proud Pharisees that think themselves righteous, that ask, <hi type="italic">Wherein shall we return?</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mal.3.7">Mal. iii. 7</reference>), Of what shall we repent? But poor publicans, that own themselves to be sinners, and are glad to be invited and encouraged to repent." It is good dealing with those that there is hope of; now there is <hi type="italic">more hope of a fool</hi> than of one that is <hi type="italic">wise in his own conceit,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.26.12">Prov. xxvi. 12</reference>.

<div eID="gen24371" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Hypocritical Rigour of the Pharisees.</title> <div sID="gen24372" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">18</hi> And the disciples of John and of the Pharisees used to fast: and they come and say unto him, Why do the disciples of John and of the Pharisees fast, but thy disciples fast not? <hi type="super">19</hi> And Jesus said unto them, Can the children of the bridechamber fast, while the bridegroom is with them? as long as they have the bridegroom with them, they cannot fast. <hi type="super">20</hi> But the days will come, when the bridegroom shall be taken away from them, and then shall they fast in those days. <hi type="super">21</hi> No man also seweth a piece of new cloth on an old garment: else the new piece that filled it up taketh away from the old, and the rent is made worse. <hi type="super">22</hi> And no man putteth new wine into old bottles: else the new wine doth burst the bottles, and the wine is spilled, and the bottles will be marred: but new wine must be put into new bottles. <hi type="super">23</hi> And it came to pass, that he went through the corn fields on the sabbath day; and his disciples began, as they went, to pluck the ears of corn. <hi type="super">24</hi> And the Pharisees said unto him, Behold, why do they on the sabbath day that which is not lawful? <hi type="super">25</hi> And he said unto them, Have ye never read what David did, when he had need, and was an hungred, he, and they that were with him? <hi type="super">26</hi> How he went into the house of God in the days of Abiathar the high priest, and did eat the showbread, which is not lawful to eat but for the priests, and gave also to them which were with him? <hi type="super">27</hi> And he said unto them, The sabbath was made for man, and not man for the sabbath: <hi type="super">28</hi> Therefore the Son of man is Lord also of the sabbath. <div eID="gen24372" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24373" type="x-p"/> Christ had been put to <hi type="italic">justify</hi> himself in conversing with <hi type="italic">publicans and sinners:</hi> here he is put to justify his disciples; and in what they do according to his will he will justify them, and bear them out. <div eID="gen24373" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24374" type="x-p"/> I. He justifies them in their <hi type="italic">not fasting,</hi> which was turned to their reproach by the Pharisees. Why do the Pharisees and the disciples of John fast? They <hi type="italic">used to fast,</hi> the Pharisees fasted <hi type="italic">twice in the week</hi> (<reference osisRef="Luke.18.12">Luke xviii. 12</reference>), and probably the disciples of John did so too; and, it should seem, this very day, when Christ and his disciples were feasting in Levi's house, was their <hi type="italic">fast-day,</hi> for the word is <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">nesteuousi</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">they do fast,</hi> or <hi type="italic">are fasting,</hi> which aggravated the offence. Thus apt are strict professors to make their own practice a standard, and to censure and condemn all that do not fully come up to it. They invidiously suggest that if Christ went among sinners to do them <hi type="italic">good,</hi> as he had pleaded, yet the disciples went to indulge their appetites, for they never knew what it was to fast, or to deny themselves. Note, Ill-will always suspects the worst. <div eID="gen24374" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24375" type="x-p"/> Two things Christ pleads in excuse of his disciples <hi type="italic">not fasting.</hi> <div eID="gen24375" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24376" type="x-p"/> 1. That these were <hi type="italic">easy days</hi> with them, and fasting was not so <hi type="italic">seasonable</hi> now as it would be hereafter, <reference osisRef="Mark.2.19-Mark.2.20">v. 19, 20</reference>. There is a time for all things. Those that enter into the married state, must expect care and <hi type="italic">trouble in the flesh,</hi> and yet, during the nuptial solemnity, they are merry, and think it becomes them to be so; it was very absurd for Samson's bride to <hi type="italic">weep before</hi> him, <hi type="italic">during the days that the feast lasted,</hi> <reference osisRef="Judg.14.17">Judg. xiv. 17</reference>. Christ and his disciples were but newly married, the bridegroom was <hi type="italic">yet with them,</hi> the nuptials were yet in the celebrating (Matthew's particularly); when the bridegroom should be removed from them to the far country, about his business, then would be a proper time to sit as a widow, in solitude and fasting. <div eID="gen24376" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24377" type="x-p"/> 2. That these were <hi type="italic">early days</hi> with them, and they were not so able for the severe exercises of religion as hereafter they would be. The Pharisees had long accustomed themselves to such austerities; and John Baptist himself came neither eating nor drinking. His disciples from the first inured themselves to hardships, and thus found it easier to bear strict and frequent fasting, but it was not so with Christ's disciples; their Master came <hi type="italic">eating and drinking,</hi> and had not bred them up to the difficult services of religion as yet, for it was all in good time. To put them upon such frequent fasting at first, would be a discouragement to them, and perhaps drive them off from following Christ; it would be of as ill consequence as <hi type="italic">putting new wine into old casks,</hi> or sewing <hi type="italic">new cloth</hi> to that which is worn thin and threadbare, <reference osisRef="Mark.2.21-Mark.2.22">v. 21, 22</reference>. Note, God graciously <hi type="italic">considers the frame</hi> of young Christians, that are <hi type="italic">weak</hi> and <hi type="italic">tender,</hi> and so must we; nor must we expect more than the <hi type="italic">work of the day in its day,</hi> and that day according to the strength, because it is not in our hands to give strength according to the day. Many contract an antipathy to some kind of food, otherwise good, by being surfeited with it when they are young; so, many entertain prejudices against the exercises of devotion by being burthened with them, and <hi type="italic">made to serve with an offering,</hi> at their setting out. Weak Christians must take heed of <hi type="italic">over-tasking</hi> themselves, and of making the yoke of Christ otherwise than as it is, easy, and sweet, and pleasant. <div eID="gen24377" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24378" type="x-p"/> II. He justifies them in <hi type="italic">plucking the ears of corn on the sabbath day,</hi> which, I will warrant you, a disciples of the Pharisees would not dare to have done; for it was contrary to an express tradition of their elders. In this instance, as in that before, they reflect upon the discipline of Christ's school, as if it were not so strict as that of theirs: so common it is for those who deny the <hi type="italic">power of godliness,</hi> to be jealous for the <hi type="italic">form,</hi> and censorious of those who affect not <hi type="italic">their</hi> form. <div eID="gen24378" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24379" type="x-p"/> Observe, 1. What a poor breakfast Christ's disciples had on a sabbath-day morning, when they were going to church (<reference osisRef="Mark.2.23">v. 23</reference>); they <hi type="italic">plucked the ears of corn,</hi> and that was the best they had. They were so intent upon spiritual dainties, that they forgot even their <hi type="italic">necessary food;</hi> and the word of Christ was to them instead of that; and their zeal for it even <hi type="italic">ate them up.</hi> The Jews made it a piece of religion, to eat dainty food on sabbath days, but the disciples were content with any thing. <div eID="gen24379" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24380" type="x-p"/> 2. How even this was <hi type="italic">grudged them</hi> by the Pharisees, upon supposition that it was not lawful to <hi type="italic">pluck the ears of corn</hi> on the sabbath day, that that was as much a servile work as <hi type="italic">reaping</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mark.2.24">v. 24</reference>); <hi type="italic">Why do they on the sabbath day that which is not lawful?</hi> Note, If Christ's disciples do that which is unlawful, Christ will be reflected upon, and upbraided with it, as he was here, and dishonour will redound to his name. It is observable, that when the Pharisees thought Christ did amiss, they told the disciples (<reference osisRef="Mark.2.16">v. 16</reference>); and now when they thought the disciples did amiss, they spoke to Christ, as make-bates, that did what they could to sow discord between Christ and his disciples, and make a breach in the family. <div eID="gen24380" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24381" type="x-p"/> 3. How Christ defended them in what they did. <div eID="gen24381" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24382" type="x-p"/> (1.) By example. They had a good precedent for it in David's eating the <hi type="italic">show-bread,</hi> when he was hungry, and there was no other bread to be had (<reference osisRef="Mark.2.25-Mark.2.26">v. 25, 26</reference>); <hi type="italic">Have ye never read?</hi> Note, Many of our mistakes would be rectified, and our unjust censures of others corrected, if we would but recollect what <hi type="italic">we have read</hi> in the scripture; appeals to that are most convincing. "You have read that David, the man after God's own heart, <hi type="italic">when he was hungry,</hi> made no difficulty of eating <hi type="italic">the show-bread,</hi> which by the law none might eat of but the priests and their families." Note, Ritual observances must give way to moral obligations; and that may be done in a case of necessity, which otherwise may not be done. This, it is said, David did in the days of <hi type="italic">Abiathar the High-Priest;</hi> or <hi type="italic">just before</hi> the days of Abiathar, who immediately succeeded Abimelech his father in the pontificate, and, it is probable, was at that time his father's deputy, or assistant, in the office; and he it was that escaped the massacre, and brought the ephod to David. <div eID="gen24382" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24383" type="x-p"/> (2.) By argument. To reconcile them to the disciples' <hi type="italic">plucking the ears of corn,</hi> let them consider, <div eID="gen24383" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24384" type="x-p"/> [1.] Whom the sabbath was <hi type="italic">made for</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mark.2.27">v. 27</reference>); <hi type="italic">it was made for man, and not man for the sabbath.</hi> This we had not in Matthew. The sabbath is a sacred and divine institution; but we must receive and embrace it as a privilege and a benefit, not as a task and a drudgery. <hi type="italic">First,</hi> God never designed it to be an <hi type="italic">imposition</hi> upon us, and therefore we must not make it so to ourselves. <hi type="italic">Man was not made for the sabbath,</hi> for he was made a day before the sabbath was instituted. Man was made <hi type="italic">for God,</hi> and for his honour and service, and he just rather die than deny him; but he was not <hi type="italic">made for the sabbath,</hi> so as to be tied up by the law of it, from that which is necessary to the support of his life. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> God did design it to be an <hi type="italic">advantage</hi> to us, and so we must make it, and improve it. He made if <hi type="italic">for man.</hi> 1. He had <hi type="italic">some</hi> regard to our <hi type="italic">bodies</hi> in the institution, that they might rest, and not be tired out with the constant business of this world (<reference osisRef="Deut.5.14">Deut. v. 14</reference>); <hi type="italic">that thy man-servant and thy maid-servant may rest.</hi> Now he that intended the <hi type="italic">sabbath-rest</hi> for the <hi type="italic">repose</hi> of our bodies, certainly never intended it should restrain us, in a case of necessity, from fetching in the necessary <hi type="italic">supports</hi> of the body; it must be construed so as not to contradict itself—for <hi type="italic">edification,</hi> and not for <hi type="italic">destruction.</hi> 2. He had <hi type="italic">much more</hi> regard to our <hi type="italic">souls.</hi> The <hi type="italic">sabbath</hi> was made a day of rest, only in order to its being a day of holy work, a day of communion with God, a day of praise and thanksgiving; and the rest from worldly business is <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> necessary, that we may closely apply ourselves to this work, and spend the whole time in it, in public and in private; but then time is allowed us for that which is necessary to the fitting of our bodies for the service of our souls in God's service, and the enabling of them to <hi type="italic">keep pace</hi> with them in that work. See here, (1.) What a <hi type="italic">good Master</hi> we serve, all whose institutions are for our own benefit, and if we be so wise as to observe them, we are <hi type="italic">wise for ourselves;</hi> it is not he, but we, that are gainers by our service. (2.) What we should aim at in our <hi type="italic">sabbath work,</hi> even the good of our own souls. If the sabbath was made for man, we should then ask ourselves at night, "What am I the better for this sabbath day?" (3.) What care we ought to take not to make those exercises of religion burthens to ourselves or others, which God ordained to be blessings; neither adding to the command by unreasonable strictness, nor indulging those corruptions which are adverse to the command, for thereby we make those devout exercises a penance to ourselves, which otherwise would be a pleasure. <div eID="gen24384" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24385" type="x-p"/> [2.] Whom the sabbath was <hi type="italic">made by</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mark.2.28">v. 28</reference>); "<hi type="italic">The Son of man is Lord also of the sabbath;</hi> and therefore he will not see the kind intentions of the institution of it frustrated by your impositions." Note, The sabbath days are <hi type="italic">days of the Son of man;</hi> he is the Lord of the day, and to his honour it must be observed; by him God made the worlds, and so it was by him that the sabbath was first instituted; by him God gave the law at mount Sinai, and so the <hi type="italic">fourth</hi> commandment was <hi type="italic">his law;</hi> and that little alteration that was shortly to be made, by the shifting of it one day forward to the first day of the week, was to be in remembrance of <hi type="italic">his</hi> resurrection, and therefore the Christian sabbath was to be called <hi type="italic">the Lord's day</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rev.1.10">Rev. i. 10</reference>), the Lord Christ's day; and the <hi type="italic">Son of man,</hi> Christ, as Mediator, is always to be looked upon as Lord of the sabbath. This argument he largely insists upon in his own justification, when he was charged with having broken the sabbath, <reference osisRef="John.5.16">John v. 16</reference>.  <chapter eID="Mark.2"/> <div eID="gen24385" type="x-p"/>

<div eID="gen24388" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen24387" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Withered Hand Restored; Multitudes Healed.</title> <div sID="gen24389" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> And he entered again into the synagogue; and there was a man there which had a withered hand. <hi type="super">2</hi> And they watched him, whether he would heal him on the sabbath day; that they might accuse him. <hi type="super">3</hi> And he saith unto the man which had the withered hand, Stand forth. <hi type="super">4</hi> And he saith unto them, Is it lawful to do good on the sabbath days, or to do evil? to save life, or to kill? But they held their peace. <hi type="super">5</hi> And when he had looked round about on them with anger, being grieved for the hardness of their hearts, he saith unto the man, Stretch forth thine hand. And he stretched <hi type="italic">it</hi> out: and his hand was restored whole as the other. <hi type="super">6</hi> And the Pharisees went forth, and straightway took counsel with the Herodians against him, how they might destroy him. <hi type="super">7</hi> But Jesus withdrew himself with his disciples to the sea: and a great multitude from Galilee followed him, and from Judæa, <hi type="super">8</hi> And from Jerusalem, and from Idumæa, and <hi type="italic">from</hi> beyond Jordan; and they about Tyre and Sidon, a great multitude, when they had heard what great things he did, came unto him. <hi type="super">9</hi> And he spake to his disciples, that a small ship should wait on him because of the multitude, lest they should throng him. <hi type="super">10</hi> For he had healed many; insomuch that they pressed upon him for to touch him, as many as had plagues. 11 And unclean spirits, when they saw him, fell down before him, and cried, saying, Thou art the Son of God. <hi type="super">12</hi> And he straitly charged them that they should not make him known. <div eID="gen24389" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24390" type="x-p"/> Here, as before, we have our Lord Jesus busy at work <hi type="italic">in the synagogue</hi> first, and then by <hi type="italic">the sea side;</hi> to teach us that his presence should not be confined either to the one or to the other, but, wherever any are gathered together in his name, whether <hi type="italic">in the synagogue</hi> or any where else, there is he in the midst of them. <hi type="italic">In every place where he records his name,</hi> he will meet his people, and <hi type="italic">bless them;</hi> it is his will that men <hi type="italic">pray every where.</hi> Now here we have some account of what he did. <div eID="gen24390" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24391" type="x-p"/> I. When he <hi type="italic">entered again into the synagogue,</hi> he improved the opportunity he had there, of doing good, and having, no doubt, preached a sermon there, he wrought a miracle for the confirmation of it, or at least for the confirmation of this truth—that <hi type="italic">it is lawful to do good on the sabbath day.</hi> We had the narrative, <reference osisRef="Matt.12.9">Matt. xii. 9</reference>. <div eID="gen24391" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24392" type="x-p"/> 1. The patient's case was piteous; he had a <hi type="italic">withered hand,</hi> by which he was disabled to work for his living; and those that are so, are the most proper objects of charity; let those be helped that cannot help themselves. <div eID="gen24392" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24393" type="x-p"/> 2. The spectators were very unkind, both to the patient and to the Physician; instead of interceding for a poor neighbour, they did what they could to hinder his cure: for they intimated that if Christ cured him now on the sabbath day, they would accuse him as a <hi type="italic">Sabbath breaker.</hi> It had been very unreasonable, if they should have opposed a physician or surgeon in helping any poor body in misery, by ordinary methods; but much more absurd was it to oppose him that cured without any labour, but by a word's speaking. <div eID="gen24393" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24394" type="x-p"/> 3. Christ dealt very fairly with the spectators, and dealt with them <hi type="italic">first,</hi> if possible to <hi type="italic">prevent</hi> the offence. <div eID="gen24394" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24395" type="x-p"/> (1.) He laboured to convince their judgment. He bade the man <hi type="italic">stand forth</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mark.3.3">v. 3</reference>), that by the sight of him they might be moved with compassion toward him, and might not, for shame, account his cure a crime. And then he appeals to their own consciences; though the thing <hi type="italic">speaks itself,</hi> yet <hi type="italic">he</hi> is pleased to <hi type="italic">speak</hi> it; "<hi type="italic">Is it lawful to do good on the sabbath days,</hi> as I design to do, <hi type="italic">or to do evil,</hi> as you design to do? Whether is better, to <hi type="italic">save life</hi> or to <hi type="italic">kill?</hi>" What fairer question could be put? And yet, because they saw it would turn against them, <hi type="italic">they held their peace.</hi> Note, Those are obstinate indeed in their infidelity, who, when they can say nothing <hi type="italic">against</hi> a truth, will say nothing <hi type="italic">to it;</hi> and, when they cannot <hi type="italic">resist,</hi> yet will not <hi type="italic">yield.</hi> <div eID="gen24395" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24396" type="x-p"/> (2.) When they rebelled against the light, he <hi type="italic">lamented their stubbornness</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mark.3.5">v. 5</reference>); <hi type="italic">He looked round about on them with anger, being grieved for the hardness of their hearts.</hi> The <hi type="italic">sin</hi> he had an eye to, was, the <hi type="italic">hardness of their hearts,</hi> their insensibleness of the evidence of his miracles, and their inflexible resolution to persist in unbelief. We hear what is said amiss, and see what is done amiss; but Christ looks at the <hi type="italic">root of bitterness</hi> in the heart, the blindness and hardness of <hi type="italic">that.</hi> Observe, [1.] How he was <hi type="italic">provoked</hi> by the sin; he looked <hi type="italic">round upon them;</hi> for they were so many, and had so placed themselves, that they surrounded him: and he looked <hi type="italic">with anger;</hi> his anger, it is probable, appeared in his countenance; his anger was, like God's, without the least <hi type="italic">perturbation</hi> to himself, but not without great <hi type="italic">provocation</hi> from us. Note, The sin of sinners is very displeasing to Jesus Christ; and the way to be angry, and not to sin, is it be angry, as Christ was, at nothing but sin. Let hard-hearted sinners tremble to think of the anger with which he will <hi type="italic">look round</hi> upon them shortly, when the <hi type="italic">great day of his wrath comes.</hi> [2.] How he <hi type="italic">pitied</hi> the sinners; he was <hi type="italic">grieved for the hardness of their hearts;</hi> as God was grieved forty years for the hardness of the hearts of their fathers in the wilderness. Note, It is a great grief to our Lord Jesus, to see sinners bent upon their own ruin, and obstinately set against the methods of their conviction and recovery, for he would not that any should perish. This is a good reason why the hardness of our own hearts and of the hearts of others, should be a grief to us. <div eID="gen24396" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24397" type="x-p"/> 4. Christ dealt very kindly with the patient; he bade him <hi type="italic">stretch forth his hand,</hi> and it was immediately <hi type="italic">restored.</hi> Now, (1.) Christ has hereby taught us to go on with resolution in the way of our duty, how violent soever the opposition is, that we meet with in it. We must deny ourselves sometimes in our ease, pleasure, and convenience, rather than give offence even to those who causelessly take it; but we must not deny ourselves the satisfaction of serving God, and doing good, though offence may unjustly be taken at it. None could be more tender of giving offence than Christ; yet, rather than send this poor man away uncured, he would venture offending all the scribes and Pharisees that compassed him about. (2.) He hath hereby given us a <hi type="italic">specimen</hi> of the cures wrought by his grace upon <hi type="italic">poor souls;</hi> our hands are spiritually <hi type="italic">withered,</hi> the powers of our souls weakened by sin, and disabled for that which is good. The great healing day is the <hi type="italic">sabbath,</hi> and the healing place the <hi type="italic">synagogue;</hi> the healing power is that of Christ. The gospel command is like this recorded here; and the command is rational and just; though our hands are withered, and we cannot of ourselves <hi type="italic">stretch them forth,</hi> we must attempt it, must, as well as we can, <hi type="italic">lift them up</hi> to God in prayer, <hi type="italic">lay hold</hi> on Christ and eternal life, and employ them in good works; and if we do our endeavour, power goes along with the word of Christ, he effects the cure. Though our hands be <hi type="italic">withered,</hi> yet, if we will not offer to <hi type="italic">stretch them out,</hi> it is our own fault that we are not healed; but if we do, and are healed, Christ and his power and grace must have all the glory. <div eID="gen24397" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24398" type="x-p"/> 5. The enemies of Christ dealt very barbarously with him. Such a work of <hi type="italic">mercy</hi> should have engaged their love <hi type="italic">to him,</hi> and such a work of <hi type="italic">wonder</hi> their faith <hi type="italic">in him.</hi> But, instead of that, the Pharisees, who pretended to be oracles in the church, and the Herodians, who pretended to be the supporters of the state, though of opposite interests one to another, <hi type="italic">took counsel together against him, how they might destroy him.</hi> Note, They that suffer for doing good, do but suffer as their Master did. <div eID="gen24398" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24399" type="x-p"/> II. When he withdrew <hi type="italic">to the sea,</hi> he did good there. While his enemies sought to <hi type="italic">destroy him,</hi> he quitted the place; to teach us in troublous times to shift for our own safety; but see here, <div eID="gen24399" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24400" type="x-p"/> 1. How he was followed into his retirement. When some had such an enmity to him, that they drove him out of their country, others had such a value for him, that they followed him wherever he went; and the enmity of their leaders to Christ did not cool their respect to him. <hi type="italic">Great multitudes</hi> followed him from all parts of the nation; as far north, as <hi type="italic">from Galilee;</hi> as far south, as from Judea and Jerusalem; nay, and from Idumea; as far east, as from beyond Jordan; and west, as from about Tyre and Sidon, <reference osisRef="Mark.3.7-Mark.3.8">v. 7, 8</reference>. Observe, (1.) What induced them to follow him; it was the report they heard of the <hi type="italic">great things he did</hi> for all that applied themselves to him; some wished <hi type="italic">to see</hi> one that had done such <hi type="italic">great things,</hi> and others hoped he would do great things <hi type="italic">for them.</hi> Note, The consideration of the <hi type="italic">great things</hi> Christ has done, should engage us to <hi type="italic">come to him.</hi> (2.) What they followed him for (<reference osisRef="Mark.3.10">v. 10</reference>); They <hi type="italic">pressed upon him, to touch him, as many as had plagues.</hi> Diseases are here called <hi type="italic">plagues,</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">mastigas</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">corrections, chastisements;</hi> so they are designed to be, to make us <hi type="italic">smart</hi> for our sins, that thereby we may be made <hi type="italic">sorry</hi> for them, and may be warned not to return to them. Those that were under these <hi type="italic">scourgings</hi> came to Jesus; this is the errand on which sickness is sent, to quicken us to enquire after Christ, and apply ourselves to him as our Physician. They <hi type="italic">pressed upon him,</hi> each striving which should get <hi type="italic">nearest to</hi> him, and which should be <hi type="italic">first served.</hi> They <hi type="italic">fell down before him</hi> (so Dr. Hammond), as petitioners for his favour; they desired leave but to <hi type="italic">touch him,</hi> having faith to be healed, not only by <hi type="italic">his</hi> touching <hi type="italic">them,</hi> but by <hi type="italic">their</hi> touching him; which no doubt they had many instances of. (3.) What provision he made to be ready to attend them (<reference osisRef="Mark.3.9">v. 9</reference>); He <hi type="italic">spoke to his disciples,</hi> who were fishermen, and had fisher-boats at command, that a <hi type="italic">small ship should</hi> constantly <hi type="italic">wait on him,</hi> to carry him from place to place on the same coast; that, when he had despatched the necessary business he had to do in one place, he might easily remove to another, where his presence was requisite, without pressing through the crowds of people that followed him for curiosity. Wise men, as much as they can, decline a crowd. <div eID="gen24400" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24401" type="x-p"/> 2. What abundance of good he did in his retirement. He did not withdraw to be idle, nor did he send back those who rudely crowded after him when he withdrew, but took it kindly, and gave them what they came for; for he never said to any that sought him diligently, <hi type="italic">Seek ye me in vain.</hi> (1.) Diseases were effectually cured; He <hi type="italic">healed many;</hi> divers sorts of patients, ill of divers sorts of diseases; though numerous, though various, he <hi type="italic">healed them.</hi> (2.) <hi type="italic">Devils</hi> were effectually <hi type="italic">conquered;</hi> those whom unclean spirits had got possession of, <hi type="italic">when they saw him,</hi> trembled at his presence, and they also <hi type="italic">fell down before him,</hi> not to supplicate his favour, but to deprecate his wrath, and by their own terrors were compelled to own that <hi type="italic">he was the Son of God,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.3.1">v. 1</reference>. It is sad that this great truth should be denied by any of the children of men, who may have the benefit of it, when a confession of it has so often been extorted from devils, who are excluded from having benefit by it. (3.) Christ sought not applause to himself in doing those great things, for <hi type="italic">he strictly charged</hi> those for whom he did them, <hi type="italic">that they should not make him known</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mark.3.12">v. 12</reference>); that they should not be <hi type="italic">industrious</hi> to spread the notice of his cures, as it were by advertisements in the newspapers, but let them leave <hi type="italic">his own works to praise him,</hi> and let the report of them <hi type="italic">diffuse itself,</hi> and make its own way. Let not those that are cured, be forward to divulge it, lest it should feed their pride who are so <hi type="italic">highly favoured;</hi> but let the <hi type="italic">standers-by</hi> carry away the intelligence of it. When we do that which is <hi type="italic">praiseworthy,</hi> and yet covet not to be <hi type="italic">praised of men</hi> for it, then <hi type="italic">the same mind is in us,</hi> which was <hi type="italic">in Christ Jesus.</hi>

<div eID="gen24401" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Calling of the Apostles.</title> <div sID="gen24402" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">13</hi> And he goeth up into a mountain, and calleth <hi type="italic">unto him</hi> whom he would: and they came unto him. <hi type="super">14</hi> And he ordained twelve, that they should be with him, and that he might send them forth to preach, <hi type="super">15</hi> And to have power to heal sicknesses, and to cast out devils: <hi type="super">16</hi> And Simon he surnamed Peter; <hi type="super">17</hi> And James the <hi type="italic">son</hi> of Zebedee, and John the brother of James; and he surnamed them Boanerges, which is, The sons of thunder: <hi type="super">18</hi> And Andrew, and Philip, and Bartholomew, and Matthew, and Thomas, and James the <hi type="italic">son</hi> of Alphæus, and Thaddæus, and Simon the Canaanite, <hi type="super">19</hi> And Judas Iscariot, which also betrayed him: and they went into a house. 20 And the multitude cometh together again, so that they could not so much as eat bread. <hi type="super">21</hi> And when his friends heard <hi type="italic">of it,</hi> they went out to lay hold on him: for they said, He is beside himself. <div eID="gen24402" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24403" type="x-p"/> In these verses, we have, <div eID="gen24403" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24404" type="x-p"/> I. The choice Christ made of the <hi type="italic">twelve apostles</hi> to be his constant followers and attendants, and to be sent abroad as there was occasion, to preach the gospel. Observe, <div eID="gen24404" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24405" type="x-p"/> 1. The introduction to this <hi type="italic">call</hi> or <hi type="italic">promotion</hi> of disciples; He <hi type="italic">goes up into a mountain,</hi> and his errand thither was <hi type="italic">to pray.</hi> Ministers must be set apart with solemn prayer for the pouring out of the Spirit upon them; though Christ had authority to confer the gifts of the Holy Ghost, yet, to set us an example, he prayed for them. <div eID="gen24405" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24406" type="x-p"/> 2. The rule he went by in his choice, and that was his own good pleasure; <hi type="italic">He called unto him whom he would.</hi> Not such as we should have thought <hi type="italic">fittest to be called, looking upon the countenance, and the height of the stature;</hi> but such as he <hi type="italic">thought fit</hi> to call, and determined to <hi type="italic">make fit</hi> for the service to which he called them: <hi type="italic">even so,</hi> blessed Jesus, <hi type="italic">because it seemed good in thine eyes.</hi> Christ calls <hi type="italic">whom he will;</hi> for he is a free Agent, and his grace is his own. <div eID="gen24406" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24407" type="x-p"/> 3. The efficacy of the call; He <hi type="italic">called them</hi> to separate themselves from the crowd, and stand by him, and they <hi type="italic">came unto him.</hi> Christ calls those who were <hi type="italic">given him</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.17.6">John xvii. 6</reference>); and <hi type="italic">all that the Father gave him, shall come to him,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.6.37">John vi. 37</reference>. Those whom it was his <hi type="italic">will</hi> to call, he made <hi type="italic">willing to come;</hi> his <hi type="italic">people shall be willing in the day of his power.</hi> Perhaps they came to him readily enough, because they were in expectation of <hi type="italic">reigning with him</hi> in temporal pomp and power; but when afterward they were <hi type="italic">undeceived</hi> in that matter, yet they had such a prospect given them of better things, that they would not say they were <hi type="italic">deceived</hi> in their Master, nor repented their leaving all to be with him. <div eID="gen24407" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24408" type="x-p"/> 4. The end and intention of this call; He <hi type="italic">ordained them</hi> (probably by the imposition of hands, which was a ceremony used among the Jews), <hi type="italic">that they should be with him</hi> constantly, to be witnesses of <hi type="italic">his doctrine, manner of life, and patience,</hi> that they might <hi type="italic">fully know it,</hi> and be able to give an account of it; and especially that they might attest the truth of his miracles; they must be <hi type="italic">with him</hi> to receive instructions <hi type="italic">from him,</hi> that they might be qualified to give instructions <hi type="italic">to others.</hi> It would <hi type="italic">require time</hi> to fit them for that which he designed them for; for they must be <hi type="italic">sent forth to preach;</hi> not to preach till they were <hi type="italic">sent,</hi> and not to be <hi type="italic">sent</hi> till by a long and intimate acquaintance with Christ they were fitted. Note, Christ's ministers must be much <hi type="italic">with him.</hi> <div eID="gen24408" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24409" type="x-p"/> 5. The power he gave them to work miracles; and hereby he put a very great honour upon them, beyond that of the great men of the earth. He ordained them to <hi type="italic">heal sicknesses and to cast out devils.</hi> This showed that the power which Christ had to work these miracles was an <hi type="italic">original</hi> power; that he had it not <hi type="italic">as a Servant,</hi> but <hi type="italic">as a Son in his own house,</hi> in that he could confer it upon others, and invest them with it: they have a rule in the law, <hi type="italic">Deputatus non potest deputare—He that is only deputed himself, cannot depute another;</hi> but our Lord Jesus had <hi type="italic">life in himself,</hi> and the Spirit without measure; for he could give this power even to the <hi type="italic">weak</hi> and <hi type="italic">foolish things</hi> of the world. <div eID="gen24409" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24410" type="x-p"/> 6. Their number and names; He <hi type="italic">ordained twelve,</hi> according to the number of the twelve tribes of Israel. They are here named not just in the same order as they were in Matthew, nor by couples, as they were there; but as there, so here, Peter is put first and Judas last. Here Matthew is put before Thomas, probably being called in that order; but in that catalogue which Matthew himself drew up, he puts himself after Thomas; so far was he from insisting upon the precedency of his consecration. But that which Mark only takes notice of in this list of the apostles, is, that Christ called James and John <hi type="italic">Boanerges,</hi> which is, <hi type="italic">The sons of thunder;</hi> perhaps they were remarkable for a loud commanding voice, they were thundering preachers; or, rather, it denotes the zeal and fervency of their spirits, which would make them active for God above their brethren. These two (saith Dr. Hammond) were to be special eminent ministers of the gospel, which is called <hi type="italic">a voice shaking the earth,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.12.26">Heb. xii. 26</reference>. Yet John, one of those <hi type="italic">sons of thunder,</hi> was full of love and tenderness, as appears by his epistles, and was the beloved disciple. <div eID="gen24410" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24411" type="x-p"/> 7. Their retirement with their Master, and close adherence to him; <hi type="italic">They went into a house.</hi> Now that this jury was impanelled, they <hi type="italic">stood together, to hearken to their evidence.</hi> They went together into the house, to settle the orders of their infant college; and now, it is likely, the bag was given to Judas, which pleased him, and made him easy. <div eID="gen24411" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24412" type="x-p"/> II. The continual crowds that attended Christ's motions (<reference osisRef="Mark.3.20">v. 20</reference>); The <hi type="italic">multitude cometh together again,</hi> unsent for, and unseasonably pressing upon him, some with one errand and some with another; so that he and his disciples could not get time <hi type="italic">so much as to eat bread,</hi> much less for a set and full meal. Yet he did not shut his doors against the petitioners, but bade them welcome, and gave to each of them <hi type="italic">an answer of peace.</hi> Note, They whose hearts are enlarged in the work of God, can easily bear with great inconveniences to themselves, in the prosecution of it, and will rather lose a meal's meat at any time than slip an opportunity of doing good. It is happy when zealous <hi type="italic">hearers</hi> and zealous <hi type="italic">preachers</hi> thus <hi type="italic">meet,</hi> and encourage one another. Now the <hi type="italic">kingdom of God was preached,</hi> and men pressed into it, <reference osisRef="Luke.16.16">Luke xvi. 16</reference>. This was a gale of opportunity worth improving; and the disciples might well afford to adjourn their meals, to lay hold on it. It is good striking while the iron is hot. <div eID="gen24412" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24413" type="x-p"/> III. The care of his relations concerning him (<reference osisRef="Mark.3.21">v. 21</reference>); <hi type="italic">When his friends</hi> in Capernaum heard how he was followed, and what pains he took, they <hi type="italic">went out, to lay hold on him,</hi> and fetch him home, for they said, <hi type="italic">He is beside himself.</hi> 1. Some understand it of an absurd preposterous care, which had more in it of reproach to him than of respect; and so we must take it as we read it, <hi type="italic">He is beside himself;</hi> either they suspected it themselves, or it was suggested to them, and they gave credit to the suggestion, that he was <hi type="italic">gone distracted,</hi> and therefore his friends ought to bind him, and put him in a dark room, to bring him to his right mind again. His kindred, many of them, had mean thoughts of him (<reference osisRef="John.7.5">John vii. 5</reference>), and were willing to hearken to this ill construction which some put upon his great zeal, and to conclude him crazed in his intellects, and under that pretence to take him off from his work. The prophets were called <hi type="italic">mad fellows,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Kgs.9.11">2 Kings ix. 11</reference>. 2. Others understand it of a <hi type="italic">well-meaning</hi> care; and then they read <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">exeste</hi></hi>—"<hi type="italic">He fainteth,</hi> he has no time to <hi type="italic">eat bread,</hi> and therefore his strength will fail him; he will be stifled with the crowd of people, and will have his spirits quite exhausted with constant speaking, and the virtue that <hi type="italic">goes out of him</hi> in his miracles; and therefore let us use a friendly violence with him, and get him a little <hi type="italic">breathing-time.</hi>" In his preaching-work, as well as his suffering-work, he was attacked with, <hi type="italic">Master, spare thyself.</hi> Note, They who go on with vigour and zeal in the work of God, must expect to meet with hindrances, both from the groundless disaffection of their enemies, and the mistaken affections of their friends, and they have need to stand upon their guard against both.

<div eID="gen24413" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Blasphemy of the Scribes.</title> <div sID="gen24414" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">22</hi> And the scribes which came down from Jerusalem said, He hath Beelzebub, and by the prince of the devils casteth he out devils. <hi type="super">23</hi> And he called them <hi type="italic">unto him,</hi> and said unto them in parables, How can Satan cast out Satan? <hi type="super">24</hi> And if a kingdom be divided against itself, that kingdom cannot stand. <hi type="super">25</hi> And if a house be divided against itself, that house cannot stand. <hi type="super">26</hi> And if Satan rise up against himself, and be divided, he cannot stand, but hath an end. 27 No man can enter into a strong man's house, and spoil his goods, except he will first bind the strong man; and then he will spoil his house. <hi type="super">28</hi> Verily I say unto you, All sins shall be forgiven unto the sons of men, and blasphemies wherewith soever they shall blaspheme: <hi type="super">29</hi> But he that shall blaspheme against the Holy Ghost hath never forgiveness, but is in danger of eternal damnation: <hi type="super">30</hi> Because they said, He hath an unclean spirit. <div eID="gen24414" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24415" type="x-p"/> I. Here is, The impudent impious brand which the scribes fastened upon Christ's casting out devils, that they might evade and invalidate the conviction of it, and have a poor excuse for not yielding to it. These <hi type="italic">scribes came down from Jerusalem,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.3.22">v. 22</reference>. It should seem they came this long journey on purpose to hinder the progress of the doctrine of Christ; such pains did they take to do mischief; and, coming from Jerusalem, where were the most polite and learned scribes, and where they had opportunity of <hi type="italic">consulting</hi> together <hi type="italic">against the Lord and his Anointed,</hi> they were in the greater capacity to do mischief; the reputation of scribes from Jerusalem would have an influence not only upon the <hi type="italic">country people,</hi> but upon the <hi type="italic">country scribes;</hi> they had never thought of this base suggestion concerning Christ's miracles till the <hi type="italic">scribes from</hi> Jerusalem put it into their heads. They could not deny but that he cast out devils, which plainly bespoke him sent of God; but they insinuated that <hi type="italic">he had Beelzebub</hi> on his side, was in league with him, and by <hi type="italic">the prince of the devils cast out devils.</hi> There is a trick in the case; Satan is not <hi type="italic">cast out,</hi> he only <hi type="italic">goes out</hi> by consent. There was nothing in the manner of Christ's <hi type="italic">casting out devils,</hi> that gave any cause to suspect this; he did it <hi type="italic">as one having authority;</hi> but so they will have it, who resolve not to believe him. <div eID="gen24415" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24416" type="x-p"/> II. The rational answer which Christ gave to this objection, demonstrating the absurdity of it. <div eID="gen24416" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24417" type="x-p"/> 1. Satan is so <hi type="italic">subtle,</hi> that he will never voluntarily quit his possession; <hi type="italic">If Satan cast out Satan, his kingdom is divided against itself,</hi> and it <hi type="italic">cannot stand,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.3.23-Mark.3.26">v. 23-26</reference>. He <hi type="italic">called them to him,</hi> as one desirous they should be convinced; he treated them with all the freedom, friendliness, and familiarity that could be; he vouchsafed to reason the case with them, <hi type="italic">that every mouth may be stopped.</hi> It was plain that the doctrine of Christ <hi type="italic">made war</hi> upon the devil's kingdom, and had a direct tendency to break his power, and crush his interest in the souls of men; and it was as plain that the casting of him out of the bodies of people confirmed that doctrine, and gave it the setting on; and therefore it cannot be imagined that he should come into such a design; every one knows that Satan is no <hi type="italic">fool,</hi> nor will act so directly against his own interest. <div eID="gen24417" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24418" type="x-p"/> 2. Christ is so <hi type="italic">wise,</hi> that, being engaged in war with him, he will attack his forces wherever he meets them, whether in the bodies or souls of people, <reference osisRef="Mark.3.27">v. 27</reference>. It is plain, Christ's design is to <hi type="italic">enter into the strong man's house,</hi> to take possession of the interest he has in the world, and to <hi type="italic">spoil his goods,</hi> and convert them to his own service; and therefore it is natural to suppose that he will thus <hi type="italic">bind the strong man,</hi> will forbid him to <hi type="italic">speak</hi> when he would, and to <hi type="italic">stay</hi> where he would, and thus show that he has gained a victory over him. <div eID="gen24418" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24419" type="x-p"/> III. The awful warning Christ gave them to take heed how they spoke such dangerous words as these; however they might make light of them, as only conjectures, and the language of <hi type="italic">free-thinking,</hi> if they persisted in it, it would be of fatal consequence to them; it would be found a sin against the last remedy, and consequently <hi type="italic">unpardonable;</hi> for what could be imagined possible to bring <hi type="italic">them</hi> to repentance for their sin in blaspheming Christ, who would set aside such a <hi type="italic">strong</hi> conviction with such a <hi type="italic">weak</hi> evasion? It is true, the gospel <hi type="italic">promiseth,</hi> because Christ hath <hi type="italic">purchased,</hi> forgiveness for the greatest sins and sinners, <reference osisRef="Mark.3.28">v. 28</reference>. Many of those who reviled Christ on the cross (which was a <hi type="italic">blaspheming of the Son of man,</hi> aggravated to the highest degree), found mercy, and Christ himself prayed, <hi type="italic">Father, forgive them;</hi> but this was <hi type="italic">blaspheming the Holy Ghost,</hi> for it was by the Holy Spirit that he <hi type="italic">cast out</hi> devils, and they said, It was <hi type="italic">by the unclean spirit,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.3.30">v. 30</reference>. By this method they would outface the conviction of all the gifts of the Holy Ghost after Christ's ascension, and defeat them all, after which there remained no more proof, and therefore they should <hi type="italic">never have forgiveness,</hi> but were <hi type="italic">liable to eternal damnation.</hi> They were in imminent danger of that everlasting punishment, from which there was <hi type="italic">no redemption,</hi> and in which there was no <hi type="italic">intermission,</hi> no <hi type="italic">remission.</hi>

<div eID="gen24419" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Family of Christ.</title> <div sID="gen24420" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">31</hi> There came then his brethren and his mother, and, standing without, sent unto him, calling him. <hi type="super">32</hi> And the multitude sat about him, and they said unto him, Behold, thy mother and thy brethren without seek for thee. <hi type="super">33</hi> And he answered them, saying, Who is my mother, or my brethren? <hi type="super">34</hi> And he looked round about on them which sat about him, and said, Behold my mother and my brethren! <hi type="super">35</hi> For whosoever shall do the will of God, the same is my brother, and my sister, and mother. <div eID="gen24420" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24421" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. The <hi type="italic">disrespect</hi> which Christ's <hi type="italic">kindred, according to the flesh,</hi> showed to him, when he was preaching (and they knew very well that he was then in his element); they not only <hi type="italic">stood without,</hi> having no desire to come in, and hear him, but they sent in a message to <hi type="italic">call him out to them</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mark.3.31-Mark.3.32">v. 31, 32</reference>), as if he must leave his work, to hearken to their <hi type="italic">impertinences;</hi> it is probable that they had <hi type="italic">no business with him,</hi> only sent for him on purpose to oblige him to <hi type="italic">break off,</hi> lest he should <hi type="italic">kill himself.</hi> He knew how far his strength would go, and preferred the salvation of souls before his own life, and soon after made it to appear with a witness; it was therefore an <hi type="italic">idle thing</hi> for them, under pretence of his sparing himself, to interrupt him; and it was worse, if really they had business with him, when they knew he preferred his business, as a Saviour, so much before any other business. <div eID="gen24421" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24422" type="x-p"/> 2. The <hi type="italic">respect</hi> which Christ showed to his spiritual kindred upon this occasion. Now, as at other times, he put a <hi type="italic">comparative neglect</hi> upon his mother, which seemed purposely designed to obviate the prevent the extravagant respect which men in aftertimes would be apt to pay her. <hi type="italic">Our</hi> respect ought to be guided and governed by Christ's; now the virgin Mary, or Christ's mother, is not equalled with, but postponed to, ordinary believers, on whom Christ here puts a <hi type="italic">superlative</hi> honour. He looked upon those that <hi type="italic">at about</hi> him, and pronounced those of them that not only heard, but did, the will of God, to be to him as <hi type="italic">his brother, and sister, and mother;</hi> as much esteemed, loved, and cared for, as his nearest relations, <reference osisRef="Mark.3.33-Mark.3.35">v. 33-35</reference>. This is a good reason why we should <hi type="italic">honour those that fear the Lord,</hi> and choose them for our people; why we should be not hearers of the word only, but doers of the work, that we may share with the saints in this honour, Surely it is good to be akin to those who are thus nearly allied to Christ, and to have fellowship with those that have fellowship with Christ; and woe to those that hate and persecute Christ's kindred, that are <hi type="italic">his bone and his flesh,</hi> every one <hi type="italic">resembling the children of a king</hi> (see <reference osisRef="Judg.8.18-Judg.8.19">Judg. viii. 18, 19</reference>); for he will with jealously plead their cause, and avenge their blood.  <chapter eID="Mark.3"/> <div eID="gen24422" type="x-p"/>

<div eID="gen24425" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen24424" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Parable of the Sower.</title> <div sID="gen24426" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> And he began again to teach by the sea side: and there was gathered unto him a great multitude, so that he entered into a ship, and sat in the sea; and the whole multitude was by the sea on the land. <hi type="super">2</hi> And he taught them many things by parables, and said unto them in his doctrine, <hi type="super">3</hi> Hearken; Behold, there went out a sower to sow: <hi type="super">4</hi> And it came to pass, as he sowed, some fell by the way side, and the fowls of the air came and devoured it up. <hi type="super">5</hi> And some fell on stony ground, where it had not much earth; and immediately it sprang up, because it had no depth of earth: <hi type="super">6</hi> But when the sun was up, it was scorched; and because it had no root, it withered away. 7 And some fell among thorns, and the thorns grew up, and choked it, and it yielded no fruit. <hi type="super">8</hi> And other fell on good ground, and did yield fruit that sprang up and increased; and brought forth, some thirty, and some sixty, and some a hundred. 9 And he said unto them, He that hath ears to hear, let him hear. <hi type="super">10</hi> And when he was alone, they that were about him with the twelve asked of him the parable. <hi type="super">11</hi> And he said unto them, Unto you it is given to know the mystery of the kingdom of God: but unto them that are without, all <hi type="italic">these</hi> things are done in parables: <hi type="super">12</hi> That seeing they may see, and not perceive; and hearing they may hear, and not understand; lest at any time they should be converted, and <hi type="italic">their</hi> sins should be forgiven them. <hi type="super">13</hi> And he said unto them, Know ye not this parable? and how then will ye know all parables? <hi type="super">14</hi> The sower soweth the word. <hi type="super">15</hi> And these are they by the way side, where the word is sown; but when they have heard, Satan cometh immediately, and taketh away the word that was sown in their hearts. <hi type="super">16</hi> And these are they likewise which are sown on stony ground; who, when they have heard the word, immediately receive it with gladness; <hi type="super">17</hi> And have no root in themselves, and so endure but for a time: afterward, when affliction or persecution ariseth for the word's sake, immediately they are offended. <hi type="super">18</hi> And these are they which are sown among thorns; such as hear the word, <hi type="super">19</hi> And the cares of this world, and the deceitfulness of riches, and the lusts of other things entering in, choke the word, and it becometh unfruitful. <hi type="super">20</hi> And these are they which are sown on good ground; such as hear the word, and receive <hi type="italic">it,</hi> and bring forth fruit, some thirtyfold, some sixty, and some a hundred. <div eID="gen24426" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24427" type="x-p"/> The foregoing chapter began with Christ's <hi type="italic">entering into the synagogue</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mark.4.1">v. 1</reference>); this chapter begins with Christ's <hi type="italic">teaching again by the sea side.</hi> Thus he changed his method, that if possible all might be reached and wrought upon. To gratify the nice and more genteel sort of people that had seats, <hi type="italic">chief seats, in the synagogue,</hi> and did not care for hearing a sermon any where else, he did not preach always by the <hi type="italic">sea side,</hi> but, having liberty, went often <hi type="italic">into the synagogue,</hi> and taught there; yet, to gratify the poor, the mob, that could not get room in the synagogue, he did not always preach there, but <hi type="italic">began again to teach by the sea side,</hi> where they could come <hi type="italic">within hearing.</hi> Thus are we <hi type="italic">debtors both to the wise and to the unwise,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.1.14">Rom. i. 14</reference>. <div eID="gen24427" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24428" type="x-p"/> Here seems to be a new convenience found out, which had not been used before, though he had before preached by the sea side (<reference osisRef="Mark.2.13">ch. ii. 13</reference>), and that was—his standing <hi type="italic">in a ship,</hi> while his hearers <hi type="italic">stood upon the land;</hi> and that inland sea of Tiberias having no tide, there was no ebbing and flowing of the waters to disturb them. Methinks Christ's carrying his doctrine into a ship, and preaching it thence, was a presage of his sending the gospel to the <hi type="italic">isles of the Gentiles,</hi> and the shipping off of the kingdom of God (that rich cargo) from the Jewish nation, to be sent to a people that would bring forth more of the fruits of it. Now observe here, <div eID="gen24428" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24429" type="x-p"/> I. The <hi type="italic">way of teaching</hi> that Christ used with the <hi type="italic">multitude</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mark.4.2">v. 2</reference>); He <hi type="italic">taught them many things,</hi> but it was <hi type="italic">by parables</hi> or similitudes, which would <hi type="italic">tempt them to hear;</hi> for people love to be spoken to in their own language, and careless hearers will catch at a plain comparison borrowed from common things, and will retain and repeat that, when they have <hi type="italic">lost,</hi> or perhaps never <hi type="italic">took,</hi> the truth which it was designed to explain and illustrate: but unless they would take pains to search into it, it would but amuse them; <hi type="italic">seeing they would see, and not perceive</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mark.4.12">v. 12</reference>); and so, while it gratified their curiosity, it was the punishment of their stupidity; they wilfully shut their eyes against the light, and therefore justly did Christ put it into the dark lantern of a parable, which had a bright side toward those who applied it to themselves, and were willing to be guided by it; but to those who were only <hi type="italic">willing for a season to play with it,</hi> it only gave a flash of light now and then, but sent them away in the dark. It is just with God to say of those that <hi type="italic">will not see,</hi> that they <hi type="italic">shall not see,</hi> and to hide from their eyes, who only look about them with a great deal of carelessness, and never look before them with any concern upon the things that belong to their peace. <div eID="gen24429" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24430" type="x-p"/> II. The way of <hi type="italic">expounding</hi> that he used with his <hi type="italic">disciples; When he was alone</hi> by himself, not only the <hi type="italic">twelve,</hi> but others that were <hi type="italic">about him with the twelve,</hi> took the opportunity to <hi type="italic">ask him</hi> the meaning of the parables, <reference osisRef="Mark.4.10">v. 10</reference>. They found it good to be <hi type="italic">about Christ;</hi> the nearer him the better; good to be <hi type="italic">with the twelve,</hi> to be conversant with those that are intimate with him. And he told them what a distinguishing favour it was to them, that they were made acquainted with the <hi type="italic">mystery of the kingdom of God,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.4.11">v. 11</reference>. <hi type="italic">The secret of the Lord was with them.</hi> That <hi type="italic">instructed</hi> them, which others were only <hi type="italic">amused</hi> with, and they were made to increase in knowledge by every parable, and understood more of the way and method in which Christ designed to set up his kingdom in the world, while others were dismissed, never the wiser. Note, Those who know the <hi type="italic">mystery</hi> of the <hi type="italic">kingdom of heaven,</hi> must acknowledge that it is <hi type="italic">given to them;</hi> they receive both the light and the sight from Jesus Christ, who, after his resurrection, both <hi type="italic">opened the scriptures,</hi> and <hi type="italic">opened the understanding,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.24.27">Luke xxiv. 27</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luke.24.45">45</reference>. <div eID="gen24430" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24431" type="x-p"/> In particular, we have here, <div eID="gen24431" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24432" type="x-p"/> 1. The parable of the sower, as we had it, <reference osisRef="Matt.13.3">Matt. xiii. 3</reference>, &c. He begins (<reference osisRef="Mark.4.3">v. 3</reference>), with, <hi type="italic">Hearken,</hi> and concludes (<reference osisRef="Mark.4.9">v. 9</reference>) with, <hi type="italic">He that hath ears to hear, let him hear.</hi> Note, The words of Christ demand attention, and those who speak from him, may command it, and should stir it up; even that which as yet we do not <hi type="italic">thoroughly</hi> understand, or not <hi type="italic">rightly,</hi> we must carefully attend to, believing it to be both intelligible and weighty, that at length we may understand it; we shall find more in Christ's sayings than at first there seemed to be. <div eID="gen24432" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24433" type="x-p"/> 2. The exposition of it to the disciples. Here is a question Christ put to them before he expounded it, which we had not in Matthew (<reference osisRef="Mark.4.13">v. 13</reference>); "<hi type="italic">Know ye not this parable?</hi> Know ye not the meaning of it? <hi type="italic">How then will ye know all parables?</hi>" (1.) "If ye know not this, which is so plain, how will ye understand other parables, which will be more dark and obscure? If ye are gravelled and run aground with this, which bespeaks so plainly the different success of the word preached upon those that hear it, which ye yourselves may see easily, how will ye understand the parables which hereafter will speak of the rejection of the Jews, and the calling of the Gentiles, which is a thing ye have no idea of?" Note, This should quicken us both to prayer and pains that we may get knowledge, that there are a great many things which we are concerned to know; and if we understand not the plain truths of the gospel, how shall we master those that are more difficult? <hi type="italic">Vita brevis, ars longa—Life is short, art is long. If we have run with the footmen, and they have wearied us,</hi> and run us down, then <hi type="italic">how shall we contend with horses?</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.12.5">Jer. xii. 5</reference>. (2.) "If ye know not this, which is intended for your direction in hearing the word, that ye may profit by it; how shall ye profit by what ye are further to hear? This parable is to teach you to be attentive to the word, and affected with it, that you may <hi type="italic">understand</hi> it. If ye receive not this, ye will not know how to use the key by which ye must be let into all the rest." If we understand not the rules we are to observe in order to our profiting by the word, how shall we profit by any other rule? Observe, Before Christ expounds the parable, [1.] He shows them how sad <hi type="italic">their</hi> case was, who were not let into the meaning of the doctrine of Christ; <hi type="italic">To you it is given, but not to them.</hi> Note, It will help us to put a value upon the privileges we enjoy as disciples of Christ, to consider the deplorable state of those who want such privileges, especially that they are out of the ordinary way of conversion; <hi type="italic">lest they should be converted, and their sins should be forgiven them.</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.4.12">v. 12</reference>. Those only who are <hi type="italic">converted,</hi> have <hi type="italic">their sins forgiven them:</hi> and it is the misery of <hi type="italic">unconverted</hi> souls, that they lie under <hi type="italic">unpardoned</hi> guilt.
