[2.] He shows them what a shame it was, that they needed such particular explanations of the word they heard, and did not apprehend it at first. Those that would improve in knowledge, must be made sensible of their ignorance. <div eID="gen24433" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24434" type="x-p"/> Having thus prepared them for it, he gives them the interpretation of the parable of the sower, as we had it before in Matthew. Let us only observe here, <div eID="gen24434" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24435" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">First,</hi> That in the great field of the church, the word of God is dispensed to all promiscuously; <hi type="italic">The sower soweth the word</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mark.4.14">v. 14</reference>), sows it at a venture, <hi type="italic">beside all waters,</hi> upon all sorts of ground (<reference osisRef="Isa.32.20">Isa. xxxii. 20</reference>), not knowing where it will light, or what fruit it will bring forth. He <hi type="italic">scatters</hi> it, in order to the <hi type="italic">increase</hi> of it. Christ was awhile <hi type="italic">sowing</hi> himself, when he went about teaching and preaching; now he sends his ministers, and sows by their hand. Ministers are sowers; they have need of the skill and discretion of the husbandman (<reference osisRef="Isa.28.24-Isa.28.26">Isa. xxviii. 24-26</reference>); they must not observe winds and clouds (<reference osisRef="Eccl.11.4">Eccl. xi. 4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eccl.11.6">6</reference>), and must look up to God, who <hi type="italic">gives seed to the sower,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.9.10">2 Cor. ix. 10</reference>. <div eID="gen24435" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24436" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> That of the many that hear the word of the gospel, and read it, and are conversant with it, there are, comparatively, but few that receive it, so as to bring forth the fruits of it; here is but one in four, that comes to good. It is sad to think, how much of the precious seed of the word of God is lost, and <hi type="italic">sown in vain;</hi> but there is a day coming when <hi type="italic">lost sermons</hi> must be accounted for. Many that have heard Christ himself <hi type="italic">preach in their streets,</hi> will hereafter be bidden to depart from him; those therefore who place all their religion in hearing, as if that alone would save them, do but deceive themselves, and build their hope upon the sand, <reference osisRef="Jas.1.22">Jam. i. 22</reference>. <div eID="gen24436" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24437" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> Many are much affected with the word for the present, who yet receive no abiding benefit by it. The motions of soul they have, answerable to what they hear, are but a mere flash, like the crackling of thorns under a pot. We read of hypocrites, that they <hi type="italic">delight to know God's ways</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.58.2">Isa. lviii. 2</reference>); of Herod, that he heard John gladly (<reference osisRef="Mark.6.20">ch. vi. 20</reference>); of others, that they <hi type="italic">rejoiced in his light</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.5.35">John v. 35</reference>); of those to whom Ezekiel was a <hi type="italic">lovely song</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.33.32">Ezek. xxxiii. 32</reference>); and those represented here by the stony ground, received the word <hi type="italic">with gladness,</hi> and yet came to nothing. <div eID="gen24437" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24438" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Fourthly,</hi> The reason why the word doth not leave commanding, abiding, impressions upon the minds of the people, is, because their hearts are not duly disposed and prepared to receive it; the fault is in themselves, not in the word; some are careless forgetful hearers, and these get <hi type="italic">no good at all</hi> by the word; it comes in at one ear, and goes out at the other; others have their convictions overpowered by their corruptions, and they lose the good impressions the word has made upon them, so that they get no <hi type="italic">abiding</hi> good by it. <div eID="gen24438" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24439" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Fifthly,</hi> The devil is very busy about loose, careless hearers, as the fowls of the air go about the seed that lies above ground; when the heart, like the <hi type="italic">highway,</hi> is unploughed, unhumbled, when it <hi type="italic">lies common,</hi> to be trodden on by every passenger, as theirs that are great company-keepers, then the devil is <hi type="italic">like the fowls;</hi> he comes swiftly, and carries away the word ere we are aware. When therefore these fowls come down upon the sacrifices, we should take care, as <hi type="italic">Abram</hi> did, to <hi type="italic">drive them away</hi> (<reference osisRef="Gen.15.11">Gen. xv. 11</reference>); that, though we cannot keep them from hovering over our heads, we may not let them nestle in our hearts. <div eID="gen24439" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24440" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Sixthly,</hi> Many that are not openly <hi type="italic">scandalized,</hi> so as to throw off their profession, as they on the stony ground did, yet have the efficacy of it secretly <hi type="italic">choked</hi> and stifled, so that it comes to nothing; they continue in a barren, hypocritical profession, which brings nothing to pass, and so go down as certainly, though more plausibly, to hell. <div eID="gen24440" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24441" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Seventhly,</hi> Impressions that are not <hi type="italic">keep,</hi> will not be <hi type="italic">durable,</hi> but will wear off in suffering, trying times; like footsteps on the sand of the sea, which are gone the next high tide of persecution; when <hi type="italic">that</hi> iniquity doth abound, the love of many to the ways of God waxeth cold; many that keep their profession in fair days, lose it in a storm; and do as those that go to sea only for pleasure, come back again when the wind arises. It is the ruin of hypocrites, that they <hi type="italic">have no root;</hi> they do not act from a living fixed principle; they do not mind <hi type="italic">heart-work,</hi> and without that religion is nothing; for he is the Christian, that is <hi type="italic">one inwardly.</hi> <div eID="gen24441" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24442" type="x-p"/> Eighthly, Many are hindered from profiting by the word of God, by their abundance of the world. Many a good lesson of humility, charity, self-denial, and heavenly-mindedness, is choked and lost by that prevailing complacency in the world, which <hi type="italic">they</hi> are apt to have, on whom it smiles. Thus many professors, that otherwise might have come to something, prove like Pharaoh's <hi type="italic">lean kine</hi> and <hi type="italic">thin ears.</hi> <div eID="gen24442" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24443" type="x-p"/> Ninthly, Those that are not encumbered with the cares of the world, and the deceitfulness of riches, may yet lose the benefit of their profession by the <hi type="italic">lusts of other things;</hi> this is added here in Mark; <hi type="italic">by the desires which are about other things</hi> (so Dr. Hammond), an inordinate appetite toward those things that are pleasing to sense or to the fancy. Those that have but little of the world, may yet be ruined by an indulgence of the body. <div eID="gen24443" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24444" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Tenthly,</hi> Fruit is the thing that God expects and requires from those that enjoy the gospel: fruit according to the <hi type="italic">seed;</hi> a temper of mind, and a course of life, agreeable to the gospel; Christian graces daily exercised, Christian duties duly performed. This is <hi type="italic">fruit,</hi> and it will abound to our account. <div eID="gen24444" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24445" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Lastly,</hi> No good fruit is to be expected but from good seed. If the seed be sown on <hi type="italic">good ground,</hi> if the heart be humble, and holy, and heavenly, there will be <hi type="italic">good fruit,</hi> and it will <hi type="italic">abound</hi> sometimes even to a <hi type="italic">hundred fold,</hi> such a crop as Isaac reaped, <reference osisRef="Gen.26.12">Gen. xxvi. 12</reference>.

<div eID="gen24445" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Gradual Advance of the Gospel.</title> <div sID="gen24446" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">21</hi> And he said unto them, Is a candle brought to be put under a bushel, or under a bed? and not to be set on a candlestick? <hi type="super">22</hi> For there is nothing hid, which shall not be manifested; neither was any thing kept secret, but that it should come abroad. <hi type="super">23</hi> If any man have ears to hear, let him hear. 24 And he said unto them, Take heed what ye hear: with what measure ye mete, it shall be measured to you: and unto you that hear shall more be given. <hi type="super">25</hi> For he that hath, to him shall be given: and he that hath not, from him shall be taken even that which he hath. <hi type="super">26</hi> And he said, So is the kingdom of God, as if a man should cast seed into the ground; <hi type="super">27</hi> And should sleep, and rise night and day, and the seed should spring and grow up, he knoweth not how. <hi type="super">28</hi> For the earth bringeth forth fruit of herself; first the blade, then the ear, after that the full corn in the ear. <hi type="super">29</hi> But when the fruit is brought forth, immediately he putteth in the sickle, because the harvest is come. <hi type="super">30</hi> And he said, Whereunto shall we liken the kingdom of God? or with what comparison shall we compare it? 31 <hi type="italic">It is</hi> like a grain of mustard seed, which, when it is sown in the earth, is less than all the seeds that be in the earth: 32 But when it is sown, it groweth up, and becometh greater than all herbs, and shooteth out great branches; so that the fowls of the air may lodge under the shadow of it. <hi type="super">33</hi> And with many such parables spake he the word unto them, as they were able to hear <hi type="italic">it.</hi> <hi type="super">34</hi> But without a parable spake he not unto them: and when they were alone, he expounded all things to his disciples. <div eID="gen24446" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24447" type="x-p"/> The lessons which our Saviour designs to teach us here by parables and figurative expressions are these:— <div eID="gen24447" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24448" type="x-p"/> I. That those who <hi type="italic">are good</hi> ought to consider the obligations they are under to <hi type="italic">do good;</hi> that is, as in the parable before, to <hi type="italic">bring forth fruit.</hi> God expects a grateful return of his gifts to us, and a useful improvement of his gifts in us; for (<reference osisRef="Mark.4.21">v. 21</reference>), <hi type="italic">Is a candle brought to be put under a bushel, or under a bed?</hi> No, but that it may be <hi type="italic">set on a candlestick.</hi> The apostles were ordained, to receive the gospel, not for themselves only, but for the good of others, to communicate it to them. All Christians, as they have <hi type="italic">received the gift,</hi> must <hi type="italic">minister the same.</hi> Note, 1. Gifts and graces make a man <hi type="italic">as a candle;</hi> the <hi type="italic">candle of the Lord</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.20.27">Prov. xx. 27</reference>), lighted by the Father of lights; the most eminent are but candles, poor lights, compared with the <hi type="italic">Sun of righteousness.</hi> A candle gives light but a <hi type="italic">little way,</hi> and but a <hi type="italic">little while,</hi> and is easily blown out, and continually burning down and wasting. 2. Many who are <hi type="italic">lighted</hi> as candles, put themselves <hi type="italic">under a bed, or under a bushel:</hi> they do not <hi type="italic">manifest</hi> grace themselves, nor <hi type="italic">minister</hi> grace to others; they have estates, and do no good with them; have their limbs and senses, wit and learning perhaps, but nobody is the better for them; they have spiritual gifts, but do not use them; like a taper in an urn, they burn to themselves. 3. Those who are lighted as candles, should set themselves <hi type="italic">on a candlestick;</hi> that is, should improve all opportunities of doing good, as those that were made for the glory of God, and the service of the communities they are members of; we are not born for ourselves. <div eID="gen24448" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24449" type="x-p"/> The reason given for this, is, because <hi type="italic">there is nothing hid, which shall not be manifested,</hi> which <hi type="italic">should not</hi> be made manifest (so it might better be read), <reference osisRef="Mark.4.22">v. 22</reference>. There is no treasure of gifts and graces lodged in any but with design to be communicated; nor was the gospel made a <hi type="italic">secret</hi> to the apostles, to be concealed, but that it should <hi type="italic">come abroad,</hi> and be divulged to all the world. Though Christ expounded the parables to his disciples privately, yet it was with design to make them the more publicly useful; they were <hi type="italic">taught,</hi> that they might teach; and it is a general rule, that <hi type="italic">the ministration of the Spirit is given to every man to profit withal,</hi> not himself only, but others also. <div eID="gen24449" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24450" type="x-p"/> II. It concerns those who hear the word of the gospel, to <hi type="italic">mark</hi> what they hear, and to <hi type="italic">make a good use</hi> of it, because their <hi type="italic">weal</hi> or <hi type="italic">woe</hi> depends upon it; what he had said before he saith again, <hi type="italic">If any man have ears to hear, let him hear,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.4.23">v. 23</reference>. Let him give the gospel of Christ a fair hearing; but that is not enough, it is added (<reference osisRef="Mark.4.24">v. 24</reference>), <hi type="italic">Take heed what ye hear,</hi> and give a due regard to that which ye do hear; <hi type="italic">Consider what ye</hi> hear, so Dr. Hammond reads it. Note, What we hear, doth us no good, unless we consider it; those especially that are to teach others must themselves be very observant of the things of God; must take notice of the message they are to deliver, that they may be exact. We must likewise <hi type="italic">take heed what we hear,</hi> by <hi type="italic">proving</hi> all things, that we may <hi type="italic">hold fast that which is good.</hi> We must be <hi type="italic">cautious,</hi> and stand upon our guard, lest we be imposed upon. To enforce this caution, consider, <div eID="gen24450" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24451" type="x-p"/> 1. As we deal with God, God will deal with us, so Dr. Hammond explains these words, "<hi type="italic">With what measure ye mete, it shall be measured to you.</hi> If ye be faithful servants to him, he will be a faithful Master to you: <hi type="italic">with the upright he will show himself upright.</hi>" <div eID="gen24451" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24452" type="x-p"/> 2. As we improve the talents we are entrusted with, we shall increase them; if we make use of the knowledge we have, for the glory of God and the benefit of others, it shall sensibly grow, as stock in trade doth by being turned; <hi type="italic">Unto you that hear, shall more be given; to you that have, it shall be given,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.4.25">v. 25</reference>. If the disciples <hi type="italic">deliver</hi> that to the church, which they have <hi type="italic">received of the Lord,</hi> they shall be <hi type="italic">led</hi> more into the <hi type="italic">secret of the Lord.</hi> Gifts and graces multiply by being exercised; and God has promised to bless the <hi type="italic">hand of the diligent.</hi> <div eID="gen24452" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24453" type="x-p"/> 3. If we do not <hi type="italic">use,</hi> we <hi type="italic">lose,</hi> what we have; <hi type="italic">From him that hath not,</hi> that doeth no good with what he hath, and so hath it in vain, is as if he had it not, <hi type="italic">shall be taken even that which he hath.</hi> Burying a talent is the betraying of a trust, and amounts to a forfeiture; and gifts and graces <hi type="italic">rust</hi> for want of <hi type="italic">wearing.</hi> <div eID="gen24453" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24454" type="x-p"/> III. The good seed of the gospel sown in the world, and sown in the heart, doth by degrees produce wonderful effects, but without noise (<reference osisRef="Mark.4.26">v. 26</reference>, &c.); <hi type="italic">So is the kingdom of God;</hi> so is the gospel, when it is sown, and received, as seed in good ground. <div eID="gen24454" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24455" type="x-p"/> 1. It will <hi type="italic">come up;</hi> though it seem lost and buried under the clods, it will find or make its way through them. The seed <hi type="italic">cast into the ground will spring.</hi> Let but the word of Christ have the place it ought to have in a soul, and it will show itself, as the <hi type="italic">wisdom from above</hi> doth in a <hi type="italic">good conversation.</hi> After a field is sown with corn, how soon is the surface of it altered! How gay and pleasant doth it look, when it is covered with green! <div eID="gen24455" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24456" type="x-p"/> 2. The husbandman cannot describe how it comes up; it is one of the mysteries of nature; It <hi type="italic">springs and grows up, he knows not how,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.4.27">v. 27</reference>. He sees it has grown, but he cannot tell in what manner it grew, or what was the cause and method of its growth. Thus we know not how the Spirit by the word makes a change in the heart, any more than we can account for the blowing of the wind, which we hear the sound of, but cannot tell whence it comes, or whither it goes. Without controversy, great is the mystery of godliness; how <hi type="italic">God manifested in the flesh</hi> came to be <hi type="italic">believed on in the world,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Tim.3.16">1 Tim. iii. 16</reference>. <div eID="gen24456" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24457" type="x-p"/> 3. The husbandman, when he hath sown the seed, doth nothing toward the springing of it up; <hi type="italic">He sleeps, and rises, night and day;</hi> goes to sleep <hi type="italic">at night,</hi> gets up <hi type="italic">in the morning,</hi> and perhaps never so much as thinks of the corn he hath sown, or ever looks upon it, but follows his pleasures or other business, and yet <hi type="italic">the earth brings forth fruit of itself,</hi> according to the ordinary course of nature, and by the concurring power of the God of nature. Thus the <hi type="italic">word of grace,</hi> when it is received in faith, is in the heart a <hi type="italic">work of grace,</hi> and the preachers contribute nothing to it. The Spirit of God is carrying it on when <hi type="italic">they sleep,</hi> and can do no business (<reference osisRef="Job.33.15-Job.33.16">Job xxxiii. 15, 16</reference>), or when they rise to go about other business. The prophets do not <hi type="italic">live for ever;</hi> but the word which they preached, is doing its work, when they are in their graves, <reference osisRef="Zech.1.5-Zech.1.6">Zech. i. 5, 6</reference>. The dew by which the seed is brought up <hi type="italic">tarrieth not for man, nor waiteth for the sons of men,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mic.5.7">Mic. v. 7</reference>. <div eID="gen24457" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24458" type="x-p"/> 4. It grows gradually; <hi type="italic">first the blade, then the ear, after that the full corn in the ear,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.4.28">v. 28</reference>. When it is sprung up, it will go forward; nature will have its course, and so will grace. Christ's interest, both in the world and in the heart, is, and will be, a <hi type="italic">growing</hi> interest; and though <hi type="italic">the beginning be small, the latter end will greatly increase.</hi> Though thou sowest not that body that shall be, but <hi type="italic">bare grain,</hi> yet God <hi type="italic">will give to every seed its own body;</hi> though at first it is but a tender <hi type="italic">blade,</hi> which the frost may nip, or the foot may crush, yet it will increase to <hi type="italic">the ear,</hi> to the <hi type="italic">full corn in the ear. Natura nil facit per saltum—Nature does nothing abruptly.</hi> God carries on his work insensibly and without noise, but insuperably and without fail. <div eID="gen24458" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24459" type="x-p"/> 5. It comes to perfection at last (<reference osisRef="Mark.4.29">v. 29</reference>); <hi type="italic">When the fruit is brought forth,</hi> that is, when it is <hi type="italic">ripe,</hi> and ready to be <hi type="italic">delivered</hi> into the owner's hand; then he <hi type="italic">puts in the sickle.</hi> This intimates, (1.) That Christ <hi type="italic">now accepts</hi> the services which are done to him by an honest heart from a good principle; from the fruit of the gospel taking place and working in the soul, Christ <hi type="italic">gathers in</hi> a harvest of honour to himself. See <reference osisRef="John.4.35">John iv. 35</reference>. (2.) That he will reward them in eternal life. When those that receive the gospel aright, have finished their course, the harvest comes, when they shall be gathered as <hi type="italic">wheat into God's barn</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.13.30">Matt. xiii. 30</reference>), as a shock of corn <hi type="italic">in his season.</hi> <div eID="gen24459" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24460" type="x-p"/> IV. The work of grace is small in its beginnings, but comes to be great and considerable at last (<reference osisRef="Mark.4.30-Mark.4.32">v. 30-32</reference>); "<hi type="italic">Whereunto shall I liken the kingdom of God,</hi> as now to be set up by the Messiah? How shall I make you to understand the designed method of it?" Christ speaks as one considering and consulting with himself, how to illustrate it with an apt similitude; <hi type="italic">With what comparison shall we compare it?</hi> Shall we fetch it from the motions of the sun, or the revolutions of the moon? No, the comparison is borrowed from this earth, it is <hi type="italic">like a grain of mustard-seed;</hi> he had compared it before to <hi type="italic">seed sown,</hi> here to <hi type="italic">that seed,</hi> intending thereby to show, <div eID="gen24460" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24461" type="x-p"/> 1. That the beginnings of the <hi type="italic">gospel kingdom</hi> would be very small, like that which is <hi type="italic">one of the least of all seeds.</hi> When a Christian church was <hi type="italic">sown in the earth</hi> for God, it was all contained in one room, and the <hi type="italic">number of the names</hi> was but one hundred and twenty (<reference osisRef="Acts.1.15">Acts i. 15</reference>), as the children of Israel, when they went down into Egypt, were but seventy souls. The work of grace in the soul, is, at first, but the <hi type="italic">day of small things;</hi> a <hi type="italic">cloud</hi> no <hi type="italic">bigger than a man's hand.</hi> Never were there such great things undertaken by such an inconsiderable handful, as that of the discipling of the nations by the ministry of the apostles; nor a work that was to end in such great glory, as the work of grace raised from such weak and unlikely beginnings. <hi type="italic">Who hath begotten me these?</hi> <div eID="gen24461" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24462" type="x-p"/> 2. That the perfection of it will be very great; <hi type="italic">When it grows up, it becomes greater than all herbs.</hi> The gospel kingdom in the world, shall increase and spread to the remotest nations of the earth, and shall continue to the latest ages of time. The <hi type="italic">church</hi> hath <hi type="italic">shot out great branches,</hi> strong ones, spreading far, and fruitful. The <hi type="italic">work of grace</hi> in the soul has mighty products, now while it is in its growth; but what will it be, when it is perfected in heaven? The difference between a <hi type="italic">grain of mustard seed</hi> and a <hi type="italic">great tree,</hi> is nothing to that between a <hi type="italic">young convert</hi> on earth and a <hi type="italic">glorified saint</hi> in heaven. See <reference osisRef="John.12.24">John xii. 24</reference>. <div eID="gen24462" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24463" type="x-p"/> After the parables thus specified the historian concludes with this general account of Christ's preaching—that <hi type="italic">with many such parables he spoke the word unto them</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mark.4.33">v. 33</reference>); probably designing to refer us to the larger account of the parables of this kind, which we had before, <reference osisRef="Matt.13.1-Matt.13.52">Matt. xiii.</reference> He spoke in parables, <hi type="italic">as they were able to hear them;</hi> he fetched his comparisons from those things that were familiar to them, and level to their capacity, and delivered them in plain expressions, in condescension to their capacity; though he did not let them into the <hi type="italic">mystery</hi> of the parables, yet his manner of expression was easy, and such as they might hereafter recollect to their edification. But, for the present, <hi type="italic">without a parable spoke he not unto them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.4.34">v. 34</reference>. The glory of the Lord was covered with a cloud, and God speaks to us in the language of the <hi type="italic">sons of men,</hi> that, though not <hi type="italic">at first,</hi> yet <hi type="italic">by degrees,</hi> we may understand his meaning; the disciples themselves understood those sayings of Christ afterward, which at first they did not rightly take the sense of. But these parables <hi type="italic">he expounded to them, when they were alone.</hi> We cannot but wish we had had that exposition, as we had of the parable of the sower; but it was not so needful; because, when the church should be enlarged, that would <hi type="italic">expound</hi> these parables to us, without any more ado.

<div eID="gen24463" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Christ and His Disciples in the Storm.</title> <div sID="gen24464" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">35</hi> And the same day, when the even was come, he saith unto them, Let us pass over unto the other side. <hi type="super">36</hi> And when they had sent away the multitude, they took him even as he was in the ship. And there were also with him other little ships. 37 And there arose a great storm of wind, and the waves beat into the ship, so that it was now full. <hi type="super">38</hi> And he was in the hinder part of the ship, asleep on a pillow: and they awake him, and say unto him, Master, carest thou not that we perish? <hi type="super">39</hi> And he arose, and rebuked the wind, and said unto the sea, Peace, be still. And the wind ceased, and there was a great calm. <hi type="super">40</hi> And he said unto them, Why are ye so fearful? how is it that ye have no faith? <hi type="super">41</hi> And they feared exceedingly, and said one to another, What manner of man is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him? <div eID="gen24464" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24465" type="x-p"/> This miracle which Christ wrought for the relief of his disciples, in stilling the storm, we had before (<reference osisRef="Matt.8.23">Matt. viii. 23</reference>, &c.); but it is here more fully related. Observe, <div eID="gen24465" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24466" type="x-p"/> 1. It was <hi type="italic">the same day</hi> that he had preached out of a ship, <hi type="italic">when the even was come,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.4.35">v. 35</reference>. When he had been <hi type="italic">labouring in the word and doctrine</hi> all day, instead of <hi type="italic">re</hi>posing himself, he <hi type="italic">ex</hi>poseth himself, to teach us not to think of a constant remaining rest till we come to heaven. The end of a toil may perhaps be but the beginning of a toss. But observe, the ship that Christ made his pulpit is taken under his special protection, and, though in danger, cannot sink. What is used for Christ, he will take particular care of. <div eID="gen24466" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24467" type="x-p"/> 2. He himself proposed putting to sea at night, because he would lose no time; <hi type="italic">Let us pass over to the other side;</hi> for we shall find, in the next chapter, he has work to do there. Christ went about doing good, and no difficulties in his way should hinder him; thus industrious we should be in serving him, and our generation according to his will. <div eID="gen24467" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24468" type="x-p"/> 3. They did not put to sea, till <hi type="italic">they had sent away the multitude,</hi> that is, had given to each of them that which they came for, and answered all their requests; for he sent none home complaining that they had attended him <hi type="italic">in vain.</hi> Or, They sent them away <hi type="italic">with a solemn blessing;</hi> for Christ came into the world, not only to pronounce, but to <hi type="italic">command,</hi> and to <hi type="italic">give,</hi> the blessing. <div eID="gen24468" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24469" type="x-p"/> 4. They took him <hi type="italic">even as he was,</hi> that is, in the same dress that he was in when he preached, without any cloak to throw over him, which he ought to have had, to keep him <hi type="italic">warm,</hi> when he went to sea at night, especially after preaching. We must not hence infer that we may be careless of our health, but we may learn hence not to be over nice and solicitous about the body. <div eID="gen24469" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24470" type="x-p"/> 5. The storm was so great, that the ship was <hi type="italic">full of water</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mark.4.37">v. 37</reference>), not by springing a leak, but perhaps partly with the shower, for the word here used signifies a <hi type="italic">tempest of wind with rain;</hi> however, the ship being little, the waves beat into it so that <hi type="italic">it was full.</hi> Note, It is no new thing for that ship to be greatly hurried and endangered, in which Christ and his disciples, Christ and his name and gospel, are embarked. <div eID="gen24470" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24471" type="x-p"/> 6. There were <hi type="italic">with him other little ships,</hi> which, no doubt, shared in the distress and danger. Probably, these <hi type="italic">little ships</hi> carried those who were desirous to go along with Christ, for the benefit of his preaching and miracles on the other side. The <hi type="italic">multitude went away</hi> when he put to sea, but some there were, that would venture upon the water with him. Those follow the Lamb aright, that follow him <hi type="italic">wherever he goes.</hi> And those that hope for a happiness in Christ, must be willing to take their lot with him, and run the same risks that he runs. One may boldly and cheerfully put to sea in Christ's company, yea though we foresee a storm. <div eID="gen24471" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24472" type="x-p"/> 7. Christ was asleep in this storm; and here we are told that it was <hi type="italic">in the hinder part of the ship,</hi> the pilot's place: he lay at the helm, to intimate that, as Mr. George Herbert expresses it, <div eID="gen24472" type="x-p"/> <lg sID="gen24473"/> <l level="1" sID="gen24474"/>When winds and waves assault my keel,<l eID="gen24474" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen24475"/>He doth preserve it, he doth steer,<l eID="gen24475" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen24476"/>Ev'n when the boat seems most to reel.<l eID="gen24476" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen24477"/>Storms are the triumph of his art;<l eID="gen24477" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen24478"/>Though he may close his eyes, yet not his heart.<l eID="gen24478" level="1"/> <lg eID="gen24473"/> <div sID="gen24479" type="x-p"/> He had a <hi type="italic">pillow</hi> there, such a one as a fisherman's ship would furnish him with. And he <hi type="italic">slept,</hi> to try the faith of his disciples and to stir up prayer: upon the trial, their faith appeared <hi type="italic">weak,</hi> and their prayers <hi type="italic">strong.</hi> Note, Sometimes when the church is in a storm, Christ seems as if he were asleep, unconcerned in the troubles of his people, and regardless of their prayers, and doth not presently appear for their relief. <hi type="italic">Verily he is a God that hideth himself,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.45.15">Isa. xlv. 15</reference>. But as, when he tarries, he doth not tarry (<reference osisRef="Hab.2.3">Hab. ii. 3</reference>), so when he sleeps he doth not sleep; the keeper of Israel doth not so much as slumber (<reference osisRef="Ps.121.3-Ps.121.4">Ps. cxxi. 3, 4</reference>); he slept, but his heart was awake, as the spouse, <reference osisRef="Song.5.2">Cant. v. 2</reference>. <div eID="gen24479" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24480" type="x-p"/> 8. His disciples encouraged themselves with their having his presence, and thought it the best way to improve that, and appeal to that, and ply the oar of prayer rather than their other oars. Their confidence lay in this, that they had their Master with them; and the ship that has Christ in it, though it may be <hi type="italic">tossed,</hi> cannot <hi type="italic">sink;</hi> the bush that has God in it, though it may <hi type="italic">burn,</hi> shall not <hi type="italic">consume.</hi> Cæsar encouraged the master of the ship, that had him on board, with this, <hi type="italic">Cæsarem vehis, et fortunam Cæsaris—Thou hast Cæsar on board, and Cæsar's fortune.</hi> They <hi type="italic">awoke Christ.</hi> Had not the necessity of the case called for it, they would not have <hi type="italic">stirred up</hi> or <hi type="italic">awoke</hi> their Master, <hi type="italic">till he had pleased</hi> (<reference osisRef="Song.2.7">Cant. ii. 7</reference>); but they knew he would <hi type="italic">forgive them this wrong.</hi> When Christ seems as if he slept in a storm, he is awaked by the prayers of his people; when we know not what to do, our eye must be to him (<reference osisRef="2Chr.20.12">2 Chron. xx. 12</reference>); we may be at our wits' end, but not at our faith's end, while we have such a Saviour to go to. Their address to Christ is here expressed very emphatically; <hi type="italic">Master, carest thou not that we perish?</hi> I confess this sounds somewhat harsh, rather like chiding him for sleeping than begging him to awake. I know no excuse for it, but the great familiarity which he was pleased to admit them into, and the freedom he allowed them; and the present distress they were in, which put them into such a fright, that they knew not what they said. <hi type="italic">They</hi> do Christ a deal of wrong, who suspect him to be <hi type="italic">careless</hi> of his people in distress. The matter is not so; he is not willing that any should perish, much less any of his little ones, <reference osisRef="Matt.18.14">Matt. xviii. 14</reference>. <div eID="gen24480" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24481" type="x-p"/> 9. The word of command with which Christ rebuked the storm, we have here, and had not in Matthew, <reference osisRef="Mark.4.39">v. 39</reference>. He says, <hi type="italic">Peace, be still</hi>—<hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">Siopa, pephimoso</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">be silent, be dumb.</hi> Let not the wind any longer roar, nor the sea rage. Thus he <hi type="italic">stills the noise of the sea, the noise of her waves;</hi> a particular emphasis is laid upon the noisiness of them, <reference osisRef="Ps.65.7">Ps. lxv. 7, and xciii. 3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.93.3-Ps.93.4">4</reference>. The noise is threatening and terrifying; let us hear no more of it. This is, (1.) A word of command to us; when our wicked hearts are <hi type="italic">like the troubled sea which cannot rest</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.57.20">Isa. lvii. 20</reference>); when our passions are up, and are unruly, let us think we hear the law of Christ, saying, <hi type="italic">Be silent, be dumb.</hi> Think not confusedly, speak not unadvisedly; but <hi type="italic">be still.</hi> (2.) A word of comfort to us, that, be the storm of trouble ever so loud, ever so strong, Jesus Christ can lay it with a word's speaking. When without are fightings, and within are fears, and the spirits are in a tumult, Christ can <hi type="italic">create the fruit of the lips, peace.</hi> If he say, <hi type="italic">Peace, be still,</hi> there is a <hi type="italic">great calm</hi> presently. It is spoken of as God's prerogative to command the seas, <reference osisRef="Jer.31.35">Jer. xxxi. 35</reference>. By this therefore Christ proves himself to be God. He that made the seas, can make them <hi type="italic">quiet.</hi> <div eID="gen24481" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24482" type="x-p"/> 10. The reproof Christ gave them for their fears, is here carried further than in Matthew. There it is, <hi type="italic">Why are ye fearful?</hi> Here, <hi type="italic">Why are ye so fearful?</hi> Though there may be cause for some fear, yet not for fear to such a degree as this. There it is, <hi type="italic">O ye of little faith.</hi> Here it is, <hi type="italic">How is it that ye have no faith?</hi> Not that the disciples were without faith. No, they believed that <hi type="italic">Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God;</hi> but at this time their fears prevailed so that they seemed to <hi type="italic">have no faith</hi> at all. It was out of the way, when they had occasion for it, and so it was as if they had not had it. "<hi type="italic">How is it, that in this matter ye have no faith,</hi> that ye think I would not come in with seasonable and effectual relief?" Those may suspect their faith, who can entertain such a thought as that Christ <hi type="italic">careth not</hi> though his <hi type="italic">people perish,</hi> and Christ justly takes it ill. <div eID="gen24482" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24483" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Lastly,</hi> The impression this miracle made upon the disciples, is here differently expressed. In Matthew it is said, <hi type="italic">The men marvelled;</hi> here it is said, <hi type="italic">They feared greatly.</hi> They <hi type="italic">feared a great fear;</hi> so the original reads it. Now their fear was rectified by their faith. When they feared the winds and the seas, it was for want of the reverence they ought to have had for Christ. But now that they saw a demonstration of his power over them, they feared <hi type="italic">them</hi> less, and <hi type="italic">him</hi> more. They <hi type="italic">feared</hi> lest they had offended Christ by their unbelieving fears; and therefore studied now to give him honour. They had <hi type="italic">feared</hi> the power and wrath of the Creator in the storm, and that fear had torment and amazement in it; but now they feared the power and grace of the Redeemer in the calm; they <hi type="italic">feared the Lord and his goodness,</hi> and it had pleasure and satisfaction in it, and by it they gave glory to Christ, as Jonah's mariners, who, when the <hi type="italic">sea ceased from her raging, feared the Lord exceedingly, and offered a sacrifice unto the Lord,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jonah.1.16">Jon. i. 16</reference>. This sacrifice they offered to the honour of Christ; they said, <hi type="italic">What manner of man is this?</hi> Surely more than a man, <hi type="italic">for even the winds and the seas obey him.</hi>  <chapter eID="Mark.4"/> <div eID="gen24483" type="x-p"/>

<div eID="gen24486" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen24485" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Expulsion of Legion.</title> <div sID="gen24487" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> And they came over unto the other side of the sea, into the country of the Gadarenes. <hi type="super">2</hi> And when he was come out of the ship, immediately there met him out of the tombs a man with an unclean spirit, <hi type="super">3</hi> Who had <hi type="italic">his</hi> dwelling among the tombs; and no man could bind him, no, not with chains: 4 Because that he had been often bound with fetters and chains, and the chains had been plucked asunder by him, and the fetters broken in pieces: neither could any <hi type="italic">man</hi> tame him. 5 And always, night and day, he was in the mountains, and in the tombs, crying, and cutting himself with stones. <hi type="super">6</hi> But when he saw Jesus afar off, he ran and worshipped him, <hi type="super">7</hi> And cried with a loud voice, and said, What have I to do with thee, Jesus, <hi type="italic">thou</hi> Son of the most high God? I adjure thee by God, that thou torment me not. <hi type="super">8</hi> For he said unto him, Come out of the man, <hi type="italic">thou</hi> unclean spirit. <hi type="super">9</hi> And he asked him, What <hi type="italic">is</hi> thy name? And he answered, saying, My name <hi type="italic">is</hi> Legion: for we are many. <hi type="super">10</hi> And he besought him much that he would not send them away out of the country. <hi type="super">11</hi> Now there was there nigh unto the mountains a great herd of swine feeding. 12 And all the devils besought him, saying, Send us into the swine, that we may enter into them. <hi type="super">13</hi> And forthwith Jesus gave them leave. And the unclean spirits went out, and entered into the swine: and the herd ran violently down a steep place into the sea, (they were about two thousand;) and were choked in the sea. 14 And they that fed the swine fled, and told <hi type="italic">it</hi> in the city, and in the country. And they went out to see what it was that was done. <hi type="super">15</hi> And they come to Jesus, and see him that was possessed with the devil, and had the legion, sitting, and clothed, and in his right mind: and they were afraid. <hi type="super">16</hi> And they that saw <hi type="italic">it</hi> told them how it befell to him that was possessed with the devil, and <hi type="italic">also</hi> concerning the swine. 17 And they began to pray him to depart out of their coasts. 18 And when he was come into the ship, he that had been possessed with the devil prayed him that he might be with him. 19 Howbeit Jesus suffered him not, but saith unto him, Go home to thy friends, and tell them how great things the Lord hath done for thee, and hath had compassion on thee. <hi type="super">20</hi> And he departed, and began to publish in Decapolis how great things Jesus had done for him: and all <hi type="italic">men</hi> did marvel. <div eID="gen24487" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24488" type="x-p"/> We have here an instance of Christ's dispossessing the strong man armed, and disposing of him as he pleased, to make it appear that he was <hi type="italic">stronger than he.</hi> This he did when he was come <hi type="italic">to the other side,</hi> whither he went through a storm; his business there was to rescue this poor creature out of the hands of Satan, and when he had done that, he returned. Thus he came from heaven to earth, and returned, in a storm, to redeem a remnant of mankind out of the hands of the devil, though but a <hi type="italic">little remnant,</hi> and did not think his pains <hi type="italic">ill bestowed.</hi> <div eID="gen24488" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24489" type="x-p"/> In Matthew, they were said to be <hi type="italic">two</hi> possessed with devils; here it is said to be a <hi type="italic">man</hi> possessed with an unclean spirit. If there were <hi type="italic">two,</hi> there was one, and Mark doth not say that there was <hi type="italic">but one;</hi> so that this difference cannot give us any just offence; it is probable that one of them was much more remarkable than the other, and said what was said. Now observe here, <div eID="gen24489" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24490" type="x-p"/> I. The miserable condition that this poor creature was in; he was under the power of an <hi type="italic">unclean spirit,</hi> the devil got possession of him, and the effect of it was not, as in many, a silent melancholy, but a raging frenzy; he was raving mad; his condition seems to have been worse than any of the possessed, that were Christ's patients. <div eID="gen24490" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24491" type="x-p"/> 1. He had <hi type="italic">his dwelling among the tombs,</hi> among the graves of dead people. Their tombs were out of the cities, in <hi type="italic">desolate places</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.3.14">Job iii. 14</reference>); which gave the devil great advantage: for <hi type="italic">woe to him that is alone.</hi> Perhaps the devil drove him to <hi type="italic">the tombs,</hi> to make people fancy that the souls of the dead were turned into dæmons, and did what mischief was done, so to excuse themselves from it. The touch of a grave was polluting, <reference osisRef="Num.19.16">Num. xix. 16</reference>. The <hi type="italic">unclean spirit</hi> drives people into that company that is <hi type="italic">defiling,</hi> and so keeps possession of them. Christ, by rescuing souls out of Satan's power, <hi type="italic">saves the living from among the dead.</hi> <div eID="gen24491" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24492" type="x-p"/> 2. He was very strong and ungovernable; <hi type="italic">No man could bind him,</hi> as it is requisite both for their own good, and for the safety of others, that those who are distracted should be. Not only cords would not hold him, but <hi type="italic">chains</hi> and <hi type="italic">fetters of iron</hi> would not, <reference osisRef="Mark.5.3-Mark.5.4">v. 3, 4</reference>. Very deplorable is the case of such as <hi type="italic">need to be</hi> thus <hi type="italic">bound,</hi> and of all miserable people in this world they are most to be pitied; but his case was worst of all, in whom the devil was so strong, that he could not be <hi type="italic">bound.</hi> This sets forth the sad condition of those souls in which the devil has dominion; those <hi type="italic">children of disobedience,</hi> in whom that unclean spirit works. Some notoriously wilful sinners are like this madman; all are herein <hi type="italic">like the horse and the mule,</hi> that they need to be <hi type="italic">held in with bit and bridle;</hi> but some are like the <hi type="italic">wild ass,</hi> that will not be so held. The commands and curses of the law are as <hi type="italic">chains</hi> and <hi type="italic">fetters,</hi> to restrain sinners from their wicked courses; but they <hi type="italic">break those bands in sunder,</hi> and it is an evidence of the power of the devil in them. <div eID="gen24492" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24493" type="x-p"/> 3. He was a terror and torment to himself and to all about him, <reference osisRef="Mark.5.5">v. 5</reference>. The devil is a <hi type="italic">cruel</hi> master to those that are <hi type="italic">led captive</hi> by him, a perfect tyrant; this wretched creature was <hi type="italic">night and day in the mountains and in the tombs, crying, and cutting himself with stones,</hi> either bemoaning his own deplorable case, or in a rage and indignation against heaven. Men in frenzies often wound and destroy themselves; what is a man, when reason is <hi type="italic">de</hi>throned and Satan <hi type="italic">en</hi>throned? The worshippers of Baal in their fury <hi type="italic">cut themselves,</hi> like this madman in his. The voice of God is, <hi type="italic">Do thyself no harm;</hi> the voice of Satan is, <hi type="italic">Do thyself all the harm thou canst;</hi> yet God's word is despised, and Satan's regarded. Perhaps his <hi type="italic">cutting himself with stones</hi> was only cutting his feet with the sharp stones he ran barefoot upon. <div eID="gen24493" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24494" type="x-p"/> II. His application to Christ (<reference osisRef="Mark.5.6">v. 6</reference>); <hi type="italic">When he saw Jesus afar off,</hi> coming ashore, he <hi type="italic">ran, and worshipped him.</hi> He usually <hi type="italic">ran upon</hi> others with <hi type="italic">rage,</hi> but he <hi type="italic">ran to</hi> Christ with <hi type="italic">reverence.</hi> That was done by an invisible hand of Christ, which could not be done with chains and fetters; his fury was all on a sudden curbed. Even the devil, in this poor creature, was forced to tremble before Christ, and bow to him: or, rather, the poor man came, and <hi type="italic">worshipped Christ,</hi> in a sense of the need he had of his help, the power of Satan in and over him being, for this instant, suspended. <div eID="gen24494" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24495" type="x-p"/> III. The word of command Christ gave to the unclean spirit, to quit his possession (<reference osisRef="Mark.5.8">v. 8</reference>); <hi type="italic">Come out of him, thou unclean spirit.</hi> He made the man desirous to be relieved, when he enabled him to <hi type="italic">run, and worship him,</hi> and then put forth his power for his relief. If Christ <hi type="italic">work in us</hi> heartily to pray for a deliverance from Satan, he will work for us that deliverance. Here is an instance of the power and authority with which Christ <hi type="italic">commanded the unclean spirits, and they obeyed him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.1.27">ch. i. 27</reference>. He said, <hi type="italic">Come out of the man.</hi> The design of Christ's gospel is to <hi type="italic">expel</hi> unclean spirits out of the souls of people; "<hi type="italic">Come out of the man, thou unclean spirit,</hi> that the Holy Spirit may enter, may take possession of the heart, and have dominion in it." <div eID="gen24495" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24496" type="x-p"/> IV. The dread which the devil had of Christ. The <hi type="italic">man ran,</hi> and <hi type="italic">worshipped Christ;</hi> but it was the devil in the man, that <hi type="italic">cried with a loud voice</hi> (making use of the poor man's tongue), <hi type="italic">What have I to do with thee?</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.5.7">v. 7</reference>. Just as that other unclean spirit, <reference osisRef="Mark.1.24">ch. i. 24</reference>. 1. He calls God the <hi type="italic">most high God,</hi> above all other gods. By the name <hi type="italic">Elion—the Most High,</hi> God was <hi type="italic">known</hi> among the Ph&#339;nicians, and the other nations that bordered upon Israel; and by that name the devil calls him. 2. He owns Jesus to be the <hi type="italic">Son of God.</hi> Note, It is no strange thing to hear the best words drop from the worst mouths. There is such a way of saying this as none can attain to but <hi type="italic">by the Holy Ghost</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Cor.12.3">1 Cor. xii. 3</reference>); yet it may be said, after a sort, by the <hi type="italic">unclean spirit.</hi> There is no judging of men by their loose sayings; but by their fruits ye shall know them. Piety from the teeth outward is an easy thing. The most fair-spoken hypocrite cannot say better than to call Jesus the Son of God, and yet that the devil did. 3. He disowns any design against Christ; "<hi type="italic">What have I to do with thee?</hi> I have no need of thee, I pretend to none; I desire to have nothing to do with thee; I <hi type="italic">cannot stand</hi> before thee, and <hi type="italic">would not</hi> fall." 4. He deprecates his wrath; I <hi type="italic">adjure thee,</hi> that is, "I earnestly beseech thee, by all that is sacred, I beg of thee for God's sake, by whose permission I have got possession of this man, that, though thou drive me out hence, yet that thou <hi type="italic">torment me not,</hi> that thou do not restrain me from doing mischief somewhere else; though I know I am <hi type="italic">sentenced,</hi> yet let me not be <hi type="italic">sent</hi> to the chains of darkness, or hindered from going to and fro, to <hi type="italic">devour.</hi>" <div eID="gen24496" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24497" type="x-p"/> V. The account Christ took from this unclean spirit of his name. This we had not in Matthew. Christ asked him, <hi type="italic">What is thy name?</hi> Not but that Christ could call all the <hi type="italic">fallen</hi> stars, as well as the <hi type="italic">morning</hi> stars, by their names; but he demands this, that the standers by might be affected with the vast numbers and power of those malignant infernal spirits, as they had reason to be, when the answer was, <hi type="italic">My name is Legion, for we are many;</hi> a <hi type="italic">legion</hi> of soldiers among the Romans consisted, some say, of six thousand men, others of twelve thousand and five hundred; but the number of a legion with them, like that of a regiment with us, was not always the same. Now this intimates that the devils, the infernal powers, are, 1. <hi type="italic">Military</hi> powers; a legion is a number of soldiers in arms. The devils war against God and his glory, Christ and his gospel, men and their holiness and happiness. They are such as we are to <hi type="italic">resist</hi> and <hi type="italic">wrestle against,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eph.6.12">Eph. vi. 12</reference>. 2. That they are <hi type="italic">numerous;</hi> he <hi type="italic">owns,</hi> or rather he <hi type="italic">boasts—We are many;</hi> as if he hoped to be <hi type="italic">too many</hi> for Christ himself to deal with. What multitudes of apostate spirits were there, and all enemies to God and man; when here were a legion posted to keep garrison in one poor wretched creature against Christ! Many there are that rise up against us. 3. That they are <hi type="italic">unanimous;</hi> they are <hi type="italic">many</hi> devils, and yet but <hi type="italic">one legion</hi> engaged in the same wicked cause; and therefore that cavil of the Pharisees, which supposed Satan to cast out Satan, and to be divided against himself, was altogether groundless. It was not <hi type="italic">one</hi> of this legion that betrayed the rest, for they all said, as one man, <hi type="italic">What have I to do with thee?</hi> 4. That they are very <hi type="italic">powerful;</hi> Who can stand before a <hi type="italic">legion?</hi> We are not a match for our spiritual enemies, in our own strength; but <hi type="italic">in the Lord, and in the power of his might,</hi> we shall be able to <hi type="italic">stand against them,</hi> though there are legions of them. 5. That there is <hi type="italic">order</hi> among them, as there is in a <hi type="italic">legion;</hi> there are <hi type="italic">principalities, and powers, and rulers of the darkness of this world,</hi> which supposes that there are those of a lower rank; the <hi type="italic">devil</hi> and his angels; the <hi type="italic">dragon</hi> and his; the prince of the devils and his subjects: which makes those enemies the more formidable. <div eID="gen24497" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24498" type="x-p"/> VI. The request of this legion, that Christ would suffer them to go into a herd of swine that was <hi type="italic">feeding nigh unto the mountains</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mark.5.11">v. 11</reference>), those mountains which the demoniacs haunted, <reference osisRef="Mark.5.5">v. 5</reference>. Their request was, 1. That he <hi type="italic">would not send them away out of the country</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mark.5.10">v. 10</reference>); not only that he would not <hi type="italic">commit</hi> them, or <hi type="italic">confine</hi> them, to their infernal prison, and so <hi type="italic">torment them before the time;</hi> but that he would not <hi type="italic">banish</hi> them <hi type="italic">that country,</hi> as justly he might, because in this poor man they had been such a terror to it, and done so much mischief. They seem to have had a particular affection for <hi type="italic">that country;</hi> or, rather, a particular spite to it; and to have liberty to walk <hi type="italic">to and fro through</hi> the rest of <hi type="italic">the earth,</hi> will not serve (<reference osisRef="Job.1.7">Job i. 7</reference>), unless the <hi type="italic">range of those mountains</hi> be allowed them for their pasture, <reference osisRef="Job.39.8">Job xxxix. 8</reference>. But why would they abide in <hi type="italic">that country?</hi> Grotius saith, Because in <hi type="italic">that country</hi> there were many <hi type="italic">apostate Jews,</hi> who had thrown themselves out of the covenant of God, and had thereby given Satan power over them. And some suggest, that, having by experience got the knowledge of the dispositions and manners of the people of that country, they could the more effectually do them mischief by their temptations. 2. That he would suffer them to <hi type="italic">enter into the swine,</hi> by destroying which they hoped to do more mischief to the souls of all the people in the country, than they could by entering into the body of any particular person, which therefore they did not ask leave to do, for they knew Christ would not grant it. <div eID="gen24498" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24499" type="x-p"/> VII. The permission Christ gave them to enter into the swine, and the immediate destruction of the swine thereby; <hi type="italic">He gave them leave</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mark.5.13">v. 13</reference>), he did not forbid or restrain them, he let them do as they had a mind. Thus he would let the Gadarenes see what powerful spiteful enemies devils are, that they might thereby be induced to make him their Friend, who alone was able to control and conquer them, and had made it appear that he was so. Immediately the <hi type="italic">unclean spirits entered into the swine,</hi> which by the law were unclean creatures, and naturally love to <hi type="italic">wallow in the mire,</hi> the fittest place for them. Those that, like the swine, delight in <hi type="italic">the mire</hi> of sensual lusts, are fit habitations for Satan, and are, like Babylon, the <hi type="italic">hold of every foul spirit,</hi> and a <hi type="italic">cage of every unclean and hateful bird</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rev.18.2">Rev. xviii. 2</reference>), as pure souls are habitations of the Holy Spirit. The consequence of the devils entering into the swine, was, that they all <hi type="italic">ran mad</hi> presently, and ran headlong into the adjoining sea, where they were all drowned, to the number of <hi type="italic">two thousand.</hi> The man they possessed did only <hi type="italic">cut himself,</hi> for God had said, <hi type="italic">He is in your hands, only save his life.</hi> But thereby it appeared, that, if he had not been so restrained, the poor man would have <hi type="italic">drowned himself.</hi> See how much we are indebted to the providence of God, and the ministration of good angels, for our preservation from malignant spirits. <div eID="gen24499" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24500" type="x-p"/> VIII. The report of all this dispersed through the country immediately. They that <hi type="italic">fed the swine,</hi> hastened to the owners, to give an account of their charge, <reference osisRef="Mark.5.14">v. 14</reference>. This drew the people together, to see what was done: and, 1. When they saw how wonderfully the poor man was cured, they hence conceived a <hi type="italic">veneration for Christ,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.5.15">v. 15</reference>. They saw him that was <hi type="italic">possessed with the devil,</hi> and knew him well enough, by the same token that they had many a time been frightened at the sight of him; and were now as much surprised to see him <hi type="italic">sitting clothed and in his right mind;</hi> when Satan was cast out, he came to himself, and was his own man presently. Note, Those who are grave and sober, and live by rule and with consideration, thereby make it appear that by the power of Christ the devil's power is broken in their souls. The sight of this <hi type="italic">made them afraid;</hi> it astonished them, and forced them to own the power of Christ, and that he is <hi type="italic">worthy to be feared.</hi> But, 2. When they found that their swine were lost, they thence conceived a <hi type="italic">dislike of Christ,</hi> and wished to have rather his room than his company; they prayed him to <hi type="italic">depart out of their coasts,</hi> for they think not any good he can do them sufficient to make them amends for the loss of so many swine, fat swine, it may be, and ready for the market. Now the devils had what they would have; for by no handle do these evil spirits more effectually manage sinful souls than by that of the love of the world. They were afraid of some further punishment, if Christ should tarry among them, whereas, if they would but part with their sins, he had life and happiness for them; but, being loth to quit either their sins or their swine, they chose rather to abandon their Saviour. Thus <hi type="italic">they</hi> do, who, rather than let go a base lust, will throw away their interest in Christ, and their expectations from him. They should rather have argued, "If he has such a power as this over devils and all creatures, it is good having him our Friend; if the devils have leave to tarry <hi type="italic">in our country</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mark.5.10">v. 10</reference>), let us entreat <hi type="italic">him</hi> to tarry in it too, who alone can control them." But, instead of this, they wished him further off. Such strange misconstructions do carnal hearts make of the just judgments of God; instead of being by them driven to him as they ought, they set him at so much the greater distance; though he hath said, <hi type="italic">Provoke me not, and I will do you no hurt,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.25.6">Jer. xxv. 6</reference>. <div eID="gen24500" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24501" type="x-p"/> IX. An account of the conduct of the poor man after his deliverance. 1. He <hi type="italic">desired that he might go along with Christ</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mark.5.18">v. 18</reference>), perhaps for fear lest the evil spirit should again seize him; or, rather, that he might receive instruction from him, being unwilling to stay among those heathenish people that desired him to depart. Those that are freed from the evil spirit, cannot but covet acquaintance and fellowship with Christ. 2. Christ <hi type="italic">would not suffer him</hi> to go with him, lest it should savour of ostentation, and to let him know that he could both protect and instruct him at a distance. And besides, he had other work for him to do; he must go home to his friends, and tell them what <hi type="italic">great things the Lord had done for him,</hi> the Lord Jesus had done; that Christ might be honoured, and his neighbours and friends might be edified, and invited to believe in Christ. He must take particular notice rather of Christ's <hi type="italic">pity</hi> than of his <hi type="italic">power,</hi> for that is it which especially he glories in; he must tell them what <hi type="italic">compassion</hi> the Lord had had on him in his misery. 3. The man, in a transport of joy, proclaimed, all the country over, what <hi type="italic">great things Jesus had done for him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.5.20">v. 20</reference>. This is a debt we owe both to Christ and to our brethren, that he may be glorified and they edified. And see what was the effect of it; <hi type="italic">All men did marvel,</hi> but few went any further. Many that cannot but wonder at the works of Christ, yet do not, as they ought, <hi type="italic">wonder after him.</hi>

<div eID="gen24501" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Healing of the Bloody Issue.</title> <div sID="gen24502" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">21</hi> And when Jesus was passed over again by ship unto the other side, much people gathered unto him: and he was nigh unto the sea. <hi type="super">22</hi> And, behold, there cometh one of the rulers of the synagogue, Jairus by name; and when he saw him, he fell at his feet, <hi type="super">23</hi> And besought him greatly, saying, My little daughter lieth at the point of death: <hi type="italic">I pray thee,</hi> come and lay thy hands on her, that she may be healed; and she shall live. 24 And <hi type="italic">Jesus</hi> went with him; and much people followed him, and thronged him. <hi type="super">25</hi> And a certain woman, which had an issue of blood twelve years, <hi type="super">26</hi> And had suffered many things of many physicians, and had spent all that she had, and was nothing bettered, but rather grew worse, <hi type="super">27</hi> When she had heard of Jesus, came in the press behind, and touched his garment. <hi type="super">28</hi> For she said, If I may touch but his clothes, I shall be whole. 29 And straightway the fountain of her blood was dried up; and she felt in <hi type="italic">her</hi> body that she was healed of that plague. 30 And Jesus, immediately knowing in himself that virtue had gone out of him, turned him about in the press, and said, Who touched my clothes? <hi type="super">31</hi> And his disciples said unto him, Thou seest the multitude thronging thee, and sayest thou, Who touched me? <hi type="super">32</hi> And he looked round about to see her that had done this thing. <hi type="super">33</hi> But the woman fearing and trembling, knowing what was done in her, came and fell down before him, and told him all the truth. <hi type="super">34</hi> And he said unto her, Daughter, thy faith hath made thee whole; go in peace, and be whole of thy plague. <div eID="gen24502" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24503" type="x-p"/> The Gadarenes having desired Christ to leave their country, he did not stay to trouble them long, but presently went by water, as he came, back <hi type="italic">to the other side</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mark.5.21">v. 21</reference>), and there <hi type="italic">much people gathered to him.</hi> Note, If there be some that reject Christ, yet there are others that receive him, and bid him welcome. A despised gospel will <hi type="italic">cross the water,</hi> and go where it will have better entertainment. Now among the many that applied themselves to him, <div eID="gen24503" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24504" type="x-p"/> I. Here is one, that comes <hi type="italic">openly</hi> to <hi type="italic">beg</hi> a cure for a sick child; and it is no less a person than one of the <hi type="italic">rulers of the synagogue,</hi> one that presided in the synagogue-worship or, as some think, one of the judges of the consistory court, which was in every city, consisting of <hi type="italic">twenty-three.</hi> He was not named in Matthew, he is here, <hi type="italic">Jairus,</hi> or <hi type="italic">Jair,</hi> <reference osisRef="Judg.10.3">Judg. x. 3</reference>. He addressed himself to Christ, though a ruler, with great humility and reverence; <hi type="italic">When he saw him, he fell at his feet,</hi> giving honour to him as one really greater than he appeared to be; and with great importunity, he <hi type="italic">besought him greatly,</hi> as one in earnest, as one that not only valued the mercy he came for, but that knew he could obtain it no where else. The case is this, He has a <hi type="italic">little daughter,</hi> about twelve years old, the darling of the family, and she <hi type="italic">lies a dying;</hi> but he believes that if Christ will but come, and <hi type="italic">lay his hands upon her,</hi> she will return even from the gates of the grave. He said, at first, when he came, <hi type="italic">She lies a dying</hi> (so Mark); but afterward, upon fresh information sent him, he saith, <hi type="italic">She is even now dead</hi> (so Matthew); but he still prosecutes his suit; see <reference osisRef="Luke.8.42-Luke.8.49">Luke viii. 42-49</reference>. Christ readily agreed, and went with him, <reference osisRef="Mark.5.24">v. 24</reference>. <div eID="gen24504" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24505" type="x-p"/> II. Here is another, that comes <hi type="italic">clandestinely</hi> to <hi type="italic">steal</hi> a cure (if I may so say) for herself; and she got the relief she came for. This cure was wrought by <hi type="italic">the way,</hi> as he was going to raise the ruler's daughter, and was followed by a crowd. See how Christ improved his time, and lost none of the precious moments of it. Many of his discourses, and some of his miracles, are dates <hi type="italic">by the way-side;</hi> we should be doing good, not only when we <hi type="italic">sit in the house,</hi> but when we <hi type="italic">walk by the way,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.6.7">Deut. vi. 7</reference>. Now observe, <div eID="gen24505" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24506" type="x-p"/> 1. The piteous case of this poor woman. She had a constant <hi type="italic">issue of blood</hi> upon her, for <hi type="italic">twelve years,</hi> which had thrown her, no doubt, into great weakness, had embittered the comfort of her life, and threatened to be her death in a little time. She had had the best advice of physicians, that she could get, and had made use of the many medicines and methods they prescribed: as long as she had any thing to give them, they had kept her in hopes that they could cure her; but now that she had spent all she had among them, they gave her up as incurable. See here, (1.) That skin for skin, and all that a man has, will be give for life and health; she spent all she had upon physicians. (2.) It is ill with those patients whose physicians are their worst disease; who <hi type="italic">suffer</hi> by their physicians, instead of being relieved by them. (3.) Those that are not <hi type="italic">bettered</hi> by medicines, commonly <hi type="italic">grow worse,</hi> and the disease gets the more ground. (4.) It is usual with people not to apply themselves to Christ, till they have tried in vain all other helpers, and find them, as certainly they will, <hi type="italic">physicians of no value.</hi> And he will be found a <hi type="italic">sure refuge,</hi> even to those who make him their <hi type="italic">last refuge.</hi> <div eID="gen24506" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24507" type="x-p"/> 2. The strong faith that she had in the power of Christ to heal her; she said within herself, though it doth not appear that she was encouraged by any preceding instance to say it, <hi type="italic">If I may but touch his clothes, I shall be whole,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.5.28">v. 28</reference>. She believed that he cured, not as a prophet, by virtue <hi type="italic">derived</hi> from God, but as the Son of God, by a virtue <hi type="italic">inherent</hi> in himself. Her case was such as she could not in modesty tell him publicly, as others did their grievances, and therefore a private cure was what she wished for, and her faith was suited to her case. <div eID="gen24507" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24508" type="x-p"/> 3. The wonderful effect produced by it; <hi type="italic">She came in the</hi> crowd <hi type="italic">behind</hi> him, and with much ado got to <hi type="italic">touch his garment,</hi> and immediately she felt the cure wrought, <reference osisRef="Mark.5.29">v. 29</reference>. The flux of blood was <hi type="italic">dried up,</hi> and she felt herself perfectly well all over her, as well as ever she was in her life, in an instant; by this it appears that the cure was altogether miraculous; for those that in such cases are cured by natural means, recover their strength slowly and gradually, and not <hi type="italic">per saltum—all at once;</hi> but <hi type="italic">as for God, his work is perfect.</hi> Note, Those whom Christ heals of the disease of sin, that bloody issue, cannot but experience in themselves a universal change for the better. <div eID="gen24508" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24509" type="x-p"/> 4. Christ's enquiry after his concealed patient, and the encouragement he gave her, upon the discovery of her; Christ <hi type="italic">knew in himself that virtue had gone out of him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.5.30">v. 30</reference>. He knew it not by any deficiency of spirits, through the exhausting of this virtue, but rather by an agility of spirits, in the exerting of it, and the innate and inseparable pleasure he had in doing good. And being desirous to see his patient, he asked, not in displeasure, as one affronted, but in tenderness, as one concerned, <hi type="italic">Who touched my clothes?</hi> The disciples, not without a show of rudeness and indecency, almost ridiculed his question (<reference osisRef="Mark.5.31">v. 31</reference>); <hi type="italic">The multitudes throng thee, and sayest thou, Who touched me?</hi> As if it had been an improper question. Christ passed by the affront, and <hi type="italic">looks around</hi> to <hi type="italic">see her that had done this thing;</hi> not that he might <hi type="italic">blame</hi> her for her presumption, but that he might <hi type="italic">commend</hi> and <hi type="italic">encourage</hi> her faith, and by his own act and deed might <hi type="italic">warrant</hi> and <hi type="italic">confirm</hi> the cure, and <hi type="italic">ratify</hi> to her that which she had <hi type="italic">surreptitiously</hi> obtained. He needed not that any should inform him, for he had presently his eye upon her. Note, As secret acts of sin, so secret acts of faith, are known to the Lord Jesus, and are under his eye. If believers derive virtue from Christ ever so closely, he knows it, and is pleased with it. The poor woman, hereupon, presented herself to the Lord Jesus (<reference osisRef="Mark.5.33">v. 33</reference>), <hi type="italic">fearing and trembling,</hi> not knowing how he would take it. Note, Christ's patients are often trembling, when they have reason to be triumphing. She might have come boldly, <hi type="italic">knowing what was done in her;</hi> yet, <hi type="italic">knowing that,</hi> she <hi type="italic">fears</hi> and <hi type="italic">trembles.</hi> It was a <hi type="italic">surprise,</hi> and was not yet, as it should have been, a <hi type="italic">pleasing</hi> surprise. However, she <hi type="italic">fell down before him.</hi> Note, There is nothing better for those that fear and tremble, than to throw themselves at the feet of the Lord Jesus; to humble themselves before him, and refer themselves to him. And she <hi type="italic">told him all the truth.</hi> Note, We must not be ashamed to own the secret transactions between Christ and our souls; but, when called to it, mention, to his praise, and the encouragement of others, what he has done for our souls, and the experience we have had of <hi type="italic">healing virtue</hi> derived from him. And the consideration of this, that nothing can be hid from Christ, should engage us to confess all to him. See what an encouraging word he gave her (<reference osisRef="Mark.5.34">v. 34</reference>); <hi type="italic">Daughter, thy faith hath made thee whole.</hi> Note, Christ puts honour upon faith, because faith gives honour to Christ. But see how <hi type="italic">what is done by faith</hi> on earth is ratified in heaven; Christ saith, <hi type="italic">Be whole of thy disease.</hi> Note, If our faith sets the seal of its <hi type="italic">amen</hi> to the power and promise of God, saying, "So it is, and so let it be to me;" God's grace will set the seal of its <hi type="italic">amen</hi> to the prayers and hopes of faith, saying, "So be it, and so it shall be, to thee." And therefore, "<hi type="italic">Go in peace;</hi> be well satisfied that thy cure is honestly come by, is effectually wrought, and take the comfort of it." Note, They that by faith are healed of their spiritual diseases, have reason to <hi type="italic">go in peace.</hi>

<div eID="gen24509" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Daughter of Jairus Restored to Life.</title> <div sID="gen24510" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">35</hi> While he yet spake, there came from the ruler of the synagogue's <hi type="italic">house certain</hi> which said, Thy daughter is dead: why troublest thou the Master any further? <hi type="super">36</hi> As soon as Jesus heard the word that was spoken, he saith unto the ruler of the synagogue, Be not afraid, only believe. <hi type="super">37</hi> And he suffered no man to follow him, save Peter, and James, and John the brother of <reference osisRef="Jas.38">James. 38</reference> And he cometh to the house of the ruler of the synagogue, and seeth the tumult, and them that wept and wailed greatly. <hi type="super">39</hi> And when he was come in, he saith unto them, Why make ye this ado, and weep? the damsel is not dead, but sleepeth. <hi type="super">40</hi> And they laughed him to scorn. But when he had put them all out, he taketh the father and the mother of the damsel, and them that were with him, and entereth in where the damsel was lying. <hi type="super">41</hi> And he took the damsel by the hand, and said unto her, Talitha cumi; which is, being interpreted, Damsel, I say unto thee, arise. <hi type="super">42</hi> And straightway the damsel arose, and walked; for she was <hi type="italic">of the age</hi> of twelve years. And they were astonished with a great astonishment. <hi type="super">43</hi> And he charged them straitly that no man should know it; and commanded that something should be given her to eat. <div eID="gen24510" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24511" type="x-p"/> Diseases and deaths came into the world by the sin and disobedience of the first Adam; but by the grace of the second Adam both are conquered. Christ, having healed an incurable disease, here goes on to triumph over death, as in the beginning of the chapter he had triumphed over an outrageous devil. <div eID="gen24511" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24512" type="x-p"/> I. The melancholy news is brought to Jairus, that his <hi type="italic">daughter is dead,</hi> and therefore, if Christ be as other physicians, he comes too late. While there is life, there is hope, and room for the use of means; but when life is gone, it is past recall; <hi type="italic">Why troublest thou the Master any further?</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.5.35">v. 35</reference>. Ordinarily, the proper thought in this case, is, "The matter is determined, the will of God is done, and I submit, I acquiesce; <hi type="italic">The Lord gave, and the Lord hath taken away. While the child was alive, I fasted and wept; for I said, Who can tell but God will yet be gracious to me,</hi> and <hi type="italic">the child shall live?</hi> But <hi type="italic">now that it is dead, wherefore should I weep?</hi> I <hi type="italic">shall go to it, but it shall not return to me.</hi>" With such words we should <hi type="italic">quiet ourselves</hi> at such a time, that our souls may be <hi type="italic">as a child that is weaned from his mother:</hi> but there the case was extraordinary; the death of the child doth not, as usually, put an end to the narrative. <div eID="gen24512" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24513" type="x-p"/> II. Christ encourageth the afflicted father yet to hope that his application to Christ on the behalf of his child should not be in vain.
