Do ye not perceive, that whatsoever thing from without entereth into the man, <hi type="italic">it</hi> cannot defile him; <hi type="super">19</hi> Because it entereth not into his heart, but into the belly, and goeth out into the draught, purging all meats? <hi type="super">20</hi> And he said, That which cometh out of the man, that defileth the man. <hi type="super">21</hi> For from within, out of the heart of men, proceed evil thoughts, adulteries, fornications, murders, <hi type="super">22</hi> Thefts, covetousness, wickedness, deceit, lasciviousness, an evil eye, blasphemy, pride, foolishness: 23 All these evil things come from within, and defile the man. <div eID="gen24600" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24601" type="x-p"/> One great design of Christ's coming, was, to set aside the ceremonial law which God made, and to put an end to it; to make way for which he begins with the ceremonial law which men had made, and added to the law of God's making, and discharges his disciples from the obligation of that; which here he doth fully, upon occasion of the offence which the Pharisees took at them for the violation of it. These Pharisees and scribes with whom he had this argument, are said to <hi type="italic">come from Jerusalem</hi> down to Galilee—fourscore or a hundred miles, to pick quarrels with our Saviour there, where they supposed him to have the greatest interest and reputation. Had they come so far to be taught by him, their zeal had been commendable; but to come so far to oppose him, and to check the progress of his gospel, was great wickedness. It should seem that the scribes and Pharisees at Jerusalem pretended not only to a pre-eminence above, but to an authority over, the country clergy, and therefore kept up their visitations and sent inquisitors among them, as they did to John when he appeared, <reference osisRef="John.1.19">John i. 19</reference>. <div eID="gen24601" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24602" type="x-p"/> Now in this passage we may observe, <div eID="gen24602" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24603" type="x-p"/> I. What the tradition of the elders was: by it all were enjoined to <hi type="italic">wash their hands</hi> before meat; a cleanly custom, and no harm in it; and yet as such to be over-nice in it discovers too great a care about the body, which is <hi type="italic">of the earth;</hi> but they placed religion in it, and would not leave it indifferent, as it was in its own nature; people were at their liberty to do it or not to do it; but they interposed their authority, and commanded all to do it upon pain of excommunication; this they kept up as a <hi type="italic">tradition of the elders.</hi> The Papists pretend to a zeal for the authority and antiquity of the church and its canons, and talk much of councils and fathers, when really it is nothing but a zeal for their own wealth, interest, and dominion, that governs them; and so it was with the Pharisees. <div eID="gen24603" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24604" type="x-p"/> We have here an account of the practice of the Pharisees and <hi type="italic">all the Jews,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.7.3-Mark.7.4">v. 3, 4</reference>. 1. They <hi type="italic">washed their hands oft;</hi> they washed them, <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">pygme</hi></hi>; the critics find a great deal of work about that word, some making it to denote the frequency of their washing (so we render it); others think it signifies the pains they took in washing their hands; they washed with great care, they washed their hands <hi type="italic">to their wrists</hi> (so some); they lifted up their hands when they were wet, that the water might <hi type="italic">run to their elbows.</hi> 2. They particularly washed before they <hi type="italic">ate bread;</hi> that is, before they sat down to a solemn meal; for that was the rule; they must be sure to wash before they ate the bread on which they begged a blessing. "Whosoever eats the bread over which they recite the benediction, <hi type="italic">Blessed be he that produceth bread,</hi> must wash his hands before and after," or else he was thought to be defiled. 3. They took special care, when they came in <hi type="italic">from the markets,</hi> to wash their hands; from the <hi type="italic">judgment-halls,</hi> so some; it signifies any place of concourse where there were people of all sorts, and, it might be supposed, some heathen or Jews under a ceremonial pollution, by coming near to whom they thought themselves polluted; saying, <hi type="italic">Stand by thyself, come not near me, I am holier than thou,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.65.5">Isa. lxv. 5</reference>. They say, The rule of the rabbies was—That, if they washed their hands well in the morning, the first thing they did, it would serve for all day, provided they kept alone; but, if they went into company, they must not, at their return, either eat or pray till they had washed their hands; thus the elders gained a reputation among the people for sanctity, and thus they exercised and kept up an authority over their consciences. 4. They added to this the washing of <hi type="italic">cups,</hi> and <hi type="italic">pots,</hi> and <hi type="italic">brazen vessels,</hi> which they suspected had been made use of by heathens, or persons polluted; nay, and the very <hi type="italic">tables</hi> on which they ate their meat. There were many cases in which, by the law of Moses, washings were appointed; but they <hi type="italic">added</hi> to them, and enforced the observation of their own impositions as much as of God's institutions. <div eID="gen24604" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24605" type="x-p"/> II. What the practice of Christ's disciples was; they knew what the law was, and the common usage; but they understood themselves so well that they would not be bound up by it: they ate bread with <hi type="italic">defiled,</hi> that is, with <hi type="italic">unwashen, hands,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.7.2">v. 2</reference>. Eating with <hi type="italic">unwashen hands</hi> they called eating with <hi type="italic">defiled</hi> hands; thus men keep up their superstitious vanities by putting every thing into an ill name that contradicts them. The disciples knew (it is probable) that the Pharisees had their eye upon them, and yet they would not humour them by a compliance with their traditions, but took their liberty as at other times, and ate bread with <hi type="italic">unwashen</hi> hands; and herein <hi type="italic">their righteousness,</hi> however it might seem to come short, did really <hi type="italic">exceed, that of the scribes and Pharisees,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.5.20">Matt. v. 20</reference>. <div eID="gen24605" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24606" type="x-p"/> III. The offence which the Pharisees took at this; They <hi type="italic">found fault</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mark.7.2">v. 2</reference>); they censured them as profane, and men of a loose conversation, or rather as men that would not submit to the power of the church, to decree rites and ceremonies, and were therefore rebellious, factious, and schismatical. They brought a complaint against them to their Master, expecting that he should check them, and order them to conform; for they that are fond of their own inventions and impositions, are commonly ready to appeal to Christ, as if he should countenance them, and as if his authority must interpose for the enforcing of them, and the rebuking of those that do not comply with them. They do not ask, Why do not thy disciples <hi type="italic">do as we do?</hi> (Though that was what they meant, coveting to make themselves the standard.) But, Why do not they <hi type="italic">walk according to the tradition of the elders?</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.7.5">v. 5</reference>. To which it was easy to answer, that, by receiving the doctrine of Christ, they had <hi type="italic">more understanding than all their teachers,</hi> yea <hi type="italic">more than the ancients,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.119.99-Ps.119.100">Ps. cxix. 99, 100</reference>. <div eID="gen24606" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24607" type="x-p"/> IV. Christ's vindication of them; in which, <div eID="gen24607" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24608" type="x-p"/> 1. He argues with the Pharisees concerning the authority by which this ceremony was imposed; and <hi type="italic">they</hi> were the fittest to be discoursed with concerning that, who were the great sticklers for it: but this he did not speak of publicly to the multitude (as appears by his <hi type="italic">calling the people</hi> to him, <reference osisRef="Mark.7.14">v. 14</reference>) lest he should have seemed to stir them up to faction and discontent at their governors; but addressed it as a reproof to the persons concerned: for the rule is, <hi type="italic">Suum cuique—Let every one have his own.</hi> <div eID="gen24608" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24609" type="x-p"/> (1.) He reproves them for their hypocrisy in pretending to honour God, when really they had no such design in their religious observances (<reference osisRef="Mark.7.6-Mark.7.7">v. 6, 7</reference>); <hi type="italic">They honour me with their lips,</hi> they pretend it is for the glory of God that they impose those things, to distinguish themselves from the heathen; but really <hi type="italic">their heart is far from God,</hi> and is governed by nothing but ambition and covetousness. They would be thought hereby to appropriate themselves as a holy people to the Lord their God, when really it is the furthest thing in their thought. They rested in the outside of all their religious exercises, and their hearts were not right with God in them, and this was worshipping God in vain; for neither was he pleased with such sham-devotions, nor were they profited by them. <div eID="gen24609" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24610" type="x-p"/> (2.) He reproves them for placing religion in the inventions and injunctions of their elders and rulers; They <hi type="italic">taught for doctrines the traditions of men.</hi> When they should have been pressing upon people the great principles of religion, they were enforcing the canons of their church, and judged of people's being Jews or no, according as they did, or did not, conform to them, without any consideration had, whether they lived in obedience to God's laws or no. It was true, there were <hi type="italic">divers washings</hi> imposed by the law of Moses (<reference osisRef="Heb.9.10">Heb. ix. 10</reference>), which were intended to signify that inward purification of the heart from worldly fleshly lusts, which God requires as absolutely necessary to our communion with him; but, instead of providing the substance, they presumptuously added to the ceremony, and were very nice in <hi type="italic">washing pots and cups;</hi> and observe, he adds, <hi type="italic">Many other such like things ye do,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.7.8">v. 8</reference>. Note, Superstition is an endless thing. If one human invention and institution be admitted, though seemingly ever so innocent, as this of washing hands, <hi type="italic">behold, a troop comes,</hi> a door is opened for <hi type="italic">many other such things.</hi> <div eID="gen24610" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24611" type="x-p"/> (3.) He reproves them for <hi type="italic">laying aside the commandment of God,</hi> and overlooking that, not urging that in their preaching, and in their discipline conniving at the violation of that, as if that were no longer of force, <reference osisRef="Mark.7.8">v. 8</reference>. Note, It is the mischief of impositions, that too often they who are zealous for them, have little zeal for the essential duties of religion, but can contentedly see them laid aside. Nay, they <hi type="italic">rejected the commandment of God,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.7.9">v. 9</reference>. <hi type="italic">He do fairly disannul and abolish the commandment of God;</hi> and even <hi type="italic">by</hi> your traditions <hi type="italic">make the word of God of no effect,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.7.13">v. 13</reference>. God's statutes shall not only <hi type="italic">lie forgotten,</hi> as antiquated obsolete laws, but they shall, in effect, <hi type="italic">stand repealed,</hi> that their traditions may take place. They were entrusted to expound the law, and to enforce it; and, under pretence of using that power, they violated the law, and dissolved the bonds of it; destroying the text with the comment. <div eID="gen24611" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24612" type="x-p"/> This he gives them a particular instance of, and a flagrant one—God commanded children to <hi type="italic">honour their parents,</hi> not only by the law of Moses, but, antecedent to that, by the law of nature; and whoso <hi type="italic">revileth,</hi> or <hi type="italic">speaketh evil of,</hi> father or mother, <hi type="italic">let him die the death,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.7.10">v. 10</reference>. Hence it is easy to infer, that it is the duty of children, if their parents be poor, to relieve them, according to their ability; and if those children are worthy to die, that curse their parents, much more those that starve them. But if a man will but conform himself in all points to the tradition of the elders, they will find him out an expedient by which he may be discharged from this obligation, <reference osisRef="Mark.7.11">v. 11</reference>. If his parents be in want and he has wherewithal to help them, but has no mind to do it, let him swear by the <hi type="italic">Corban,</hi> that is, by the <hi type="italic">gold of the temple,</hi> and the <hi type="italic">gift upon the altar,</hi> that his parents shall not be profited by him, that he will not relieve them; and, if they ask any thing of him, let him tell them this, and it is enough; as if by the obligation of this wicked vow he had discharged himself from the obligation of God's holy law; thus Dr. Hammond understands it: and it is said to be an ancient canon of the rabbin, That vows take place in things commanded by the law, as well as in things indifferent; so that, if a man make a vow which cannot be ratified without breaking a commandment, the vow must be ratified, and the commandment violated; so Dr. Whitby. Such doctrine as this the Papists teach, discharging children from all obligation to their parents by their monastic vows, and their entrance into religion, as they call it. He concludes, <hi type="italic">Any many such like things do ye.</hi> Where will men stop, when once they have made the word of God give way to their tradition? These eager imposers of such ceremonies, at first only <hi type="italic">made light</hi> of God's commandments <hi type="italic">in comparison</hi> with their traditions, but afterward <hi type="italic">made void</hi> God's commandments, if they stood <hi type="italic">in competition</hi> with them. All this, in effect, Isaiah prophesied of them; what he said of the hypocrites of his own day, was applicable to the scribes and Pharisees, <reference osisRef="Mark.7.6">v. 6</reference>. Note, When we see, and complain of, the wickedness of the present times, yet we do not <hi type="italic">enquire wisely of that matter,</hi> if we say that all <hi type="italic">the former days were better than these,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.10">Eccl. vii. 10</reference>. The worst of hypocrites and evil doers have had their predecessors. <div eID="gen24612" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24613" type="x-p"/> 2. He instructs the people concerning the principles upon which this ceremony was grounded. It was requisite that this part of his discourse should be public, for it related to daily practice, and was designed to rectify a great mistake which the people were led into by their elders; he therefore <hi type="italic">called the people unto him</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mark.7.14">v. 14</reference>), and bid them <hi type="italic">hear and understand.</hi> Note, It is not enough for the common people to <hi type="italic">hear,</hi> but they must <hi type="italic">understand</hi> what they hear. When Christ would run down the tradition of the Pharisees about washing before meat, he strikes at the opinion which was the root of it. Note, Corrupt customs are best cured by rectifying corrupt notions. <div eID="gen24613" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24614" type="x-p"/> Now that which he goes about to set them right in, is, what the pollution is, which we are in danger of being damaged by, <reference osisRef="Mark.7.15">v. 15</reference>. (1.) Not by the <hi type="italic">meat we eat,</hi> though it be eaten with unwashen hands; that is but from without, and goes through a man. But, (2.) It is by the breaking out of the corruption that is in our hearts; the mind and conscience are defiled, guilt is contracted, and we become odious in the sight of God by that which <hi type="italic">comes out</hi> of us; our wicked thoughts and affections, words and actions, these defile us, and these only. Our care must therefore be, to <hi type="italic">wash our heart from wickedness.</hi> <div eID="gen24614" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24615" type="x-p"/> 3. He gives his disciples, in private, an explication of the instructions he gave the people. They <hi type="italic">asked</hi> him, when they had him by himself, <hi type="italic">concerning the parable</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mark.7.17">v. 17</reference>); for to them, it seems, it was a parable. Now, in answer to their enquiry, (1.) He reproves their dulness; "<hi type="italic">Are ye so without understanding also?</hi> Are ye dull <hi type="italic">also,</hi> as dull as the people that <hi type="italic">cannot</hi> understand, as dull as the Pharisees that <hi type="italic">will not?</hi> Are ye <hi type="italic">so</hi> dull?" He doth not expect they should understand every thing; "But are ye so weak as not to understand <hi type="italic">this?</hi>" (2.) He explains this truth to them, that they might <hi type="italic">perceive</hi> it, and then they would <hi type="italic">believe</hi> it, for it carried its own evidence along with it. Some truths prove themselves, if they be but rightly explained and apprehended. If we understand the spiritual nature of God and of his law, and what it is that is offensive to him, and disfits us for communion with him, we shall soon perceive, [1.] That that which we eat and drink cannot defile us, so as to call for any religious washing; it <hi type="italic">goes into the stomach,</hi> and passes the several digestions and secretions that nature has appointed, and what there may be in it that is defiling is voided and gone; <hi type="italic">meats for the belly, and the belly for meats,</hi> but <hi type="italic">God shall destroy both it and them.</hi> But, [2.] It is that which <hi type="italic">comes out from</hi> the heart, the corrupt heart, that defiles us. As by the ceremonial law, whatsoever (almost) comes out of a man, defiles him (<reference osisRef="Lev.15.2">Lev. xv. 2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.23.13">Deut. xxiii. 13</reference>), so what comes out from the <hi type="italic">mind</hi> of a man is that which defiles him before God, and calls for a religious washing (<reference osisRef="Mark.7.21">v. 21</reference>); <hi type="italic">From within, out of the heart of men,</hi> which they boast of the <hi type="italic">goodness</hi> of, and think is the best part of them, thence that which defiles proceeds, thence comes all the mischief. As a corrupt fountain sends forth corrupt streams, so doth a corrupt heart send forth corrupt reasonings, corrupt appetites and passions, and all those wicked words and actions which are produced by them. Divers particulars are specified, as in Matthew; we had one there, which is not here, and that is, <hi type="italic">false witness-bearing;</hi> but <hi type="italic">seven</hi> are mentioned here, to be added to those we had there. <hi type="italic">First, Covetousnesses,</hi> for it is plural; <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">pleonexiai</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">immoderate desires</hi> of more of the wealth of the world, and the gratifications of sense, and still more, still crying, <hi type="italic">Give, give.</hi> Hence we read of a <hi type="italic">heart exercised with covetous practices,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Pet.2.14">2 Pet. ii. 14</reference>. <hi type="italic">Secondly, Wickedness</hi>—<hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">poneriai</hi></hi>; malice, hatred, and ill-will, a desire to do mischief, and a delight in mischief done. <hi type="italic">Thirdly, Deceit;</hi> which is wickedness covered and disguised, that it may be the more securely and effectually committed. <hi type="italic">Fourthly, Lasciviousness;</hi> that filthiness and foolish talking which the apostle condemns; the eye full of adultery, and all wanton dalliances. <hi type="italic">Fifthly,</hi> The <hi type="italic">evil eye;</hi> the envious eye, and the covetous eye, grudging others the good we give them, or do for them (<reference osisRef="Prov.23.6">Prov. xxiii. 6</reference>), or grieving at the good they do or enjoy. <hi type="italic">Sixthly, Pride</hi>—<hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">hyperephania</hi></hi>; exalting ourselves in our own conceit above others, and looking down with scorn and contempt upon others. <hi type="italic">Seventhly, Foolishness</hi>—<hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">aphrosyne</hi></hi>; imprudence, inconsideration; some understand it especially of vainglorious boasting, which St. Paul calls <hi type="italic">foolishness</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Cor.11.1">2 Cor. xi. 1</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.11.19">19</reference>), because it is here joined with <hi type="italic">pride;</hi> I rather take it for that rashness in speaking and acting, which is the cause of so much evil. <hi type="italic">Ill-thinking</hi> is put first, as that which is the spring of all our <hi type="italic">com</hi>missions, and <hi type="italic">unthinking</hi> put last, as that which is the spring of all our <hi type="italic">o</hi>missions. Of all these he concludes (<reference osisRef="Mark.7.23">v. 23</reference>), 1. That they <hi type="italic">come from within,</hi> from the corrupt nature, the carnal mind, the evil treasure in the heart; justly is it said, that the <hi type="italic">inward part is very wickedness,</hi> it must needs be so, when all this comes from within. 2. That they <hi type="italic">defile the man;</hi> they render a man unfit for communion with God, they bring a stain upon the conscience; and, if not mortified and rooted out, will shut men out of the new Jerusalem, into which no <hi type="italic">unclean thing shall enter.</hi>

<div eID="gen24615" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Syrophenician Woman.</title> <div sID="gen24616" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">24</hi> And from thence he arose, and went into the borders of Tyre and Sidon, and entered into a house, and would have no man know <hi type="italic">it:</hi> but he could not be hid. <hi type="super">25</hi> For a <hi type="italic">certain</hi> woman, whose young daughter had an unclean spirit, heard of him, and came and fell at his feet: <hi type="super">26</hi> The woman was a Greek, a Syrophenician by nation; and she besought him that he would cast forth the devil out of her daughter. <hi type="super">27</hi> But Jesus said unto her, Let the children first be filled: for it is not meet to take the children's bread, and to cast <hi type="italic">it</hi> unto the dogs. <hi type="super">28</hi> And she answered and said unto him, Yes, Lord: yet the dogs under the table eat of the children's crumbs. <hi type="super">29</hi> And he said unto her, For this saying go thy way; the devil is gone out of thy daughter. <hi type="super">30</hi> And when she was come to her house, she found the devil gone out, and her daughter laid upon the bed. <div eID="gen24616" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24617" type="x-p"/> See here, I. How <hi type="italic">humbly</hi> Christ was pleased to <hi type="italic">conceal himself.</hi> Never man was so cried up as he was in Galilee, and therefore, to teach us, though not to decline any opportunity of doing good, yet not to be fond of popular applause, he arose from thence, and <hi type="italic">went into the borders</hi> of Tyre and Sidon, where he was little known; and there he entered, not into a synagogue, or place of concourse, but <hi type="italic">into a</hi> private <hi type="italic">house,</hi> and he <hi type="italic">would have no man to know it;</hi> because it was foretold concerning him, <hi type="italic">He shall not strive nor cry, neither shall his voice be heard in the streets.</hi> Not but that he was willing to preach and heal here as well as in other places, but for this he would be sought unto. Note, As there is a time to <hi type="italic">appear,</hi> so there is a time to <hi type="italic">retire.</hi> Or, he would not be known, because he was upon the borders of Tyre and Sidon, among Gentiles, to whom he would not be so forward to show himself as to the tribes of Israel, whose glory he was to be. <div eID="gen24617" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24618" type="x-p"/> II. How <hi type="italic">graciously</hi> he was pleased to <hi type="italic">manifest himself,</hi> notwithstanding. Though he would not carry a harvest of miraculous cures into those parts, yet, it should seem, he came on purpose to drop a handful, to let fall this one which we have here an account of. <hi type="italic">He could not be hid;</hi> for, though a candle may be put under a bushel, the sun cannot. Christ was too well known to be long <hi type="italic">incognito—hid,</hi> any where; the oil of gladness which he was anointed with, like ointment of the right hand, would betray itself, and fill the house with its odours. Those that had only heard his fame, could not converse with him, but they would soon say, "This must be Jesus." Now observe, <div eID="gen24618" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24619" type="x-p"/> 1. The application made to him by a poor woman in distress and trouble. She was a Gentile, a Greek, <hi type="italic">a stranger to the commonwealth of Israel, an alien to the covenant of promise;</hi> she was by extraction a Syrophenician, and not in any degree proselyted to the Jewish religion; she had a <hi type="italic">daughter,</hi> a <hi type="italic">young</hi> daughter, that was possessed <hi type="italic">with the devil.</hi> How many and grievous are the calamities that young children are subject to! Her address was, (1.) Very humble, pressing, and importunate; <hi type="italic">She heard of him,</hi> and <hi type="italic">came, and fell at his feet.</hi> Note, Those that would obtain mercy from Christ, must throw themselves at his feet; must refer themselves to him, humble themselves before him, and give up themselves to be ruled by him. Christ never put any from him, that fell at his feet, which a poor trembling soul may do, that has not boldness and confidence to throw itself into his arms. (2.) It was very particular; she tells him what she wanted. Christ gave poor supplicants leave to be thus free with him; she besought him that he would <hi type="italic">cast forth the devil out of her daughter,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.7.26">v. 26</reference>. Note, The greatest blessing we can ask of Christ for our children is, that he would break the power of Satan, that is, the power of sin, in their souls; and particularly, that he would cast forth the <hi type="italic">unclean spirit,</hi> that they may be temples of the Holy Ghost, and he may dwell in them. <div eID="gen24619" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24620" type="x-p"/> 2. The discouragement he gave to this address (<reference osisRef="Mark.7.27">v. 27</reference>); He said unto her, "<hi type="italic">Let the children first be filled;</hi> let the Jews have all the miracles wrought for them, that they have occasion for, who are in a particular manner God's chosen people; and let not that which was intended for them, be thrown to those who are not of God's family, and who have not that knowledge of him, and interest in him, which they have, and who are as <hi type="italic">dogs in comparison of them,</hi> vile and profane, and who are as <hi type="italic">dogs to them,</hi> snarling at them, spiteful toward them, and ready to worry them." Note, Where Christ knows the faith of poor supplicants to be strong, he sometimes delights to try it, and put it to the stretch. But his saying, <hi type="italic">Let the children first be filled,</hi> intimates that there was mercy in reserve for the Gentiles, and not far off; for the Jews began already to be surfeited with the gospel of Christ, and some of them had desired him to <hi type="italic">depart out of their coasts.</hi> The children begin to play with their meat, and their leavings, their loathings, would be a feast for the Gentiles. The apostles went by this rule, <hi type="italic">Let the children first be filled,</hi> let the Jews have the first offer; and if their full souls loathe this honeycomb, <hi type="italic">Lo, we turn to the Gentiles!</hi> <div eID="gen24620" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24621" type="x-p"/> 3. The turn she gave to this word of Christ, which made against her, and her improvement of it, to make for her, <reference osisRef="Mark.7.28">v. 28</reference>. She said, "<hi type="italic">Yes, Lord,</hi> I own it is true that the <hi type="italic">children's bread</hi> ought not to be cast to the dogs; but they were never denied the <hi type="italic">crumbs</hi> of that bread, nay it belongs to them, and they are allowed a place <hi type="italic">under the table,</hi> that they may be ready to receive them. I ask not for a <hi type="italic">loaf,</hi> no, nor for a <hi type="italic">morsel,</hi> only for a <hi type="italic">crumb;</hi> do not refuse me that." This she speaks, not as undervaluing the mercy, or making light of it in itself, but magnifying the abundance or miraculous cures with which she heard the Jews were feasted, in comparison with which a single cure was but as a crumb. Gentiles do not come in crowds, as the Jews do; <hi type="italic">I come alone.</hi> Perhaps she had heard of Christ's feeding five thousand lately at once, after which, even when they had gathered up the fragments, there could not but be some crumbs left for the dogs. <div eID="gen24621" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24622" type="x-p"/> 4. The grant Christ thereupon made of her request. Is she thus humble, thus earnest? For <hi type="italic">this saying, Go thy way,</hi> thou shalt have what thou camest for, <hi type="italic">the devil is gone out of thy daughter,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.7.29">v. 29</reference>. This encourages us to <hi type="italic">pray</hi> and not to <hi type="italic">faint,</hi> to continue instant in prayer, not doubting but to prevail at last; the vision at the end shall <hi type="italic">speak, and not lie.</hi> Christ's saying that is <hi type="italic">was done,</hi> did it effectually, as at other times his saying, <hi type="italic">Let it be done;</hi> for (<reference osisRef="Mark.7.30">v. 30</reference>) she <hi type="italic">came to her house,</hi> depending upon the word of Christ, that her daughter was healed, and so she <hi type="italic">found it,</hi> the <hi type="italic">devil was gone out.</hi> Note, Christ can conquer Satan at a distance; and it was not only when the demoniacs <hi type="italic">saw him,</hi> that they yielded to his power (as <reference osisRef="Mark.3.11">ch. iii. 11</reference>), but when they saw him not, for the Spirit of the Lord is not <hi type="italic">bound,</hi> nor <hi type="italic">bounded.</hi> She found her daughter not in any toss or agitation, but very quietly <hi type="italic">laid on the bed,</hi> and reposing herself; waiting for her mother's return, to rejoice with her, that she was so <hi type="italic">finely well.</hi>

<div eID="gen24622" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Cure of a Deaf and Dumb Person.</title> <div sID="gen24623" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">31</hi> And again, departing from the coasts of Tyre and Sidon, he came unto the sea of Galilee, through the midst of the coasts of Decapolis. <hi type="super">32</hi> And they bring unto him one that was deaf, and had an impediment in his speech; and they beseech him to put his hand upon him. <hi type="super">33</hi> And he took him aside from the multitude, and put his fingers into his ears, and he spit, and touched his tongue; <hi type="super">34</hi> And looking up to heaven, he sighed, and saith unto him, Ephphatha, that is, Be opened. <hi type="super">35</hi> And straightway his ears were opened, and the string of his tongue was loosed, and he spake plain. <hi type="super">36</hi> And he charged them that they should tell no man: but the more he charged them, so much the more a great deal they published <hi type="italic">it;</hi> <hi type="super">37</hi> And were beyond measure astonished, saying, He hath done all things well: he maketh both the deaf to hear, and the dumb to speak. <div eID="gen24623" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24624" type="x-p"/> Our Lord Jesus seldom staid long in a place, for he knew where his work lay, and attended the changes of it. When he had cured the woman of Canaan's daughter, he had done what he had to do in that place, and therefore presently left those parts, and returned <hi type="italic">to the sea of Galilee,</hi> whereabout his usual residence was; yet he did not come directly thither, but fetched a compass <hi type="italic">through the midst of the coasts of Decapolis,</hi> which lay mostly on the other side Jordan; such long walks did our Lord Jesus take, when he <hi type="italic">went about doing good.</hi> <div eID="gen24624" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24625" type="x-p"/> Now here we have the story of a cure that Christ wrought, which is not recorded by any other of the evangelists; it is of one that was <hi type="italic">deaf</hi> and <hi type="italic">dumb.</hi> <div eID="gen24625" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24626" type="x-p"/> I. His case was sad, <reference osisRef="Mark.7.32">v. 32</reference>. There were those that brought to him one that was <hi type="italic">deaf;</hi> some think, born deaf, and then he must be dumb of course; others think that by some distemper or disaster he was become deaf, or, at least, thick of hearing; and he had an <hi type="italic">impediment in his speech.</hi> He was <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">mogilalos</hi></hi>; some think that he was quite dumb; others, that he could not speak but with great difficulty to himself, and so as scarcely to be understood by those that heard him. He was <hi type="italic">tongue-tied,</hi> so that he was perfectly unfit for conversation, and deprived both of the pleasure and of the profit of it; he had not the satisfaction either of hearing other people talk, or of telling his own mind. Let us take occasion from hence to give thanks to God for preserving to us the sense of hearing, especially that we may be capable of hearing the word of God; and the faculty of speech, especially that we may be capable of speaking God's praises; and let us look with compassion upon those that are deaf or dumb, and treat them with great tenderness. They that brought this poor man to Christ, besought him that he would <hi type="italic">put his hand upon him,</hi> as the prophets did upon those whom they <hi type="italic">blessed</hi> in the name of the Lord. It is not said, They besought him to <hi type="italic">cure him,</hi> but to <hi type="italic">put his hand upon him,</hi> to take cognizance of his case, and put forth his power to do to him as he pleased. <div eID="gen24626" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24627" type="x-p"/> II. His cure was solemn, and some of the circumstances of it were singular. <div eID="gen24627" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24628" type="x-p"/> 1. Christ <hi type="italic">took him aside from the multitude,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.7.33">v. 33</reference>. Ordinarily, he wrought his miracles publicly before all the people, to show that they would bear the strictest scrutiny and inspection; but this he did privately, to show that he did not seek his own glory, and to teach us to avoid every thing that savours of ostentation. Let us learn of Christ to be humble, and to do good where no eye sees, but his that is <hi type="italic">all eye.</hi> <div eID="gen24628" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24629" type="x-p"/> 2. He used more significant actions, in the doing of this cure, than usual. (1.) He <hi type="italic">put his fingers into his ears,</hi> as if he would <hi type="italic">syringe</hi> them, and fetch out that which stopped them up. (2.) He spit upon his own finger, and then <hi type="italic">touched his tongue,</hi> as if he would moisten his mouth, and so loosen that with which his tongue was tied; these were no causes that could in the least contribute to his cure, but only signs of the exerting of that power which Christ had in himself to cure him, for the encouraging of his faith, and theirs that brought him. The application was all from himself, it was his own <hi type="italic">fingers</hi> that he put into his ears, and his own <hi type="italic">spittle</hi> that he put upon his tongue; for he alone heals. <div eID="gen24629" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24630" type="x-p"/> 3. He <hi type="italic">looked up to heaven,</hi> to give his Father the praise of what he did; for he sought his praise, and did his will, and, as Mediator, acted in dependence on him, and with an eye to him. Thus he signified that it was by a divine power, a power her had as the Lord from heaven, and brought with him thence, that he did this; for the <hi type="italic">hearing ear</hi> and the <hi type="italic">seeing eye</hi> the <hi type="italic">Lord has made,</hi> and can remake even <hi type="italic">both of them.</hi> He also hereby directed his patient who could <hi type="italic">see,</hi> though he could not <hi type="italic">hear,</hi> to look up to heaven for relief. Moses with his stammering tongue is directed to look that way (<reference osisRef="Exod.4.11">Exod. iv. 11</reference>); <hi type="italic">Who hath made man's mouth? Or who maketh the dumb or deaf, or the seeing or the blind? Have not I the Lord?</hi> <div eID="gen24630" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24631" type="x-p"/> 4. He sighed; not as if he found any difficulty in working this miracle, or obtaining power to do it from his father; but thus he expressed his pity for the miseries of human life, and his sympathy with the afflicted in their afflictions, as one that was himself <hi type="italic">touched with the feeling of their infirmities.</hi> And as to this man, he <hi type="italic">sighed,</hi> not because he was loth to do him this kindness, or did it with reluctancy; but because of the many temptations which he would be exposed to, and the sins he would be in danger of, the tongue-sins, after the restoring of his speech to him, which before he was free from. He had better be <hi type="italic">tongue-tied</hi> still, unless he have grace to <hi type="italic">keep his mouth as with a bridle,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.39.1">Ps. xxxix. 1</reference>. <div eID="gen24631" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24632" type="x-p"/> 5. He said, <hi type="italic">Ephphatha;</hi> that is, <hi type="italic">Be opened.</hi> This was nothing that looked like <hi type="italic">spell</hi> or <hi type="italic">charm,</hi> such as they used, who had <hi type="italic">familiar spirits,</hi> who <hi type="italic">peeped and muttered,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.8.19">Isa. viii. 19</reference>. Christ speaks as one having authority, and power went along with the word. <hi type="italic">Be opened,</hi> served both parts of the cure; "Let the <hi type="italic">ears</hi> be <hi type="italic">opened,</hi> let the <hi type="italic">lips</hi> be <hi type="italic">opened,</hi> let him hear and speak freely, and let the restraint be taken off;" and the effect was answerable (<reference osisRef="Mark.7.35">v. 35</reference>); <hi type="italic">Straightway his ears were opened, and the string of his tongue was loosed,</hi> and all was well: and happy he who, as soon as he had his hearing and speech, had the blessed Jesus so near him to converse with. <div eID="gen24632" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24633" type="x-p"/> Now this cure was, (1.) A proof of Christ's being the Messiah; for it was foretold that by his power the <hi type="italic">ears of the deaf should be unstopped,</hi> and the <hi type="italic">tongue of the dumb</hi> should be made to <hi type="italic">sing,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.35.5-Isa.35.6">Isa. xxxv. 5, 6</reference>. (2.) It was a specimen of the operations of his gospel upon the minds of men. The great command of the gospel, and grace of Christ to poor sinners, is <hi type="italic">Ephphatha-Be opened.</hi> Grotius applies it thus, that the internal impediments of the mind are removed by the Spirit of Christ, as those bodily impediments were by the word of his power. He <hi type="italic">opens the heart,</hi> as he did Lydia's, and thereby opens the ear to receive the word of God, and opens the mouth in prayer and praises. <div eID="gen24633" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24634" type="x-p"/> 6. He ordered it to be kept very private, but it was made very public (1.) It was his humility, that he <hi type="italic">charged them they should tell no man,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.7.36">v. 36</reference>. Most men will proclaim their own goodness, or, at least, desire that others should proclaim it; but Christ, though he was himself in no danger of being puffed up with it, knowing that we are, would thus set us an example of self-denial, as in other things, so especially in praise and applause. We should take pleasure in doing good, but not in its being known. (2.) It was their zeal, that, though he charged them to say nothing of it, yet they published it, before Christ would have had it published. But they meant honestly, and therefore it is to be reckoned rather an act of indiscretion than an act of disobedience, <reference osisRef="Mark.7.36">v. 36</reference>. But they that told it, and they that heard it, were <hi type="italic">beyond measure astonished,</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">hyperperissos</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">more than above measure;</hi> they were exceedingly affected with it, and this was said by every body, it was the common verdict, <hi type="italic">He hath done all things well</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mark.7.37">v. 37</reference>); whereas there were those that hated and persecuted him as an <hi type="italic">evil-doer,</hi> they are ready to witness for him, not only that he has done no evil, but that he has done a great deal of good, and has done it well, modestly and humbly, and very devoutly, and all gratis, <hi type="italic">without money and without price,</hi> which added much to the lustre of his good works. He <hi type="italic">maketh both the deaf to hear, and the dumb to speak;</hi> and that is <hi type="italic">well,</hi> it is well for them, it is well for their relations, to whom they had been a burthen; and therefore <hi type="italic">they</hi> are inexcusable who speak ill of him.  <chapter eID="Mark.7"/> <div eID="gen24634" type="x-p"/>

<div eID="gen24637" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen24636" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Christ Feeds the Four Thousand.</title> <div sID="gen24638" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> In those days the multitude being very great, and having nothing to eat, Jesus called his disciples <hi type="italic">unto him,</hi> and saith unto them, <hi type="super">2</hi> I have compassion on the multitude, because they have now been with me three days, and have nothing to eat: <hi type="super">3</hi> And if I send them away fasting to their own houses, they will faint by the way: for divers of them came from far. <hi type="super">4</hi> And his disciples answered him, From whence can a man satisfy these <hi type="italic">men</hi> with bread here in the wilderness? 5 And he asked them, How many loaves have ye? And they said, Seven. <hi type="super">6</hi> And he commanded the people to sit down on the ground: and he took the seven loaves, and gave thanks, and brake, and gave to his disciples to set before <hi type="italic">them;</hi> and they did set <hi type="italic">them</hi> before the people. <hi type="super">7</hi> And they had a few small fishes: and he blessed, and commanded to set them also before <hi type="italic">them.</hi> <hi type="super">8</hi> So they did eat, and were filled: and they took up of the broken <hi type="italic">meat</hi> that was left seven baskets. 9 And they that had eaten were about four thousand: and he sent them away. <div eID="gen24638" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24639" type="x-p"/> We had the story of a miracle very like this before, in this gospel (<reference osisRef="Mark.6.35">ch. vi. 35</reference>), and of this same miracle (<reference osisRef="Matt.15.32">Matt. xv. 32</reference>), and here is little or no addition or alternation as to the circumstances. Yet observe, <div eID="gen24639" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24640" type="x-p"/> 1. That our Lord Jesus was greatly followed; <hi type="italic">The multitude was very great</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mark.8.1">v. 1</reference>); notwithstanding the wicked arts of the scribes and Pharisees to blemish him, and to blast his interest, the common people, who had more honesty, and therefore more true wisdom, than their leaders, kept up their high thoughts of him. We may suppose that this multitude were generally of the meaner sort of people, with such Christ conversed, and was familiar; for thus he humbled himself, and made himself of no reputation, and thus encouraged the meanest to come to him for life and grace. <div eID="gen24640" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24641" type="x-p"/> 2. Those that followed him, underwent a great deal of difficulty in following him; <hi type="italic">They were with him three days, and had nothing to eat,</hi> that was hard service. Never let the Pharisee say, that <hi type="italic">Christ's disciples fast not.</hi> There were those, probably, that brought some food with them from home; but by this time it was all spent, and they had a great way home; and yet they <hi type="italic">continued</hi> with Christ, and did not speak of leaving him till he spoke of dismissing them. Note, True zeal makes nothing of hardships in the way of duty. They that have a full feast for their souls may be content with slender provision for their bodies. It was an old saying among the Puritans, <hi type="italic">Grown bread and the gospel are good fare.</hi> <div eID="gen24641" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24642" type="x-p"/> 3. As Christ has a <hi type="italic">compassion</hi> for all that are in wants and straits, so he has a special <hi type="italic">concern</hi> for those that are reduced to straits by their zeal and diligence in attending on him. Christ said, <hi type="italic">I have compassion on the multitude.</hi> Whom the proud Pharisees looked upon with disdain, the humble Jesus looked upon with pity and tenderness; and thus must we <hi type="italic">honour all men.</hi> But that which he chiefly considers, is, <hi type="italic">They have been with me three days, and have nothing to eat.</hi> Whatever losses we sustain, or hardships we go through, for Christ's sake, and in love to him, he will take care that they shall be made up to us one way or other. <hi type="italic">They that seek the Lord, shall not</hi> long <hi type="italic">want any good thing,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.34.10">Ps. xxxiv. 10</reference>. Observe with what sympathy Christ saith (<reference osisRef="Mark.8.3">v. 3</reference>), <hi type="italic">If I send them away fasting to their own houses, they will faint by the way,</hi> for hunger. Christ knows and considers our frame; and he is <hi type="italic">for the body,</hi> if we glorify him, <hi type="italic">verily we shall be fed.</hi> He considered that <hi type="italic">many of them came from afar,</hi> and had a great way home. When we see <hi type="italic">multitudes</hi> attending upon the word preached, it is comfortable to think that Christ knows whence they all come, though we do not. <hi type="italic">I know thy works, and where thou dwellest,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.2.13">Rev. ii. 13</reference>. Christ would by no means have them go home fasting, for it is not his manner to send those <hi type="italic">empty</hi> way from him, that in a right manner attend on him. <div eID="gen24642" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24643" type="x-p"/> 4. The doubts of Christians are sometimes made to work for the magnifying of the power of Christ. The disciples could not imagine whence so many men should be <hi type="italic">satisfied with bread</hi> here in the wilderness, <reference osisRef="Mark.8.4">v. 4</reference>. That therefore must needs be <hi type="italic">wonderful,</hi> and appear so much the more so, which the disciples looked upon as <hi type="italic">impossible.</hi> <div eID="gen24643" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24644" type="x-p"/> 5. Christ's time to act for the relief of his people, is, when things are brought to the last extremity; when they were ready to <hi type="italic">faint,</hi> Christ provided for them. That he might not invite them to follow him for the <hi type="italic">loaves,</hi> he did not supply them but when they were utterly reduced, and then he <hi type="italic">sent them away.</hi> <div eID="gen24644" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24645" type="x-p"/> 6. The bounty of Christ is inexhaustible, and, to evidence that, Christ <hi type="italic">repeated</hi> this miracle, to show that he is still the same for the succour and supply of his people that attend upon him. His favours are renewed, as our wants and necessities are. In the former miracle, Christ used all the bread he had, which was <hi type="italic">five loaves,</hi> and fed all the guests he had, which were <hi type="italic">five thousand,</hi> and so he did now; though he might have said, "If five loaves would feed five thousand, four may feed four thousand;" he took all the seven loaves, and fed with them the four thousand; for he would teach us to take things as they are, and accommodate ourselves to them; to use what we have, and make the best of that which is. Here it was, as in the dispensing of manna, <hi type="italic">He that gathered much had nothing over, and he that gathered little had no lack.</hi> <div eID="gen24645" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24646" type="x-p"/> 7. In our Father's house, in our Master's house, <hi type="italic">there is bread enough, and to spare;</hi> there is a fulness in Christ, which he communicates to all that passes through his hands; so that from it we receive, and <hi type="italic">grace for grace,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.1.16">John i. 16</reference>. Those need not fear wanting, that have Christ to live upon. <div eID="gen24646" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24647" type="x-p"/> 8. It is good for those that follow Christ, <hi type="italic">to keep together;</hi> these followers of Christ continued in a body, <hi type="italic">four thousand</hi> of them together, and Christ fed them all. Christ's sheep must abide by the flock, and go forth by their footsteps, and verily they shall be fed.

<div eID="gen24647" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Leaven of Herod and the Pharisees; Christ Reproves His Disciples.</title> <div sID="gen24648" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">10</hi> And straightway he entered into a ship with his disciples, and came into the parts of Dalmanutha. <hi type="super">11</hi> And the Pharisees came forth, and began to question with him, seeking of him a sign from heaven, tempting him. <hi type="super">12</hi> And he sighed deeply in his spirit, and saith, Why doth this generation seek after a sign? verily I say unto you, There shall no sign be given unto this generation. <hi type="super">13</hi> And he left them, and entering into the ship again departed to the other side. <hi type="super">14</hi> Now <hi type="italic">the disciples</hi> had forgotten to take bread, neither had they in the ship with them more than one loaf. <hi type="super">15</hi> And he charged them, saying, Take heed, beware of the leaven of the Pharisees, and <hi type="italic">of</hi> the leaven of Herod. <hi type="super">16</hi> And they reasoned among themselves, saying, <hi type="italic">It is</hi> because we have no bread. <hi type="super">17</hi> And when Jesus knew <hi type="italic">it,</hi> he saith unto them, Why reason ye, because ye have no bread? perceive ye not yet, neither understand? have ye your heart yet hardened? <hi type="super">18</hi> Having eyes, see ye not? and having ears, hear ye not? and do ye not remember? 19 When I brake the five loaves among five thousand, how many baskets full of fragments took ye up? They say unto him, Twelve. <hi type="super">20</hi> And when the seven among four thousand, how many baskets full of fragments took ye up? And they said, Seven. <hi type="super">21</hi> And he said unto them, How is it that ye do not understand? <div eID="gen24648" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24649" type="x-p"/> Still Christ is upon motion; now he visits the parts of Dalmanutha, that no corner of the land of Israel might say that they had not had his presence with them. He came thither <hi type="italic">by ship</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mark.8.10">v. 10</reference>); but, meeting with occasions of dispute there, and not with opportunities of doing good, he <hi type="italic">entered into the ship again</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mark.8.13">v. 13</reference>), and came back. In these verses, we are told, <div eID="gen24649" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24650" type="x-p"/> I. How he refused to gratify the Pharisees, who challenged him to give them a <hi type="italic">sign from heaven.</hi> They <hi type="italic">came forth</hi> on purpose to <hi type="italic">question with him;</hi> not to propose questions to him, that they might learn of him, but to cross question with him, that they might ensnare him. <div eID="gen24650" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24651" type="x-p"/> 1. They demanded of him a <hi type="italic">sign from heaven,</hi> as if the signs he gave them on earth, which were more familiar to them, and were more capable of being examined and enquired into, were not sufficient. There was a sign <hi type="italic">from heaven</hi> at his baptism, in the descent of the dove, and the voice (<reference osisRef="Matt.3.16-Matt.3.17">Matt. iii. 16, 17</reference>); it was public enough; and if they had attended John's baptism as they ought to have done, they might themselves have seen it. Afterward, when he was nailed to the cross, they prescribed a new sign; <hi type="italic">Let him come down from the cross, and we will believe him;</hi> thus obstinate infidelity will still have something to say, though ever so unreasonable. They demanded this sign, <hi type="italic">tempting him;</hi> not in hopes that he would give it them, that they might be satisfied, but in hopes that he would not, that they might imagine themselves to have a pretence for their infidelity. <div eID="gen24651" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24652" type="x-p"/> 2. He denied them their demand; He <hi type="italic">sighed deeply in his spirit,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.8.12">v. 12</reference>. He <hi type="italic">groaned</hi> (so some), being grieved for the <hi type="italic">hardness of their hearts,</hi> and the little influence that his preaching and miracles had had upon them. The infidelity of those that have long enjoyed the means of conviction, is a great grief to the Lord Jesus; it troubles him, that sinners should thus stand in their own light, and put a bar in their own door. (1.) He expostulates with them upon this demand; "<hi type="italic">Why doth this generation seek after a sign;</hi> this generation, that is so unworthy to have the gospel brought to it, and to have any sign accompanying it; <hi type="italic">this generation,</hi> that so greedily swallows the traditions of the elders, without the confirmation of any sign at all; <hi type="italic">this generation,</hi> into which, by the calculating of the times prefixed in the Old Testament, they might easily perceive that the coming of the Messiah must fall; <hi type="italic">this generation,</hi> that has had such plenty of sensible and merciful signs given them in the cure of their sick? What an absurdity is it for them to desire a sign!" (2.) He refuses to answer their demand; <hi type="italic">Verily, I say unto you, there shall no sign,</hi> no such sign, <hi type="italic">be given to this generation.</hi> When God spoke to particular persons in a particular case, out of the road of his common dispensation, they were encouraged to ask a sign, as Gideon and Ahaz; but when he speaks in general to all, as in the law and the gospel, sending each with their own evidence, it is presumption to prescribe other signs than what he has given. <hi type="italic">Shall any teach God knowledge?</hi> He denied them, and then <hi type="italic">left them,</hi> as men not fit to be talked with; if they will not be convinced, they shall not; leave them to their strong delusions. <div eID="gen24652" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24653" type="x-p"/> II. How he warned his disciples against the leaven of the Pharisees and of Herod. Observe here, <div eID="gen24653" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24654" type="x-p"/> 1. What the caution was (<reference osisRef="Mark.8.15">v. 15</reference>); "<hi type="italic">Take heed, beware,</hi> lest ye partake of the <hi type="italic">leaven of the Pharisees,</hi> lest ye embrace the tradition of the elders, which they are so wedded to, lest ye be proud, and hypocritical, and ceremonious, like them." Matthew adds, <hi type="italic">and of the Sadducees;</hi> Mark adds, <hi type="italic">and of Herod:</hi> whence some gather, that Herod, and his courtiers were generally Sadducees, that is, deists, men of no religion. Others give this sense, The Pharisees demanded a <hi type="italic">sign from heaven;</hi> and Herod was long <hi type="italic">desirous</hi> to see some miracle wrought by Christ (<reference osisRef="Luke.23.8">Luke xxiii. 8</reference>); such as he should prescribe, so that the leaven of both was the same; they were unsatisfied with the signs they had, and would have others of their own devising; "Take heed of <hi type="italic">this leaven</hi>" (saith Christ), "be convinced by the miracles ye have seen, and covet not to see more." <div eID="gen24654" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24655" type="x-p"/> 2. How they misunderstood this caution. It seems, at their putting to sea this time, they had <hi type="italic">forgotten to take bread,</hi> and <hi type="italic">had not in their ship more than one loaf,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.8.14">v. 14</reference>. When therefore Christ bid them <hi type="italic">beware of the leaven of the Pharisees,</hi> they understood it as an intimation to them, not to apply themselves to any of the Pharisees for relief, when they came to the other side, for they had lately been offended at them for eating with <hi type="italic">unwashen hands.</hi> They <hi type="italic">reasoned among themselves,</hi> what should be the meaning of this caution, and concluded, "<hi type="italic">It is because we have no bread;</hi> he saith this, to reproach us for being so careless as to go to sea, and go among strangers, with but one loaf of bread; he doth, in effect, tell us, we must be brought to <hi type="italic">short allowance,</hi> and must eat our bread by weight." They <hi type="italic">reasoned it</hi>—<hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">dielogizonto</hi></hi>, they <hi type="italic">disputed</hi> about it; one said, "It was owing to you;" and the other said, "It was owing to you, that we are so ill provided for this voyage." Thus distrust of God makes Christ's disciples quarrel among themselves. <div eID="gen24655" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24656" type="x-p"/> 3. The reproof Christ gave them for their uneasiness in this matter, as it argued a disbelief of his power to supply them, notwithstanding the abundant experience they had had of it. The reproof is given with some warmth, for he knew their hearts, and knew they needed to be thus soundly chidden; "<hi type="italic">Perceive ye not yet, neither understand,</hi> that which you have had so many demonstrations of? <hi type="italic">Have ye your hearts yet hardened,</hi> so as that nothing will make any impression upon them, or bring them to compliance with your Master's designs? <hi type="italic">Having eyes, see ye not</hi> that which is plain before your eyes? <hi type="italic">Having ears, hear ye not</hi> that which you have been so often told? How strangely stupid and senseless are ye! <hi type="italic">Do ye not remember</hi> that which was done but the other day, <hi type="italic">when I broke the five loaves among the five thousand,</hi> and soon after, the <hi type="italic">seven loaves among the four thousand?</hi> Do ye not remember <hi type="italic">how many baskets full ye took up</hi> of the fragments?" Yes, they did remember, and could tell that they took up <hi type="italic">twelve</hi> baskets full one time, and <hi type="italic">seven</hi> another; "Why then," said he, "<hi type="italic">how is it that ye do not understand?</hi> As if he that multiplied <hi type="italic">five</hi> loaves, and <hi type="italic">seven,</hi> could not multiply one." They seemed to suspect that the one was not matter enough to work upon, if he should have a mind to entertain his hearers a third time: and if that was their thought, it was indeed a very senseless one, as if it were not all alike to the Lord, to save by many or few, and as easy to make one loaf to feed five thousand as five. It was therefore proper to remind them, not only of the sufficiency, but of the overplus, of the former meals; and justly were they chidden for not understanding what Christ therein designed, and what they from thence might have learned. Note, (1.) The experiences we have had of God's goodness to us in the way of duty, greatly aggravate our distrust of him, which is <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> very provoking to the Lord Jesus. (2.) Our <hi type="italic">not understanding</hi> of the true intent and meaning of God's favours to us, is equivalent to our not remembering of them. (3.) We are <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> overwhelmed with present cares and distrusts, because we do not <hi type="italic">understand,</hi> and remember, what we have known and seen of the power and goodness of our Lord Jesus. It would be a great support to us, to <hi type="italic">consider the days of old,</hi> and we are wanting both to God and ourselves if we do not. (4.) When we thus <hi type="italic">forgot the works of God,</hi> and distrust him, we should chide ourselves severely for it, as Christ doth his disciples here; "Am I thus without understanding? How is it that my heart is thus hardened?"

<div eID="gen24656" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">A Blind Man Restored to Sight.</title> <div sID="gen24657" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">22</hi> And he cometh to Bethsaida; and they bring a blind man unto him, and besought him to touch him. <hi type="super">23</hi> And he took the blind man by the hand, and led him out of the town; and when he had spit on his eyes, and put his hands upon him, he asked him if he saw ought. <hi type="super">24</hi> And he looked up, and said, I see men as trees, walking. <hi type="super">25</hi> After that he put <hi type="italic">his</hi> hands again upon his eyes, and made him look up: and he was restored, and saw every man clearly. <hi type="super">26</hi> And he sent him away to his house, saying, Neither go into the town, nor tell <hi type="italic">it</hi> to any in the town. <div eID="gen24657" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24658" type="x-p"/> This cure is related only by this evangelist, and there is something singular in the circumstances. <div eID="gen24658" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24659" type="x-p"/> I. Here is a <hi type="italic">blind man</hi> brought to Christ by his friends, with a desire that he would <hi type="italic">touch him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.8.22">v. 22</reference>. Here appears the faith of those that brought him—they doubted not but that one touch of Christ's hand would recover him his sight; but the man himself showed not that earnestness for, or expectation of, a cure that other blind men did. If those that are spiritually blind, do not pray for themselves, yet let their friends and relations pray for them, that Christ would be pleased to <hi type="italic">touch them.</hi> <div eID="gen24659" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24660" type="x-p"/> II. Here is Christ <hi type="italic">leading</hi> this blind man, <reference osisRef="Mark.8.23">v. 23</reference>. He did not bid his friends lead him, but (which bespeaks his wonderful condescension) he himself <hi type="italic">took him by the hand, and led him,</hi> to teach us to be as Job was, <hi type="italic">eyes to the blind,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.29.15">Job xxix. 15</reference>. Never had poor blind man such a Leader. He led him <hi type="italic">out of the town.</hi> Had he herein only designed privacy, he might have led him into a house, into an inner chamber, and have cured him there; but he intended hereby to upbraid Bethsaida with the <hi type="italic">mighty works</hi> that had <hi type="italic">in vain</hi> been done <hi type="italic">in her</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.11.21">Matt. xi. 21</reference>), and was telling her, in effect, she was unworthy to have any more done within her walls. Perhaps Christ took the blind man <hi type="italic">out of the town,</hi> that he might have a larger prospect in the <hi type="italic">open fields,</hi> to try his sight with, than he could have in the <hi type="italic">close streets.</hi> <div eID="gen24660" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24661" type="x-p"/> III. Here is the cure of the blind man, by that blessed Oculist, who came into the world to <hi type="italic">preach the recovering of sight to the blind</hi> (<reference osisRef="Luke.4.18">Luke iv. 18</reference>), and to <hi type="italic">give</hi> what he <hi type="italic">preached.</hi> In this cure we may observe, 1. That Christ used a <hi type="italic">sign;</hi> he <hi type="italic">spat on his eyes</hi> (spat <hi type="italic">into</hi> them, so some), and <hi type="italic">put his hand upon him.</hi> He could have cured him, as he did others, with a word speaking, but thus he was pleased to assist his faith which was very weak, and to help him against his <hi type="italic">unbelief.</hi> And this spittle signified the <hi type="italic">eye-salve</hi> wherewith Christ anoints the eyes of those that are spiritually blind, <reference osisRef="Rev.3.18">Rev. iii. 18</reference>. 2. That the cure was wrought <hi type="italic">gradually,</hi> which was not usual in Christ's miracles. He <hi type="italic">asked him if he saw aught,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.8.23">v. 23</reference>. Let him tell what condition his sight was in, for the satisfaction of those about him. And he <hi type="italic">looked up;</hi> so far he <hi type="italic">recovered his sight,</hi> that he could open his eyes, and he said, <hi type="italic">I see men as trees walking;</hi> he could not distinguish men from trees, otherwise than he could discern them to move. He had some glimmerings of sight, and betwixt him and the sky could perceive a man erect like a tree, but <hi type="italic">could not discern the form thereof,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.4.16">Job iv. 16</reference>. But, 3. It was soon completed; Christ never doeth <hi type="italic">his work</hi> by the halves, nor leaves it till he can say, <hi type="italic">It is finished.</hi> He <hi type="italic">put his hands again upon his eyes,</hi> to disperse the remaining darkness, and then bade him look up again, and he <hi type="italic">saw every man clearly,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.8.25">v. 25</reference>. Now Christ took this way, (1.) Because he would not <hi type="italic">tie himself to a method,</hi> but would show with what liberty he acted in all he did. He did not cure by <hi type="italic">rote,</hi> as I may say, and in a <hi type="italic">road,</hi> but <hi type="italic">varied</hi> as he thought fit. Providence gains the same end in different ways, that men may attend its motions with an <hi type="italic">implicit faith.</hi> (2.) Because it should be to the patient <hi type="italic">according to his faith;</hi> and perhaps this man's faith was at first very weak, but afterward gathered strength, and accordingly his cure was. Not that Christ always went by this rule, but thus he would sometimes put a rebuke upon those who came to him, doubting. (3.) Thus Christ would show how, and in what method, those are healed by his grace, who by nature are <hi type="italic">spiritually blind;</hi> at first, their knowledge is confused, they see <hi type="italic">men as trees walking;</hi> but, like the light of the morning, it <hi type="italic">shines more and more to the perfect day,</hi> and then they <hi type="italic">see all things clearly,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.4.18">Prov. iv. 18</reference>. Let us enquire then, if we <hi type="italic">see aught</hi> of those things which <hi type="italic">faith</hi> is the <hi type="italic">substance</hi> and <hi type="italic">evidence</hi> of; and if through grace we see <hi type="italic">any thing</hi> of them, we may hope that we shall see yet <hi type="italic">more</hi> and <hi type="italic">more,</hi> for Jesus Christ will <hi type="italic">perfect</hi> for ever those that are <hi type="italic">sanctified.</hi> <div eID="gen24661" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24662" type="x-p"/> IV. The directions Christ gave the man he had cured, not to <hi type="italic">tell it to any in the town of Bethsaida,</hi> nor so much as to <hi type="italic">go into the town,</hi> where probably there were some expecting him to come back, who had seen Christ lead him out of the town, but, having been eyewitnesses of so many miracles, had not so much as the curiosity to follow him: let not those be gratified with the sight of him when he was cured, who would not show so much respect to Christ as to go a step out of the town, to see this cure wrought. Christ doth not forbid him to tell it to others, but he must not tell it to <hi type="italic">any in the town.</hi> Slighting Christ's favours is forfeiting them; and Christ will make those know the worth of their privileges by the want of them, that would not know them otherwise. Bethsaida, in the day of her visitation, would not know the things that belonged to her peace, and now they are <hi type="italic">hid from her eyes.</hi> They will not see, and therefore shall not see.

<div eID="gen24662" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Peter's Enlightened Testimony; Peter Rebuked.</title> <div sID="gen24663" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">27</hi> And Jesus went out, and his disciples, into the towns of Cæsarea Philippi: and by the way he asked his disciples, saying unto them, Whom do men say that I am? <hi type="super">28</hi> And they answered, John the Baptist: but some <hi type="italic">say,</hi> Elias; and others, One of the prophets. <hi type="super">29</hi> And he saith unto them, But whom say ye that I am? And Peter answereth and saith unto him, Thou art the Christ. <hi type="super">30</hi> And he charged them that they should tell no man of him. <hi type="super">31</hi> And he began to teach them, that the Son of man must suffer many things, and be rejected of the elders, and <hi type="italic">of</hi> the chief priests, and scribes, and be killed, and after three days rise again. <hi type="super">32</hi> And he spake that saying openly. And Peter took him, and began to rebuke him. <hi type="super">33</hi> But when he had turned about and looked on his disciples, he rebuked Peter, saying, Get thee behind me, Satan: for thou savourest not the things that be of God, but the things that be of men. <hi type="super">34</hi> And when he had called the people <hi type="italic">unto him</hi> with his disciples also, he said unto them, Whosoever will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow me. <hi type="super">35</hi> For whosoever will save his life shall lose it; but whosoever shall lose his life for my sake and the gospel's, the same shall save it. <hi type="super">36</hi> For what shall it profit a man, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul? <hi type="super">37</hi> Or what shall a man give in exchange for his soul? <hi type="super">38</hi> Whosoever therefore shall be ashamed of me and of my words in this adulterous and sinful generation; of him also shall the Son of man be ashamed, when he cometh in the glory of his Father with the holy angels. <div eID="gen24663" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24664" type="x-p"/> We have read a great deal of the doctrine Christ preached, and the miracles he wrought, which were many, and strange, and well-attested, of various kinds, and wrought in several places, to the astonishment of the multitudes that were eye-witnesses of them. It is now time for us to pause a little, and to consider what these things mean; the wondrous works which Christ then forbade the publishing of, being recorded in these sacred writings, are thereby published to all the world, to us, to all ages; now what shall we think of them? Is the record of those things designed only for an amusement, or to furnish us with matter for discourse? No, certainly <hi type="italic">these things are written, that we may believe that Jesus is the Christ the Son of God</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.20.31">John xx. 31</reference>); and this discourse which Christ had with his disciples, will assist us in making the necessary reflections upon the miracles of Christ, and a right use of them. Three things we are here taught to infer from the miracles Christ wrought. <div eID="gen24664" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24665" type="x-p"/> I. They <hi type="italic">prove</hi> that he is <hi type="italic">the true Messiah,</hi> the Son of God, and Saviour of the world: this the works he did witnessed concerning him; and this his disciples, who were the eye-witnesses of those works, here profess their belief of; which cannot but be a satisfaction to us in making the same inference from them. <div eID="gen24665" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24666" type="x-p"/> 1. Christ enquired of them what the sentiments of the people were concerning him; <hi type="italic">Who did men say that I am?</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.8.27">v. 27</reference>. Note, Though it is a small thing for us to be judged of men, yet it may sometimes do us good to know what people say of us, not that we may seek our own glory, but that we may hear our faults. Christ asked them, not that he might be informed, but that they might observe it themselves, and inform one another. <div eID="gen24666" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24667" type="x-p"/> 2. The account they gave him, was such as plainly intimated the <hi type="italic">high opinion</hi> the people had of him. Though they came short of the truth, yet they were convinced by his miracles that he was an extraordinary person, sent from the invisible world with a divine commission. It is probable that they would have acknowledged him to be the Messiah, if they had not been possessed by their teachers with a notion that the Messiah must be a temporal Prince, appearing in external pomp and power, which the figure Christ made, would not comport with; yet (whatever the Pharisees said, whose copyhold was touched by the strictness and spirituality of his doctrine) none of the people said that he was a Deceiver, but some said that <hi type="italic">he was John Baptist,</hi> others <hi type="italic">Elias,</hi> others <hi type="italic">one of the prophets,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.8.28">v. 28</reference>. All agreed that he was one <hi type="italic">risen from the dead.</hi> <div eID="gen24667" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24668" type="x-p"/> 3. The account they gave him of their own sentiments concerning him, intimated their abundant satisfaction in him, and in their having left all to follow him, which now, after some time of trial, they see no reason to repent; <hi type="italic">But whom say ye that I am?</hi> To this they have an answer ready, <hi type="italic">Thou art the Christ,</hi> the Messiah often promised, and long expected, <reference osisRef="Mark.8.29">v. 29</reference>. To be a Christian indeed, is, sincerely to believe that Jesus is the Christ, and to act accordingly; and that he is so, plainly appears by his wondrous works. This they knew, and must shortly publish and maintain; but for the present they must keep it secret (<reference osisRef="Mark.8.30">v. 30</reference>), till the proof of it was completed, and they were completely qualified to maintain it, by the pouring out of the Holy Ghost; and then <hi type="italic">let all the house of Israel know assuredly that God has made this same Jesus, whom ye crucified, both Lord and Christ,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.2.36">Acts ii. 36</reference>. <div eID="gen24668" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24669" type="x-p"/> II. These miracles of Christ <hi type="italic">take off the offence of the cross,</hi> and assure us that Christ was, in it, not conquered, but a Conqueror. Now that the disciples are convinced that Jesus is the Christ, they may bear to hear of his sufferings, which Christ now <hi type="italic">begins</hi> to give them notice of, <reference osisRef="Mark.8.31">v. 31</reference>. <div eID="gen24669" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24670" type="x-p"/> 1. Christ <hi type="italic">taught</hi> his disciples that he must <hi type="italic">suffer many things,</hi> Though they had got over the vulgar error of the Messiah's being a temporal Prince, so far as to believe their Master to be the Messiah, notwithstanding his present meanness, yet still they retained it, so far as to expect that he would <hi type="italic">shortly</hi> appear in outward pomp and grandeur, and <hi type="italic">restore the kingdom to Israel;</hi> and therefore, to rectify that mistake, Christ here gives them a prospect of the contrary, that he must be <hi type="italic">rejected of the elders, and the chief priests,</hi> and <hi type="italic">the scribes,</hi> who, they expected, should be brought to own and prefer him; that, instead of being crowned, <hi type="italic">he must be killed,</hi> he must be crucified, and <hi type="italic">after three days he must rise again</hi> to a heavenly life, and to be <hi type="italic">no more in this world.</hi> This he spoke <hi type="italic">openly</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mark.8.32">v. 32</reference>), <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">parresia</hi></hi>. He said it freely and plainly, and did not wrap it up in ambiguous expressions. The disciples might easily understand it, if they had not been very much under the power of prejudice: or, it intimates that he spoke it cheerfully and without any terror, and would have them to hear it so: he spoke that saying <hi type="italic">boldly,</hi> as one that not only knew he <hi type="italic">must</hi> suffer and die, but was resolved he <hi type="italic">would,</hi> and made it his own act and deed. <div eID="gen24670" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24671" type="x-p"/> 2. Peter opposed it; <hi type="italic">He took him, and began to rebuke him.</hi> Here Peter showed more love than discretion, a zeal for Christ and his safety, but not according to knowledge. He <hi type="italic">took him</hi>—<hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">proslabomenos auton</hi></hi>.
