We do not find that Christ met with food elsewhere, when he missed of it on the fig-tree; but the zeal of God's house so ate him up, and made him forget himself, that he came, hungry as he was, to Jerusalem, and went straight to the temple, and began to reform those abuses which the day before he had marked out; to show that when the Redeemer came to Zion, his errand was, <hi type="italic">to turn away ungodliness from Jacob</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rom.11.26">Rom. xi. 26</reference>), and that he came not, as he was falsely accused, to <hi type="italic">destroy</hi> the temple, but to purify and refine it, and reduce his church to its primitive rectitude. <div eID="gen24797" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24798" type="x-p"/> 1. He cast out the <hi type="italic">buyers</hi> and <hi type="italic">sellers, overthrew the tables of the money-changers</hi> (and threw the money to the ground, the fitter place for it), and threw down the <hi type="italic">seats of them that sold doves.</hi> This he did as one having authority, as <hi type="italic">a Son in his own house.</hi> The filth of the daughter of Zion is purged away, not by might, nor by power, but by <hi type="italic">the spirit of judgment, and the spirit of burning.</hi> And he did it without opposition; for what he did, was manifested to be right and good, even in the consciences of those that had connived at it, and countenanced it, because they got money by it. Note, It may be some encouragement to zealous reformers, that frequently the purging out of corruptions, and the correcting of abuses, prove an easier piece of work than was apprehended. Prudent attempts sometimes prove successful beyond expectation, and there are not those lions <hi type="italic">found</hi> in the way, that were feared to be. <div eID="gen24798" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24799" type="x-p"/> 2. He <hi type="italic">would not suffer that any man should carry any vessel,</hi> any sort of goods or wares, <hi type="italic">through the temple,</hi> or any of the courts of it, because it was the nearer way, and would save them the labour of going about, <reference osisRef="Mark.11.16">v. 16</reference>. The Jews owned that it was one of the instances of honour due to the temple, not to make the mountain of the house, or the court of the Gentiles, a road, or common passage, or to come into it with any bundle. <div eID="gen24799" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24800" type="x-p"/> 3. He gave a good reason for this; because it was written, <hi type="italic">My house shall be called of all nations, The house of prayer,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.11.17">v. 17</reference>. So it is written, <reference osisRef="Isa.56.7">Isa. lvi. 7</reference>. It shall pass among all people under that character. <hi type="italic">It shall be the house of prayer to all nations;</hi> it was so in the first institution of it; when Solomon dedicated it, it was with an eye to the sons of the strangers, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.8.41">1 Kings viii. 41</reference>. And it was prophesied that it should be yet more so. Christ will have the temple, as a type of the gospel-church, to be, (1.) A <hi type="italic">house of prayer.</hi> After he had turned out the oxen and doves, which were things for sacrifice, he revived the appointment of it as a <hi type="italic">house of prayer,</hi> to teach us that when all sacrifices and offerings should be abolished, the spiritual sacrifices of prayer and praise should continue and remain for ever. (2.) That it should be so <hi type="italic">to all nations,</hi> and not to the people of the Jews only; for <hi type="italic">whosoever shall call upon the name of the Lord, shall be saved,</hi> though not of the seed of Jacob, according to the flesh. It was therefore insufferable for them to <hi type="italic">make it a den of thieves,</hi> which would prejudice those nations against it, whom they should have invited to it. When Christ drove out the buyers and sellers at the beginning of his ministry, he only charged them with making the temple a <hi type="italic">house of merchandise</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.2.16">John ii. 16</reference>); but now he chargeth them with making it a <hi type="italic">den of thieves,</hi> because since then they had twice gone about to stone him in the temple (<reference osisRef="John.8.59">John viii. 59</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.10.31">x. 31</reference>), or because the traders there were grown notorious for cheating their customers, and imposing upon the ignorance and necessity of the country people, which is no better than downright thievery. Those that suffer vain worldly thoughts to lodge within them when they are at their devotions, turn the <hi type="italic">house of prayer</hi> into a <hi type="italic">house of merchandise;</hi> but they that make long prayers for pretence to devour widows' houses, turn it into a <hi type="italic">den of thieves.</hi> <div eID="gen24800" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24801" type="x-p"/> 4. The scribes and the chief priests were extremely nettled at this, <reference osisRef="Mark.11.18">v. 18</reference>. They hated him, and hated to be reformed by him; and yet they <hi type="italic">feared him,</hi> lest he should next overthrow <hi type="italic">their</hi> seats, and expel <hi type="italic">them,</hi> being conscious to themselves of the profaning and abusing of their power. They found that he had a great interest, that <hi type="italic">all the people were astonished at his doctrine,</hi> and that every thing he said, was an oracle and a law to them; and what durst <hi type="italic">he</hi> not attempt, what could <hi type="italic">he</hi> not effect, being thus supported? They therefore sought, not how he might make their peace with him, but <hi type="italic">how they might destroy him.</hi> A desperate attempt, and which, one would think, they themselves could not but fear was <hi type="italic">fighting against God.</hi> But they care not what they do, to support their own power and grandeur. <div eID="gen24801" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24802" type="x-p"/> III. His discourse with his disciples, upon occasion of the fig-tree's withering away which he had cursed. At <hi type="italic">even,</hi> as usual, he <hi type="italic">went out of the city</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mark.11.19">v. 19</reference>), to Bethany; but it is probable that it was in the dark, so that they could not see the fig-tree; but the next morning, as they <hi type="italic">passed by,</hi> they observed the <hi type="italic">fig-tree dried up from the roots,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.11.20">v. 20</reference>. More is <hi type="italic">included</hi> many times in Christ's curses than is <hi type="italic">expressed,</hi> as appears by the effects of them. The curse was no more than that it should never bear fruit again, but the effect goes further, <hi type="italic">it is dried up from the roots.</hi> If it bear no fruit, it shall bear no leaves to cheat people. Now observe, <div eID="gen24802" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24803" type="x-p"/> 1. How the disciples were affected with it. Peter remembered Christ's words, and said, with surprise, <hi type="italic">Master, behold, the fig-tree which thou cursedst is withered away,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.11.21">v. 21</reference>. Note, Christ's curses have wonderful effects, and make those to wither presently, that flourished like the green bay-tree. <hi type="italic">Those whom he curseth are cursed indeed.</hi> This represented the character and state of the Jewish church; which, from henceforward, was a tree dried up from the roots; no longer fit for food, but for fuel only. The first establishment of the Levitical priesthood was ratified and confirmed by the miracle of a <hi type="italic">dry rod,</hi> which in <hi type="italic">one night</hi> budded, and blossomed, and brought forth almonds (<reference osisRef="Num.17.8">Num. xvii. 8</reference>), a happy omen of the fruitlessness and flourishing of that priesthood. And now, by a contrary miracle, the expiration of that priesthood was signified by a flourishing tree dried up in a night; the just punishment of those priests that had abused it. And this seemed very strange to the disciples, and scarcely credible, that the Jews, who had been so long God's own, his only professing people in the world, should be thus abandoned; they could not imagine how that <hi type="italic">fig-tree</hi> should <hi type="italic">so soon wither away:</hi> but this comes of rejecting Christ, and being rejected by him. <div eID="gen24803" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24804" type="x-p"/> 2. The good instructions Christ gave them from it; for of <hi type="italic">those</hi> even this <hi type="italic">withered</hi> tree was <hi type="italic">fruitful.</hi> <div eID="gen24804" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24805" type="x-p"/> (1.) Christ teacheth them from hence to <hi type="italic">pray in faith</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mark.11.22">v. 22</reference>); <hi type="italic">Have faith in God.</hi> They admired the power of Christ's word of command; "Why," said Christ, "a lively active faith would put as great a power into your prayers, <reference osisRef="Mark.11.23-Mark.11.24">v. 23, 24</reference>. <hi type="italic">Whosoever shall say to this mountain,</hi> this mount of Olives, <hi type="italic">Be removed, and be cast into the sea;</hi> if he has but any word of God, general or particular, to build his faith upon, and if he <hi type="italic">shall not doubt in his heart, but shall believe that those things which he saith,</hi> according to the warrant he has from what God hath said, <hi type="italic">shall come to pass, he shall have whatsoever he saith.</hi>" Through the strength and power of God in Christ, the greatest difficulty shall be got over, and the thing shall be effected. And therefore (<reference osisRef="Mark.11.24">v. 24</reference>), "<hi type="italic">What things soever ye desire, when ye pray believe that ye shall</hi> receive them; nay, believe that ye <hi type="italic">do receive them,</hi> and he that has power to give them, saith, <hi type="italic">Ye shall have them. I say unto you,</hi> Ye shall, <reference osisRef="Mark.11.24">v. 24</reference>. <hi type="italic">Verily</hi> I say unto you, Ye shall," <reference osisRef="Mark.11.23">v. 23</reference>. Now this is to be applied, [1.] To that <hi type="italic">faith of miracles</hi> which the apostles and first preachers of the gospel were endued with, which did wonders in <hi type="italic">things natural,</hi> healing the sick, raising the dead, casting out devils; these were, in effect, the removing of mountains. The apostles speak of a faith which would do that, and yet might be found where holy love was not, <reference osisRef="1Cor.13.2">1 Cor. xiii. 2</reference>. [2.] It may be applied to that <hi type="italic">miracle of faith,</hi> which all true Christians are endued with, which doeth wonders in <hi type="italic">things spiritual.</hi> <hi type="italic">It justifies</hi> us (<reference osisRef="Rom.5.1">Rom. v. 1</reference>), and so removes the mountains of guilt, and casts them into the <hi type="italic">depths of the sea,</hi> never to rise up in judgment against us, <reference osisRef="Mic.7.19">Mic. vii. 19</reference>. It <hi type="italic">purifies</hi> the heart (<reference osisRef="Acts.15.9">Acts xv. 9</reference>), and so removes mountains of corruption, and <hi type="italic">makes them plains</hi> before the grace of God, <reference osisRef="Zech.4.7">Zech. iv. 7</reference>. It is by faith that the world is conquered, Satan's fiery darts are quenched, a soul is crucified with Christ, and yet lives; by faith we set the Lord always before us, and see him that is invisible, and have him present to our minds; and this is effectual to remove mountains, for at the presence of the Lord, at the presence of the God of Jacob, the mountains were not only moved, but <hi type="italic">re</hi>moved, <reference osisRef="Ps.114.4-Ps.114.7">Ps. cxiv. 4-7</reference>. <div eID="gen24805" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24806" type="x-p"/> (2.) To this is added here that necessary qualification of the prevailing prayer, that we freely forgive those who have been any way injurious to us, and be in charity with all men (<reference osisRef="Mark.11.25-Mark.11.26">v. 25, 26</reference>); <hi type="italic">When ye stand praying,</hi> forgive. Note, Standing is no improper posture for prayer; it was generally used among the Jews; hence they called their prayers, their <hi type="italic">standings;</hi> when they would say how the world was <hi type="italic">kept up</hi> by prayer, they expressed it thus, <hi type="italic">Stationibus stat mundus—The world is held up by standings.</hi> But the primitive Christians generally used more humble and reverent gesture of kneeling, especially on fast days, though not on Lord's days. When we are at prayer, we must remember to pray for others, particularly for our enemies, and those that have wronged us; now we cannot pray sincerely that God would do them good, if we bear malice to them, and wish them ill. If we have injured others before we pray, we must go and <hi type="italic">be reconciled to them;</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.5.23-Matt.5.24">Matt. v. 23, 24</reference>. But if they have injured us, we go a nearer way to work, and must immediately from our hearts <hi type="italic">forgive</hi> them. [1.] Because this is a <hi type="italic">good step</hi> towards obtaining the <hi type="italic">pardon</hi> of our own sins: <hi type="italic">Forgive,</hi> that <hi type="italic">your Father may forgive you;</hi> that is, "that he may be qualified to receive forgiveness, that he may forgive you without injury to his honour, as it would be, if he should suffer those to have such benefit by his mercy, as are so far from being conformable to the pattern of it." [2.] Because the want of this is a certain bar to the obtaining of the pardon of our sins; "<hi type="italic">If ye do not forgive</hi> those who have injured you, if he hate their persons, bear them a grudge, meditate revenge, and take all occasion to speak ill of them, <hi type="italic">neither will your Father forgive your trespasses.</hi>" This ought to be remembered in prayer, because one great errand we have to the throne of grace, is, to pray for the pardon of our sins: and care about it ought to be our daily care, because prayer is a part of our daily work. Our Saviour often insists on this, for it was his great design to engage his disciples to love one another.

<div eID="gen24806" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Pharisees Nonplussed.</title> <div sID="gen24807" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">27</hi> And they come again to Jerusalem: and as he was walking in the temple, there come to him the chief priests, and the scribes, and the elders, <hi type="super">28</hi> And say unto him, By what authority doest thou these things? and who gave thee this authority to do these things? <hi type="super">29</hi> And Jesus answered and said unto them, I will also ask of you one question, and answer me, and I will tell you by what authority I do these things. <hi type="super">30</hi> The baptism of John, was <hi type="italic">it</hi> from heaven, or of men? answer me. 31 And they reasoned with themselves, saying, If we shall say, From heaven; he will say, Why then did ye not believe him? 32 But if we shall say, Of men; they feared the people: for all <hi type="italic">men</hi> counted John, that he was a prophet indeed. <hi type="super">33</hi> And they answered and said unto Jesus, We cannot tell. And Jesus answering saith unto them, Neither do I tell you by what authority I do these things. <div eID="gen24807" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24808" type="x-p"/> We have here Christ examined by the great Sanhedrim concerning his authority; for they claimed a power to call prophets to an account concerning their mission. They came to him when he was <hi type="italic">walking in the temple,</hi> not for his diversion, but <hi type="italic">teaching</hi> the people, first one company and then another. The Peripatetic philosophers were so called from the custom they had of <hi type="italic">walking</hi> when they taught. The cloisters, or piazzas, in the courts of the temple, were fitted for this purpose. The great men were vexed to see him followed and heard with attention, and therefore <hi type="italic">came to him</hi> with some solemnity, and did as it were arraign him at the bar with this question, <hi type="italic">By what authority doest thou these things?</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.11.28">v. 28</reference>. Now observe, <div eID="gen24808" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24809" type="x-p"/> I. How they designed hereby to run him aground, and embarrass him. If they could make it out before the people, that he had not a <hi type="italic">legal mission,</hi> that he was not duly <hi type="italic">ordained,</hi> though he was ever so well qualified, and preached ever so profitably and well, they would tell the people that they <hi type="italic">ought not to hear him.</hi> This they made the last refuge of an obstinate unbelief; because they were resolved not to receive his doctrine, they were resolved to find some flaw or other in his commission, and will conclude it invalid, if it be not produced and ratified in their court. Thus the Papists resolve their controversy with us very much into the mission of our ministers, and if they have but any pretence to overthrow that, they think they have gained their point, though we have the scripture ever so much on our side. But this is indeed a question, which all that act either as magistrates or ministers, ought to be furnished with a good answer to, and often put to themselves, <hi type="italic">By what authority do I these things?</hi> For <hi type="italic">how can men preach except they be sent?</hi> Or how can they act with comfort, or confidence, or hope of success, except they be authorized? <reference osisRef="Jer.23.32">Jer. xxiii. 32</reference>. <div eID="gen24809" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24810" type="x-p"/> II. How he effectually ran them aground, and embarrassed them, with this question, "What are your thoughts concerning <hi type="italic">the baptism of John?</hi> <hi type="italic">Was it from heaven, or of men?</hi> By what authority did John preach, and baptize, and gather disciples? <hi type="italic">Answer me,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.11.30">v. 30</reference>. Deal fairly and ingenuously, and give a categorical answer, one way or the other." By this resolve of <hi type="italic">their</hi> question into <hi type="italic">this,</hi> our Saviour intimates how near akin his doctrine and baptism were to John's; they had the same original, and the same design and tendency—to introduce the gospel kingdom. Christ might with the better grace put this question to <hi type="italic">them,</hi> because they had sent a committee of their own house to examine John, <reference osisRef="John.1.19">John i. 19</reference>. "Now," saith Christ, "what was the result of your enquiries concerning him?" <div eID="gen24810" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24811" type="x-p"/> They knew what they <hi type="italic">thought</hi> of this question; they could not but think that <hi type="italic">John Baptist</hi> was a man sent of God. But the difficulty was, what they should <hi type="italic">say to it</hi> now. Men that oblige not themselves to speak <hi type="italic">as they think</hi> (which is a certain rule) cannot avoid perplexing themselves thus. <div eID="gen24811" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24812" type="x-p"/> 1. If they own the baptism of John to be <hi type="italic">from heaven,</hi> as really it was, they <hi type="italic">shame themselves;</hi> for Christ will presently turn it upon them, <hi type="italic">Why did ye not then believe him,</hi> and receive his baptism? They could not bear that Christ should say this, but they could bear it that their own consciences should say so, because they had an art of stifling and silencing them, and because what conscience said, though it might gall and grate them a little, would not <hi type="italic">shame them;</hi> and then <hi type="italic">they</hi> would do well enough, who looked no further than Saul's care, when he was convicted, <hi type="italic">Honour me now before this people,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.30">1 Sam. xv. 30</reference>. <div eID="gen24812" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24813" type="x-p"/> 2. If they say, "<hi type="italic">It is of men,</hi> he was not sent of God, but his doctrine and baptism were inventions of his own," they <hi type="italic">expose themselves,</hi> the people will be ready to do them a mischief, or a least clamour upon them; for <hi type="italic">all men counted John that he was a prophet indeed,</hi> and therefore they could not bear that he should be reflected on. Note, There is a carnal slavish fear, which not only wicked subjects but wicked rulers likewise are liable to, which God makes use of as a means to keep the world in some order, and to suppress <hi type="italic">violence,</hi> that it shall not always <hi type="italic">grow up into a rod of wickedness.</hi> Now by this dilemma to which Christ brought them, (1.) They were confounded and baffled, and forced to make a dishonourable retreat; to pretend ignorance—<hi type="italic">We cannot tell</hi> (and that was mortification enough to those proud men), but really to discover the greatest malice and wilfulness. What Christ did by his wisdom, we must labour to do by our well doing—<hi type="italic">put to silence the ignorance of foolish men,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Pet.2.15">1 Pet. ii. 15</reference>. (2.) Christ came off with honour, and justified himself in refusing to give them an answer to their imperious demand; <hi type="italic">Neither tell I you by what authority I do these things.</hi> They did not deserve to be told; for it was plain that they contended not for truth, but victory; nor did <hi type="italic">he</hi> need to <hi type="italic">tell them,</hi> for the works which he did, told them plainly that he had authority from God to do what he did; since no man could do those miracles which he did unless God were with him. Let them wait but three or four days, and his resurrection shall tell them who gave him his authority, for by that he will be <hi type="italic">declared to be the Son of God with power,</hi> as by their rejecting of him, notwithstanding, they will be declared to be the enemies of God.  <chapter eID="Mark.11"/> <div eID="gen24813" type="x-p"/>

<div eID="gen24816" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen24815" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Vineyard and Husbandmen.</title> <div sID="gen24817" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> And he began to speak unto them by parables. A <hi type="italic">certain</hi> man planted a vineyard, and set a hedge about <hi type="italic">it,</hi> and digged <hi type="italic">a place for</hi> the winefat, and built a tower, and let it out to husbandmen, and went into a far country. 2 And at the season he sent to the husbandmen a servant, that he might receive from the husbandmen of the fruit of the vineyard. <hi type="super">3</hi> And they caught <hi type="italic">him,</hi> and beat him, and sent <hi type="italic">him</hi> away empty. <hi type="super">4</hi> And again he sent unto them another servant; and at him they cast stones, and wounded <hi type="italic">him</hi> in the head, and sent <hi type="italic">him</hi> away shamefully handled. <hi type="super">5</hi> And again he sent another; and him they killed, and many others; beating some, and killing some. <hi type="super">6</hi> Having yet therefore one son, his wellbeloved, he sent him also last unto them, saying, They will reverence my son. <hi type="super">7</hi> But those husbandmen said among themselves, This is the heir; come, let us kill him, and the inheritance shall be ours. <hi type="super">8</hi> And they took him, and killed <hi type="italic">him,</hi> and cast <hi type="italic">him</hi> out of the vineyard. <hi type="super">9</hi> What shall therefore the lord of the vineyard do? he will come and destroy the husbandmen, and will give the vineyard unto others. <hi type="super">10</hi> And have ye not read this scripture; The stone which the builders rejected is become the head of the corner: <hi type="super">11</hi> This was the Lord's doing, and it is marvellous in our eyes? <hi type="super">12</hi> And they sought to lay hold on him, but feared the people: for they knew that he had spoken the parable against them: and they left him, and went their way. <div eID="gen24817" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24818" type="x-p"/> Christ had formerly in parables showed how he designed to set up the gospel church; now he begins in parables to show how he would lay aside the Jewish church, which it might have been grafted into the <hi type="italic">stock of,</hi> but was built upon the <hi type="italic">ruins of.</hi> This parable we had just as we have it here, <reference osisRef="Matt.21.33">Matt. xxi. 33</reference>. We may observe here, <div eID="gen24818" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24819" type="x-p"/> I. They that enjoy the privileges of the visible church, have a vineyard let out to them, which is capable of great improvement, and from the occupiers of which rent is justly expected. When God <hi type="italic">showed his word unto Jacob, his statutes and judgments unto Israel</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.147.19">Ps. cxlvii. 19</reference>), when he set up his temple among them, his priesthood, and his ordinances, then he <hi type="italic">let out</hi> to them the <hi type="italic">vineyard</hi> he had <hi type="italic">planted;</hi> which he <hi type="italic">hedged,</hi> and in which he <hi type="italic">built a tower,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.12.1">v. 1</reference>. Members of the church are God's tenants, and they have both a good Landlord and a good bargain, and may live well upon it, if it be not their own fault. <div eID="gen24819" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24820" type="x-p"/> II. Those whom God lets out his vineyard to, he sends his servants to, to put them in mind of his just expectations from them, <reference osisRef="Mark.12.2">v. 2</reference>. He was not <hi type="italic">hasty</hi> in his demands, nor <hi type="italic">high,</hi> for he did not send for the rent till they could make it, <hi type="italic">at the season;</hi> nor did he put them to the trouble of making money of it, but was willing to take it <hi type="italic">in specie.</hi> <div eID="gen24820" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24821" type="x-p"/> III. It is sad to think what base usage God's faithful ministers have met with, in all ages, from those that have enjoyed the privileges of the church, and have not brought forth fruit answerable. The Old-Testament prophets were persecuted even by those that went under the name of the Old-Testament church. They <hi type="italic">beat them,</hi> and <hi type="italic">sent them empty away</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mark.12.3">v. 3</reference>); that was bad: they <hi type="italic">wounded them,</hi> and <hi type="italic">sent them away shamefully entreated</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mark.12.4">v. 4</reference>); that was worse: nay, at length, they came to such a pitch of wickedness, that they <hi type="italic">killed</hi> them, <reference osisRef="Mark.12.5">v. 5</reference>. <div eID="gen24821" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24822" type="x-p"/> IV. It was no wonder if those who abused the prophets, abused Christ himself. God did at length send them his Son, his <hi type="italic">well-beloved;</hi> it was therefore so much the greater kindness in him to send him; as in Jacob to send Joseph to visit his brethren, <reference osisRef="Gen.37.14">Gen. xxxvii. 14</reference>. And it might be expected that he whom their Master <hi type="italic">loved,</hi> they also should respect and love (<reference osisRef="Mark.12.6">v. 6</reference>); "<hi type="italic">They will reverence my son,</hi> and, in reverence to him, will pay their rent." But, instead of <hi type="italic">reverencing</hi> him because he was the son and heir, they <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> hated him, <reference osisRef="Mark.12.7">v. 7</reference>. Because Christ, in calling to repentance and reformation, made his demands with more authority than the prophets had done, they were the more enraged against him, and determined to put him to death, that they might engross all church power to themselves, and that all the respect and obedience of the people might be paid to them only; "<hi type="italic">The inheritance shall be ours,</hi> we will be lords paramount, and bear all the sway." There is an <hi type="italic">inheritance,</hi> which, if they had duly <hi type="italic">reverenced the Son,</hi> might have been theirs, a heavenly inheritance; but they slighted that, and would have their inheritance in the wealth, and pomp, and powers, of this world. So they <hi type="italic">took him, and killed him;</hi> they had not done it yet, but they would do it in a little time; and they <hi type="italic">cast him out of the vineyard,</hi> they refused to admit his gospel when he was gone; it would by no means agree with their scheme, and so they threw it out with disdain and detestation. <div eID="gen24822" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24823" type="x-p"/> V. For such sinful and shameful doings nothing can be expected but a fearful doom (<reference osisRef="Mark.12.9">v. 9</reference>); <hi type="italic">What shall therefore the Lord of the vineyard do?</hi> It is easy to say what, for nothing could be done more provoking. <div eID="gen24823" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24824" type="x-p"/> 1. He will <hi type="italic">come, and destroy the husbandmen,</hi> whom he would have saved. When they only denied the fruit, he did not <hi type="italic">distrain</hi> upon them for rent, nor <hi type="italic">disseize</hi> them and <hi type="italic">dispossess</hi> them for <hi type="italic">non-payment;</hi> but when they killed his servants, and his Son, he determined to <hi type="italic">destroy</hi> them; and this was fulfilled when Jerusalem was laid waste, and the Jewish nation extirpated and made a desolation. <div eID="gen24824" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24825" type="x-p"/> 2. He will <hi type="italic">give the vineyards to others.</hi> If he have not the rent from them, he will have it from another people, for God will be no loser by any. This was fulfilled in the taking in of the Gentiles, and the abundance of fruit which the <hi type="italic">gospel brought forth in all the world,</hi> <reference osisRef="Col.1.6">Col. i. 6</reference>. If some from whom we expected well, prove bad, it doth not follow but that others will be better. Christ encouraged himself with this in his undertaking; <hi type="italic">Though Israel be not gathered,</hi> not gathered to him, but gathered against him, <hi type="italic">yet shall I be glorious</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.49.5-Isa.49.6">Isa. xlix. 5, 6</reference>), as a <hi type="italic">Light to lighten the Gentiles.</hi> <div eID="gen24825" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24826" type="x-p"/> 3. Their opposition to Christ's exaltation shall be no obstruction to it (<reference osisRef="Mark.12.10-Mark.12.11">v. 10, 11</reference>); <hi type="italic">The stone which the builders rejected,</hi> notwithstanding that, is become <hi type="italic">the Head of the corner,</hi> is highly advanced as the <hi type="italic">Head-stone,</hi> and of necessary use and influence as the <hi type="italic">Corner-stone.</hi> God will set Christ as <hi type="italic">his King,</hi> upon his <hi type="italic">holy hill of Zion,</hi> in spite of <hi type="italic">their</hi> project, who would <hi type="italic">break his bands asunder.</hi> And all the world shall see and own this to <hi type="italic">be the Lord's doing,</hi> in justice to the Jews, and in compassion to the Gentiles. The exaltation of Christ <hi type="italic">was the Lord's doing,</hi> and it is <hi type="italic">his doing</hi> to exalt him in our hearts, and to set up his throne there; and if it be done, it cannot but be marvellous in our eyes. <div eID="gen24826" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24827" type="x-p"/> Now what effect had this parable upon the chief priests and scribes, whose conviction was designed by it? They knew <hi type="italic">he spoke this parable against them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.12.12">v. 12</reference>. They could not but see their own faces in the glass of it; and one would think it showed them their sin so very heinous, and their ruin so certain and great, that it should have frightened them into a compliance with Christ and his gospel, should have prevailed to bring them to repentance, at least to make them desist from their malicious purpose against him: but, instead of that, (1.) They <hi type="italic">sought to lay hold on him,</hi> and make him their prisoner immediately, and so to fulfil what he had just now said they would do to him, <reference osisRef="Mark.12.8">v. 8</reference>. (2.) Nothing restrained them from it but the awe they stood in of the people; they did not <hi type="italic">reverence</hi> Christ, nor had an <hi type="italic">fear of</hi> God before their eyes, but were afraid, if they should publicly lay hold on Christ, the mob would rise, and lay hold on them, and rescue them. (3.) They <hi type="italic">left him, and went their way;</hi> if they could not do hurt to him, they resolved he should not do good to them, and therefore they got out of the hearing of his powerful preaching, <hi type="italic">lest they should be converted and healed.</hi> Note, If men's prejudices be not conquered by the evidence of truth, they are but confirmed; and if the corruptions of the heart be not subdued by faithful reproofs, they are but enraged and exasperated. If the gospel be not a <hi type="italic">savour of life unto life,</hi> it will be a <hi type="italic">savour of death unto death.</hi>

<div eID="gen24827" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Question Respecting Tribute.</title> <div sID="gen24828" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">13</hi> And they send unto him certain of the Pharisees and of the Herodians, to catch him in <hi type="italic">his</hi> words. 14 And when they were come, they say unto him, Master, we know that thou art true, and carest for no man: for thou regardest not the person of men, but teachest the way of God in truth: Is it lawful to give tribute to Cæsar, or not? <hi type="super">15</hi> Shall we give, or shall we not give? But he, knowing their hypocrisy, said unto them, Why tempt ye me? bring me a penny, that I may see <hi type="italic">it.</hi> 16 And they brought <hi type="italic">it.</hi> And he saith unto them, Whose <hi type="italic">is</hi> this image and superscription? And they said unto him, Cæsar's. <hi type="super">17</hi> And Jesus answering said unto them, Render to Cæsar the things that are Cæsar's, and to God the things that are God's. And they marvelled at him. <div eID="gen24828" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24829" type="x-p"/> When the enemies of Christ, who thirsted for his blood, could not find occasion against him from what he said against them, they tried to ensnare him by putting questions to him. Here we have him tempted, or <hi type="italic">at</hi>tempted rather, with a question about the lawfulness of paying tribute to Cæsar. We had this narrative, <reference osisRef="Matt.22.15">Matt. xxii. 15</reference>. <div eID="gen24829" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24830" type="x-p"/> I. The persons they employed were the <hi type="italic">Pharisees</hi> and the <hi type="italic">Herodians,</hi> men that in this matter were contrary to one another, and yet concurred against Christ, <reference osisRef="Mark.12.13">v. 13</reference>. The Pharisees were great sticklers for the liberty of the Jews, and, if he should say, It is lawful to give tribute to Cæsar, they would incense the common people against him, and the Herodians would, underhand, assist them in it. The Herodians were great sticklers for the Roman power, and, if he should discountenance the paying of tribute to Cæsar, they would incense the governor against hum, yea, and the Pharisees, against their own principles, would join with them in it. It is no new thing for those that are at variance in other things, to join in a confederacy against Christ. <div eID="gen24830" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24831" type="x-p"/> II. The pretence they made was, that they desired him to resolve them a case of conscience, which was of great importance in the present juncture; and they take on them to have a high opinion of his ability to resolve it, <reference osisRef="Mark.12.14">v. 14</reference>. They complimented him at a high rate, called him <hi type="italic">Master,</hi> owned him for a Teacher of the <hi type="italic">way of God,</hi> a Teacher of it <hi type="italic">in truth,</hi> one who taught what was good, and upon principles of truth, who would not be brought by smiles or frowns to depart a step from the rules of equity and goodness; "<hi type="italic">Thou carest for no man,</hi> nor <hi type="italic">regardest the person of men,</hi> thou art not afraid of offending either the jealous prince on one hand, or the jealous people on the other; <hi type="italic">thou art right,</hi> and always in the right, and dost in a right manner declare good and evil, truth and falsehood." If they spoke as they thought concerning Christ, when they said, <hi type="italic">We know that thou art right,</hi> their persecuting him, and putting him to death, as a deceiver, was sin against knowledge; they knew him, and yet crucified him. However, a man's testimony shall be taken most strongly against himself, and <hi type="italic">out of their own mouths are they judged;</hi> they knew that he taught the way of God in truth, and yet rejected the counsel of God against themselves. The professions and pretences of hypocrites will be produced in evidence against them, and they will be self-condemned. But if they did not know or believe it, they <hi type="italic">lied unto God with their mouth, and flattered him with their tongue.</hi> <div eID="gen24831" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24832" type="x-p"/> III. The question they put was, <hi type="italic">Is it lawful to give tribute to Cæsar, or not?</hi> They would be thought desirous to know their duty. <hi type="italic">As a nation that did righteousness, they ask of God the ordinances of justice,</hi> when really they desired nothing but to know what he would say, in hopes that, which side soever he took of the question, they might take occasion from it to accuse him. Nothing is more likely to ensnare ministers, than bringing them to meddle with controversies about civil rights, and to settle land-marks between the prince and the subject, which it is fit should be done, while it is not at all fit that they should have the doing of it. They seemed to refer the determining of this matter to Christ; and he indeed was fit to determine it, for <hi type="italic">by him kings reign, and princes decree justice;</hi> they put the question fairly, <hi type="italic">Shall we give, or shall we not give?</hi> They seemed resolved to stand to his award; "If thou sayest that we must pay tribute, we will do it, thou we be made beggars by it. If thou sayest that we must not, we will not, though we be made traitors for it." Many seemed desirous to do it; as those proud men, <reference osisRef="Jer.42.20">Jer. xlii. 20</reference>. <div eID="gen24832" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24833" type="x-p"/> IV. Christ determined the question, and evaded the snare, by referring them to their national concessions already made, by which they were precluded from disputing this matter, <reference osisRef="Mark.12.15-Mark.12.17">v. 15-17</reference>. He <hi type="italic">knew their hypocrisy,</hi> the malice that was in their hearts against him, while <hi type="italic">with their mouth they showed all this love.</hi> Hypocrisy, though ever so artfully managed, cannot be concealed from the Lord Jesus. He sees the <hi type="italic">potsherd</hi> that is <hi type="italic">covered</hi> with the <hi type="italic">silver dross.</hi> He knew they intended to ensnare him, and therefore contrived the matter so as to ensnare them, and to oblige them by their own words to do what they were unwilling to do, which was, to pay their taxes honestly and quietly, and yet at the same time to screen himself against their exceptions. He made them acknowledge that the current money of their nation was Roman money, had the emperor's image on one side, and his <hi type="italic">superscription</hi> on the reverse; and if so, 1. Cæsar might command their money for the public benefit, because he had the custody and conduct of the state, wherein he ought to have his charges borne; <hi type="italic">Render to Cæsar the things that are Cæsar's.</hi> The circulation of the money is from him as the fountain, and therefore it must return to him. As far as it is <hi type="italic">his,</hi> so far it must be rendered to him; and how far it is <hi type="italic">his,</hi> and may be commanded by him, is to be judged by the constitution of the government, according as it is, and hath settled the prerogative of the prince and the property of the subject. 2. Cæsar might not command their consciences, nor did he pretend to it; he offered not to make any alteration in their religion. "Pay your tribute, therefore, without murmuring or disputing, but be sure to <hi type="italic">render to God the things that are God's.</hi>" Perhaps he referred to the parable he had just now put forth, in which he had condemned them for not <hi type="italic">rendering</hi> the fruits to the Lord of the vineyard, <reference osisRef="Mark.12.2">v. 2</reference>. Many that seem careful to give to men their due, are in no care to give God <hi type="italic">the glory due to his name;</hi> whereas our hearts and best affections are as much due to him as ever rent was to a landlord, or tribute to a prince. All that heard Christ, <hi type="italic">marvelled</hi> at the discretion of his answer, and how ingenuously he avoided the snare; but I doubt none were brought by it, as they ought to be, to render to God themselves and their devotions. Many will commend the wit of a sermon, that will not be commanded by the divine laws of a sermon.

<div eID="gen24833" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Question of the Sadducees.</title> <div sID="gen24834" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">18</hi> Then come unto him the Sadducees, which say there is no resurrection; and they asked him, saying, <hi type="super">19</hi> Master, Moses wrote unto us, If a man's brother die, and leave <hi type="italic">his</hi> wife <hi type="italic">behind him,</hi> and leave no children, that his brother should take his wife, and raise up seed unto his brother. 20 Now there were seven brethren: and the first took a wife, and dying left no seed. <hi type="super">21</hi> And the second took her, and died, neither left he any seed: and the third likewise. <hi type="super">22</hi> And the seven had her, and left no seed: last of all the woman died also. <hi type="super">23</hi> In the resurrection therefore, when they shall rise, whose wife shall she be of them? for the seven had her to wife. <hi type="super">24</hi> And Jesus answering said unto them, Do ye not therefore err, because ye know not the scriptures, neither the power of God? <hi type="super">25</hi> For when they shall rise from the dead, they neither marry, nor are given in marriage; but are as the angels which are in heaven. <hi type="super">26</hi> And as touching the dead, that they rise: have ye not read in the book of Moses, how in the bush God spake unto him, saying, I <hi type="italic">am</hi> the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob? <hi type="super">27</hi> He is not the God of the dead, but the God of the living: ye therefore do greatly err. <div eID="gen24834" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24835" type="x-p"/> The Sadducees, who were the deists of that age, here attack our Lord Jesus, it should seem, not as the scribes, and Pharisees, and chief-priests, with any malicious design upon his person; they were not bigots and persecutors, but sceptics and infidels, and their design was upon his doctrine, to hinder the spreading of that: they denied that there was any resurrection, and world of spirits, any state of rewards and punishments on the other side of death: now those great and fundamental truths which they denied, Christ had made it his business to establish and prove, and had carried the notion of them much further that ever it was before carried; and therefore they set themselves to perplex his doctrine. <div eID="gen24835" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24836" type="x-p"/> I. See here the method they take to entangle it; they quote the ancient law, by which, if a man died without issue, his brother was obliged to marry his widow, <reference osisRef="Mark.12.19">v. 19</reference>. They suppose a case to happen that, according to that law, seven brothers were, successively, the husbands of one woman, <reference osisRef="Mark.12.20">v. 20</reference>. Probably, these Sadducees, according to their wonted profaneness, intended hereby to ridicule that law, and so to bring the whole frame of the Mosaic institution into contempt, as absurd and inconvenient in the practice of it. Those who deny divine truths, commonly set themselves to disparage divine laws and ordinances. But this was only by the by; their design was to expose the doctrine of the resurrection; for they suppose that if there be a future state, it must be such a one as this, and then the doctrine, they think, is clogged either with this invincible absurdity, that a woman in that state must have seven husbands, or else with this insolvable difficulty, whose wife must she be. See with what subtlety these heretics <hi type="italic">undermine</hi> the truth; they do not <hi type="italic">deny</hi> it, nor say, <hi type="italic">There can be</hi> no resurrection; nay, they do not seem to doubt of it, nor say, <hi type="italic">If there be a resurrection,</hi> whose wife shall she be? as the devil to Christ, <hi type="italic">If thou be the Son of God.</hi> But, as though these beasts of the field were more subtle than the serpent himself, they pretend to own the truth, as if they were not Sadducees, no not they; who said that they denied the resurrection? They take it for granted that there is a resurrection, and would be thought to desire instruction concerning it, when really they are designing to give a fatal stab, and think that they shall do it. Note, It is the common artifice of heretics and Sadducees to perplex and entangle the truth, which they have not the impudence to deny. <div eID="gen24836" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24837" type="x-p"/> II. See here the method Christ takes to clear and establish this truth, which they attempted to darken, and give a shock to. This was a matter of moment, and therefore Christ does not pass it over lightly, but enlarges upon it, that, if they should not be reclaimed, yet others might be confirmed. <div eID="gen24837" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24838" type="x-p"/> 1. He charges the Sadducees with <hi type="italic">error,</hi> and charges that upon their <hi type="italic">ignorance.</hi> They who banter the doctrine of the resurrection as some do in our age, would be thought the only knowing men, because the only <hi type="italic">free thinkers,</hi> when really they are the fools in Israel, and the most <hi type="italic">enslaved</hi> and, prejudiced thinkers in the world. <hi type="italic">Do ye not therefore err?</hi> Ye cannot but be sensible of it yourselves, and that the cause of your error is, (1.) Because ye do not <hi type="italic">know the scriptures.</hi> Not but that the Sadducees had read the scriptures, and perhaps were ready in them; yet they might be truly said not to <hi type="italic">know the scriptures,</hi> because they did not know the sense and meaning of them, but put false constructions upon them; or they did not receive the scriptures as the word of God, but set up their own corrupt reasonings in opposition to the scripture, and would believe nothing but what they could see. Note, A right knowledge of the scripture, as the fountain whence all revealed religion now flows, and the foundation on which it is built, is the best preservative against error. Keep the truth, the scripture-truth, and it shall keep thee. (2.) Because ye <hi type="italic">know not the power of God.</hi> They could not but know that God is almighty, but they would not apply that doctrine to this matter, but gave up the truth to the objections of the impossibility of it, which would all have been answered, if they had but stuck to the doctrine of God's omnipotence, to which <hi type="italic">nothing is impossible.</hi> This therefore which God hath spoken once, we are concerned to hear twice, to hear and believe, to hear and apply—that <hi type="italic">power belongs to God,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.62.11">Ps. lxii. 11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.4.19-Rom.4.21">Rom. iv. 19-21</reference>. The same power that made soul and body and preserved them while they were together, can preserve the body safe, and the soul active, when they are parted, and can unite them together again; for <hi type="italic">behold, the Lord's arm is not shortened.</hi> The power of God, seen in the return of the spring (<reference osisRef="Ps.104.30">Ps. civ. 30</reference>), in the reviving of the corn (<reference osisRef="John.12.24">John xii. 24</reference>), in the restoring of an abject people to their prosperity (<reference osisRef="Ezek.37.12-Ezek.37.14">Ezek. xxxvii. 12-14</reference>), in the raising of so many to life, miraculously, both in the Old Testament and in the New, and especially in the resurrection of Christ (<reference osisRef="Eph.1.19-Eph.1.20">Eph. i. 19, 20</reference>), are all earnests of our resurrection by the same power (<reference osisRef="Phil.3.21">Phil. iii. 21</reference>); <hi type="italic">according to the mighty working whereby he is able to subdue all things to himself.</hi> <div eID="gen24838" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24839" type="x-p"/> 2. He sets aside all the force of their objection, by setting the doctrine of the future state in a true light (<reference osisRef="Mark.12.25">v. 25</reference>); <hi type="italic">When they shall rise from the dead, they neither marry, nor are given in marriage.</hi> It is a folly to ask, <hi type="italic">Whose wife shall she be of the seven?</hi> For the relation between husband and wife, though instituted in the earthly paradise, will not be known in the heavenly one. Turks and infidels expect sensual pleasures in their fools' paradise, but Christians <hi type="italic">know</hi> better things—that <hi type="italic">flesh and blood shall not inherit the kingdom of God</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Cor.15.50">1 Cor. xv. 50</reference>); and <hi type="italic">expect</hi> better things—even a full satisfaction in God's love and likeness (<reference osisRef="Ps.17.15">Ps. xvii. 15</reference>); they are <hi type="italic">as the angels of God in heaven,</hi> and we know that they have neither wives nor children. It is no wonder if we confound ourselves with endless absurdities, when we measure our ideas of the world of spirits by the affairs of this world of sense. <div eID="gen24839" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24840" type="x-p"/> III. He builds the doctrine of the future state, and of the blessedness of the righteous in that state, upon the covenant of God with Abraham, which God was pleased to own, being after Abraham's death, <reference osisRef="Mark.12.26-Mark.12.27">v. 26, 27</reference>. He appeals to the scriptures; <hi type="italic">Have ye not read in the book of Moses?</hi> We have some advantage in dealing with those that have <hi type="italic">read the scriptures,</hi> though many that have read them, <hi type="italic">wrest them,</hi> as these Sadducees did, to <hi type="italic">their own destruction.</hi> Now that which he refers them to is, what God says to Moses at the bush, <hi type="italic">I am the God of Abraham;</hi> not only, I <hi type="italic">was</hi> so, but I <hi type="italic">am</hi> so; I am the portion and happiness of Abraham, a God all-sufficient to him. Note, It is absurd to think that God's relation to Abraham should be continued, and thus solemnly recognised, if Abraham was annihilated, or that the <hi type="italic">living God</hi> should be the portion and happiness of a man that is dead, and must be for ever so; and therefore you must conclude, 1. That Abraham's soul exists and acts as a state of separation from the body. 2. That therefore, some time or other, the body must rise again; for there is such an innate inclination in a human soul towards its body, as would make a total and everlasting separation inconsistent with the ease and repose, much more with the bliss and joy of those souls that have the Lord for their God. Upon the whole matter, he concludes, <hi type="italic">Ye therefore do greatly err.</hi> Those that deny the resurrection, greatly err, and ought to be told so.

<div eID="gen24840" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Hopeful Scribe.</title> <div sID="gen24841" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">28</hi> And one of the scribes came, and having heard them reasoning together, and perceiving that he had answered them well, asked him, Which is the first commandment of all? <hi type="super">29</hi> And Jesus answered him, The first of all the commandments <hi type="italic">is,</hi> Hear, O Israel; The Lord our God is one Lord: <hi type="super">30</hi> And thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy mind, and with all thy strength: this <hi type="italic">is</hi> the first commandment. <hi type="super">31</hi> And the second <hi type="italic">is</hi> like, <hi type="italic">namely</hi> this, Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself. There is none other commandment greater than these. 32 And the scribe said unto him, Well, Master, thou hast said the truth: for there is one God; and there is none other but he: <hi type="super">33</hi> And to love him with all the heart, and with all the understanding, and with all the soul, and with all the strength, and to love <hi type="italic">his</hi> neighbour as himself, is more than all whole burnt offerings and sacrifices. <hi type="super">34</hi> And when Jesus saw that he answered discreetly, he said unto him, Thou art not far from the kingdom of God. And no man after that durst ask him <hi type="italic">any question.</hi> <div eID="gen24841" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24842" type="x-p"/> The scribes and Pharisees were (however bad otherwise) enemies to the Sadducees; now one would have expected that, when they heard Christ argue so well against the Sadducees, they would have countenanced him, as they did Paul when he appeared against the Sadducees (<reference osisRef="Acts.23.9">Acts xxiii. 9</reference>); but it had not the effect: because he did not fall in with them in the ceremonials of religion, he agreeing with them in the essentials, gained him no manner of respect with them. Only we have here an account of <hi type="italic">one</hi> of them, a scribe, who had so much civility in him as to take notice of Christ's answer to the Sadducees, and to own that he had <hi type="italic">answered well,</hi> and much to the purpose (<reference osisRef="Mark.12.28">v. 28</reference>); and we have reason to hope that he did not join with the other scribes in persecuting Christ; for here we have his application to Christ for instruction, and it was such as became him; not tempting Christ, but desiring to improve his acquaintance with him. <div eID="gen24842" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24843" type="x-p"/> I. He enquired, <hi type="italic">Which is the first commandment of all?</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.12.28">v. 28</reference>. He doth not mean the first in <hi type="italic">order,</hi> but the first in <hi type="italic">weight</hi> and <hi type="italic">dignity;</hi> "Which is that command which we ought to have in a special manner an eye to, and our obedience to which will lay a foundation for our obedience to all the rest?" Not that any commandment of God is little (they are all the commands of a great God), but some are greater than others, moral precepts than rituals, and of some we may say, They are the <hi type="italic">greatest of all.</hi> <div eID="gen24843" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24844" type="x-p"/> II. Christ gave him a direct answer to this enquiry, <reference osisRef="Mark.12.29-Mark.12.31">v. 29-31</reference>. Those that sincerely desire to be instructed concerning their duty, Christ will <hi type="italic">guide in judgment,</hi> and <hi type="italic">teach his way.</hi> He tells him, <div eID="gen24844" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24845" type="x-p"/> 1. That the great commandment of all, which is indeed inclusive of all, is, that of <hi type="italic">loving God with all our hearts.</hi> (1.) Where there is a commanding principle in the soul, there is a disposition to every other duty. Love is the leading affection of the soul; the love of God is the leading grace in the renewed soul. (2.) Where this is not, nothing else that is good is done, or done aright, or accepted, or done long. Loving God with all our heart, will effectually take us off from, and arm us against, all those things that are rivals with him for the throne in our souls, and will engage us to every thing by which he may be honoured, and with which he will be pleased; and no commandment will be grievous where this principle commands, and has the ascendant. Now here in, Mark, our Saviour prefixes to this command the great doctrinal truth upon which it is built (<reference osisRef="Mark.12.29">v. 29</reference>); <hi type="italic">Hear, O Israel, The Lord our God is one Lord;</hi> if we firmly believe this, it will follow, that we shall love him <hi type="italic">with all our heart.</hi> He is Jehovah, who has all amiable perfections in himself; he is <hi type="italic">our God,</hi> to whom we stand related and obliged; and therefore we ought to <hi type="italic">love him,</hi> to set our affections on him, let out own desire toward him, and take a delight in him; and he is <hi type="italic">one Lord,</hi> therefore he must be loved with our <hi type="italic">whole heart;</hi> he has the sole <hi type="italic">right to us,</hi> and therefore ought to have the sole <hi type="italic">possession of us.</hi> If he be one, our hearts must be one with him, and since there is no God besides, no rival must be admitted with him upon the throne. <div eID="gen24845" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24846" type="x-p"/> 2. That the second great commandment is, to <hi type="italic">love our neighbour as ourselves</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mark.12.31">v. 31</reference>), as truly and sincerely as we love ourselves, and in the same instances, and we must show it by <hi type="italic">doing as we would be done by.</hi> As we must therefore love God better than ourselves, because he is Jehovah, a being infinitely better than we are, and must love him with <hi type="italic">all our heart,</hi> because he is <hi type="italic">one Lord,</hi> and there is no other like him; so we must <hi type="italic">love our neighbour as ourselves,</hi> because he is of the same nature with ourselves; our hearts are fashioned alike, and my neighbour and myself are of one body, of one society, that of the world of mankind; and if a fellow-Christian, and of the same sacred society, the obligation is the stronger. <hi type="italic">Hath not one God created us?</hi> <reference osisRef="Mal.2.10">Mal. ii. 10</reference>. Has not one Christ redeemed us? Well might Christ say, <hi type="italic">There is no other commandment greater than these;</hi> for in these all the law is fulfilled, and if we make conscience of obedience to these, all other instances of obedience will follow of course. <div eID="gen24846" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24847" type="x-p"/> III. The scribe consented to what Christ said, and descanted upon it, <reference osisRef="Mark.12.32-Mark.12.33">v. 32, 33</reference>. 1. He commends Christ's decision of this question; <hi type="italic">Well, Master, thou hast said the truth.</hi> Christ's assertions needed not the scribe's attestations; but this scribe, being a man in authority, thought it would put some reputation upon what Christ said, to have it commended by him; and it shall be brought in evidence against those who persecuted Christ, as a deceiver, that one of themselves, even a scribe of their own, confessed that he <hi type="italic">said the truth,</hi> and said it <hi type="italic">well.</hi> And thus must we subscribe to Christ's sayings, must set to our seal that they are true. 2. He comments upon it. Christ had quoted that great doctrine, that <hi type="italic">the Lord our God is one Lord;</hi> and this he not only assented to, but added, "<hi type="italic">There is none other but he;</hi> and therefore we must have no other God besides." This excludes all rivals with him, and secures the throne in the heart entire for him. Christ had laid down that great law, of loving God <hi type="italic">with all our hearts;</hi> and this also he explains—that it is loving him <hi type="italic">with the understanding,</hi> as those that know what abundant reason we have to love him. Our love to God, as it must be an <hi type="italic">entire,</hi> so it must be an <hi type="italic">intelligent,</hi> love; we must love him with <hi type="italic">all</hi> the understanding, <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">ex holes tes syneseos</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">out of the whole understanding;</hi> our rational powers and faculties must all be set on work to lead out the affections of our souls toward God. Christ has said, "To love God and our neighbour is the greatest commandment of all;" "Yea," saith the scribe, "it is better, it is <hi type="italic">more than all whole-burnt-offerings and sacrifices,</hi> more acceptable to God, and will turn to a better account to ourselves." There were those who held, that the law of <hi type="italic">sacrifices</hi> was the <hi type="italic">greatest commandment</hi> of all; but this scribe readily agreed with our Saviour in this—that the law of love to God and our neighbour is greater than that of <hi type="italic">sacrifice,</hi> even than that of <hi type="italic">whole-burnt-offerings,</hi> which were intended purely for the honour of God. <div eID="gen24847" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24848" type="x-p"/> IV. Christ approved of what he said, and encouraged him to proceed in his enquiries of him, <reference osisRef="Mark.12.34">v. 34</reference>. 1. He owned that he understood well, as far as he went; so far, so good. <hi type="italic">Jesus saw that he answered discreetly,</hi> and was the more pleased with it, because he had of late met with so many even of the scribes, men of letters, that answered <hi type="italic">indiscreetly,</hi> as those that had <hi type="italic">no understanding,</hi> nor desired to have any. He answered <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">nounechos</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">as one that had a mind;</hi> as a rational intelligent man, as one that had his wits about him; as one whose reason was not blinded, whose judgment was not biassed, and whose forethought was not fettered, by the prejudices which other scribes were so much under the power of. He answered as one that allowed himself liberty and leisure to consider, as one that had considered. 2. He owned that he stood fair for a further advance; "<hi type="italic">Thou art not far from the kingdom of God,</hi> the kingdom of grace and glory; thou art in a likely way to be a Christian, a disciple of Christ. For the doctrine of Christ insists most upon these things, and is designed, and has a tendency direct, to bring thee to this." Note, There is hope of those who make a good use of the light they have, and go as far as that will carry them, that by the grace of God they will be led further, by the clearer discoveries God has to make to them. What became of this scribe we are not told, but would willingly hope that he took the hint Christ hereby gave him, and that, having been told by him, so much to his satisfaction, what was the great commandment of the law, he proceeded to enquire of him, or his apostles, what was the great commandment of the gospel too. Yet, if he did not, but took, up here, and went no further, we are not to think it strange; for there are many who are <hi type="italic">not far from the kingdom of God,</hi> and yet never come thither. Now, one would think, this should have invited many to consult him: but it had a contrary effect; <hi type="italic">No man, after that, durst ask him any question;</hi> every thing he said, was spoken with such authority and majesty, that every one stood in awe of him; those that desired to <hi type="italic">learn,</hi> were <hi type="italic">ashamed</hi> to ask, and those that designed to <hi type="italic">cavil,</hi> were <hi type="italic">afraid</hi> to ask.

<div eID="gen24848" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Christ the Son and Lord of David.</title> <div sID="gen24849" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">35</hi> And Jesus answered and said, while he taught in the temple, How say the scribes that Christ is the Son of David? 36 For David himself said by the Holy Ghost, The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> said to my Lord, Sit thou on my right hand, till I make thine enemies thy footstool. <hi type="super">37</hi> David therefore himself calleth him Lord; and whence is he <hi type="italic">then</hi> his son? And the common people heard him gladly. <hi type="super">38</hi> And he said unto them in his doctrine, Beware of the scribes, which love to go in long clothing, and <hi type="italic">love</hi> salutations in the marketplaces, <hi type="super">39</hi> And the chief seats in the synagogues, and the uppermost rooms at feasts: <hi type="super">40</hi> Which devour widows' houses, and for a pretence make long prayers: these shall receive greater damnation. <div eID="gen24849" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24850" type="x-p"/> Here, I. Christ shows the people how weak and defective the scribes were in their preaching, and how unable to solve the difficulties that occurred in the scriptures of the Old Testament, which they undertook to expound. Of this he gives an instance, which is not so fully related here as it was in Matthew. Christ was <hi type="italic">teaching in the temple:</hi> many things he said, which were not written; but notice is taken of this, because it will stir us up to enquire <hi type="italic">concerning Christ,</hi> and to enquire <hi type="italic">of him;</hi> for none can have the right knowledge of him but <hi type="italic">from himself;</hi> it is not to be had from <hi type="italic">the scribes,</hi> for they will soon be run aground. <div eID="gen24850" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24851" type="x-p"/> 1. They told the people that the Messiah was to be the <hi type="italic">Son of David</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mark.12.35">v. 35</reference>), and they were in the right; he was not only to descend from his loins, but to fill his throne (<reference osisRef="Luke.1.32">Luke i. 32</reference>); <hi type="italic">The Lord shall give him the throne of his father David.</hi> The scripture said it often, but the people took it as what the scribes said; whereas the truths of God should rather be quoted from our Bibles than from our ministers, for there is the original of them. <hi type="italic">Dulcius ex ipso fonte bibuntur aquæ—The waters are sweetest when drawn immediately from their source.</hi> <div eID="gen24851" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24852" type="x-p"/> 2. Yet they could not tell them how, notwithstanding that it was very proper for David, in spirit, the spirit of prophecy, to call him <hi type="italic">his Lord,</hi> as he doth, <reference osisRef="Ps.110.1">Ps. cx. 1</reference>. They had taught the people that concerning the Messiah, which would be for the honour of their nation—that he should be a branch of their royal family; but they had not taken care to teach them that which was for the honour of the Messiah himself—that he should be the Son of God, and, as such, and not otherwise, <hi type="italic">David's Lord.</hi> Thus they <hi type="italic">held the truth in unrighteousness,</hi> and were <hi type="italic">partial</hi> in the gospel, as well as in the law, of the Old Testament. They were able to say it, and prove it—that Christ was to be David's son; but if any should object, <hi type="italic">How then doth David himself call him Lord?</hi> they would not know how to avoid the force of the objection. Note, Those are unworthy to sit in Moses's seat, who, though they are able to preach the truth, are not in some measure able to defend it when they have preached it, and to convince gainsayers. <div eID="gen24852" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24853" type="x-p"/> Now this galled the scribes, to have their ignorance thus exposed, and, no doubt, incensed them more against Christ; but the <hi type="italic">common people heard him gladly,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.12.37">v. 37</reference>. What he preached was surprising and affecting; and though it reflected upon the scribes, it was instructive to them, and they had never heard such preaching. Probably there was something more than ordinarily commanding and charming in his voice and way of delivery, which recommended him to the affections of the common people; for we do not find that any were wrought upon to <hi type="italic">believe</hi> in him, and to <hi type="italic">follow</hi> him, but he was to them as a <hi type="italic">lovely song of one that could play well on an instrument;</hi> as Ezekiel was to his hearers, <reference osisRef="Ezek.33.32">Ezek. xxxiii. 32</reference>. And perhaps some of these cried, <hi type="italic">Crucify him,</hi> as Herod heard John Baptist gladly, and yet cut off his head. <div eID="gen24853" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24854" type="x-p"/> II. He cautions the people to take heed of suffering themselves to be imposed upon by the scribes, and of being infected with their pride and hypocrisy; <hi type="italic">He said unto them in his doctrine, "Beware of the scribes</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mark.12.38">v. 38</reference>); stand upon your guard, that you neither imbibe their peculiar opinions, nor the opinions of the people concerning them." The charge is long as drawn up against them in the parallel place (<reference osisRef="Matt.23.1-Matt.23.39">Matt. xxiii.</reference>); it is here contracted. <div eID="gen24854" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24855" type="x-p"/> 1. They affect to appear <hi type="italic">very great;</hi> for they go in <hi type="italic">long clothing,</hi> with vestures <hi type="italic">down to their feet,</hi> and in those they walk <hi type="italic">about the streets,</hi> as princes, or judges, or gentlemen of the long robe. Their going in such clothing was not sinful, but their <hi type="italic">loving</hi> to go in it, priding themselves in it, valuing themselves on it, commanding respect by it, saying to their long clothes, as Saul to Samuel, <hi type="italic">Honour me now before this people,</hi> this was a product of pride. Christ would have his disciples go with <hi type="italic">their loins girt.</hi> <div eID="gen24855" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24856" type="x-p"/> 2. They affect to appear <hi type="italic">very good;</hi> for they pray, they make <hi type="italic">long prayers,</hi> as if they were very intimate with heaven, and had a deal of business there. They took care it should be known that they prayed, that they prayed long, which, some think, intimates that they prayed not for themselves only, but for others, and therein were very particular and very large; this they did <hi type="italic">for a pretence,</hi> that they might seem to love prayer, not only for God's sake, whom hereby they pretended to glorify, but for their neighbour's sake, whom hereby they pretended to be serviceable to. <div eID="gen24856" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24857" type="x-p"/> 3. They here aimed to <hi type="italic">advance</hi> themselves: they coveted applause, and were fond of it; they loved <hi type="italic">salutations in the marketplaces,</hi> and the <hi type="italic">chief seats in the synagogues, and the uppermost rooms at feasts;</hi> these pleased a vain fancy; to have these given them, they thought, expressed the value <hi type="italic">they</hi> had for them, who did know them, and gained them respect for those who did not. <div eID="gen24857" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24858" type="x-p"/> 4. They herein aimed to <hi type="italic">enrich</hi> themselves. They <hi type="italic">devoured widows' houses,</hi> made themselves masters of their estates by some trick or other; it was to screen themselves from the suspicion of dishonesty, that they put on the mask of piety; and that they might not be thought as bad as the worst, they were studious to seem as good as the best. Let fraud and oppression be thought the worse of for their having <hi type="italic">profaned</hi> and <hi type="italic">disgraced</hi> long prayers; but let not prayers, no nor <hi type="italic">long prayers,</hi> be thought the worse of, if made in humility and sincerity, for their having been by some thus abused. But as iniquity, thus disguised with a show of piety, is <hi type="italic">double</hi> iniquity, so its doom will be doubly heavy; <hi type="italic">These shall receive great damnation;</hi> greater than those that live without prayer, greater than they would have received for the wrong done to the poor widows, if it had not been thus disguised. Note, The damnation of hypocrites will be of all others the greatest damnation.

<div eID="gen24858" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Christ Commendeth the Poor Widow.</title> <div sID="gen24859" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">41</hi> And Jesus sat over against the treasury, and beheld how the people cast money into the treasury: and many that were rich cast in much. <hi type="super">42</hi> And there came a certain poor widow, and she threw in two mites, which make a farthing. <hi type="super">43</hi> And he called <hi type="italic">unto him</hi> his disciples, and saith unto them, Verily I say unto you, That this poor widow hath cast more in, than all they which have cast into the treasury: <hi type="super">44</hi> For all <hi type="italic">they</hi> did cast in of their abundance; but she of her want did cast in all that she had, <hi type="italic">even</hi> all her living. <div eID="gen24859" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24860" type="x-p"/> This passage of story was not in Matthew, but is here and in Luke; it is Christ's commendation of the poor widow, that cast <hi type="italic">two mites</hi> into the treasury, which our Saviour, busy as he was in preaching, found leisure to take notice of. Observe, <div eID="gen24860" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24861" type="x-p"/> I. There was a <hi type="italic">public fund</hi> for charity, into which contributions were brought, and out of which distributions were made; a poor's-box, and this in <hi type="italic">the temple;</hi> for works of charity and works of piety very fitly go together; where God is honoured by our worship, it is proper he should be honoured by the relief of his poor; and we often find <hi type="italic">prayers</hi> and <hi type="italic">alms</hi> in conjunction, as <reference osisRef="Acts.10.2">Acts x. 2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.10.4">4</reference>. It is good to erect public receptacles of charity for the inviting and directing of private hands in giving to the poor; nay it is good for those who are of ability to have funds of their own, to <hi type="italic">lay by as God has prospered them</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Cor.16.2">1 Cor. xvi. 2</reference>), that they might have something ready to give when an object of charity offers itself, which is before dedicated to such uses. <div eID="gen24861" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24862" type="x-p"/> II. Jesus Christ had <hi type="italic">an eye</hi> upon it; <hi type="italic">He sat over against the treasury, and beheld now the people cast money into it;</hi> not grudging either that he had none to cast in, or had not the disposal of that which was cast in, but observing what was cast in. Note, Our Lord Jesus takes notice of what we contribute to pious and charitable uses; whether we give liberally or sparingly; whether cheerfully or with reluctance and ill-will; nay, he looks at the heart; he observes what principles we act upon, and what our views are, in giving alms; and whether we do it as unto the Lord, or only to be seen of men. <div eID="gen24862" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24863" type="x-p"/> III. He saw <hi type="italic">many that were rich cast in much:</hi> and it was a good sight to see rich people charitable, to see <hi type="italic">many</hi> rich people so, and to see them not only cast in, but cast in <hi type="italic">much.</hi> Note, Those that are rich, ought to give richly; if God give abundantly to us, he expects we should give abundantly to the poor; and it is not enough for those that are rich, to say, that they give as much as others do, who perhaps have much less of the world than they have, but they must give in proportion to their estates; and if objects of charity do not present themselves, that require so much, they ought to enquire them out, and to <hi type="italic">devise liberal things.</hi> <div eID="gen24863" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24864" type="x-p"/> IV. There was a <hi type="italic">poor widow that cast in two mites, which make a farthing</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mark.12.42">v. 42</reference>); and our Lord Jesus highly commended her; <hi type="italic">called his disciples</hi> to him, and bid them take notice of it (<reference osisRef="Mark.12.43">v. 43</reference>); told them that she could very ill spare that which she gave, she had scarcely enough for herself, it was <hi type="italic">all her living,</hi> all she had to live upon for that day, and perhaps a great part of what she had earned by her labour the day before; and that forasmuch as he knew she did it from a truly charitable disposition, he reckoned it more than all that put together, which the rich people threw in; for they did <hi type="italic">cast in of their abundance, but she of her want,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.12.44">v. 44</reference>. Now many would have been ready to censure this <hi type="italic">poor widow,</hi> and to think she did ill; why should she give to others, when she had little enough for herself? Charity begins at home; or, if she would give it, why did she not bestow it upon some poor body that she knew? What occasion was there for her bringing it to the <hi type="italic">treasury</hi> to be disposed of by the chief priests, who, we have reason to fear, were partial in the disposal of it? It is so rare a thing to find any that would not blame this widow, that we cannot expect to find any that will imitate her; and yet our Saviour commends her, and therefore we are sure that she did very well and wisely. If Christ saith, <hi type="italic">Well-done,</hi> no matter who saith otherwise; and we must hence learn, 1. That <hi type="italic">giving alms,</hi> is an excellent good thing, and highly pleasing to the Lord Jesus; and if we be humble and sincere in it, he will graciously accept of it, though in some circumstances there may not be all the discretion in the world. 2.
