Those that have but a <hi type="italic">little,</hi> ought to give alms out of <hi type="italic">their little.</hi> Those that live by their labour, from hand to mouth, must <hi type="italic">give to those that need,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eph.4.28">Eph. iv. 28</reference>. 3. It is very good for us to straiten and deny ourselves, that we may be able to give the more to the poor; to deny ourselves not only superfluities, but even conveniences, for the sake of charity. We should in many cases pinch ourselves, that we may supply the necessities of others; this is loving our neighbours as ourselves. 4. Public charities should be encouraged, for they bring upon a nation public blessings; and though there may be some mismanagement of them, yet that is not a good reason why we should not bring in our <hi type="italic">quota</hi> to them. 5. Though we can give but a <hi type="italic">little</hi> in charity, yet if it be according to our ability, and be given with an upright heart, it shall be accepted of Christ, who requires <hi type="italic">according to what a man has, and not according to what he has not;</hi> two mites shall be put upon the score, and brought to account, if given in a right manner, as if they had been two pounds. 6. It is much to the praise of charity, when we give not only <hi type="italic">to our power,</hi> but <hi type="italic">beyond our power,</hi> as the Macedonian churches, whose <hi type="italic">deep poverty abounded to the riches of their liberality,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.8.2-2Cor.8.3">2 Cor. viii. 2, 3</reference>. When we can cheerfully provide for others, out of our own necessary provision, as the widow of Sarepta for Elijah, and Christ for his five thousand guests, and trust God to provide for us some other way, <hi type="italic">this is thank-worthy.</hi>  <chapter eID="Mark.12"/> <div eID="gen24864" type="x-p"/>

<div eID="gen24867" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen24866" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Destruction of the Temple Foretold.</title> <div sID="gen24868" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> And as he went out of the temple, one of his disciples saith unto him, Master, see what manner of stones and what buildings <hi type="italic">are here!</hi> <hi type="super">2</hi> And Jesus answering said unto him, Seest thou these great buildings? there shall not be left one stone upon another, that shall not be thrown down. <hi type="super">3</hi> And as he sat upon the mount of Olives over against the temple, Peter and James and John and Andrew asked him privately, <hi type="super">4</hi> Tell us, when shall these things be? and what <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> the sign when all these things shall be fulfilled? <div eID="gen24868" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24869" type="x-p"/> We may here see, <div eID="gen24869" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24870" type="x-p"/> I. How apt many of Christ's own disciples are to idolize things that look <hi type="italic">great,</hi> and have been long looked upon as <hi type="italic">sacred.</hi> They had heard Christ complain of those who had made the temple a <hi type="italic">den of thieves;</hi> and yet, when he quitted it, for the wickedness that remained in it, they court him to be as much in love as they were with the stately structure and adorning of it. One of them said to him, "Look, Master, <hi type="italic">what manner of stones, and what buildings are here,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.13.1">v. 1</reference>. We never saw the like in Galilee; O do not leave this fine place." <div eID="gen24870" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24871" type="x-p"/> II. How little Christ values external pomp, where there is not real purity; "<hi type="italic">Seest thou these great buildings</hi>" (saith Christ), "and admirest thou them? I tell thee, the time is at hand when <hi type="italic">there shall not be left one stone upon another, that shall not be thrown down,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Mark.13.2">v. 2</reference>. And the sumptuousness of the fabric shall be no security to it, no nor move any compassion in the Lord Jesus towards it. He looks with <hi type="italic">pity</hi> upon the ruin of precious souls, and weeps over them, for on them he has put great value; but we do not find him look with any pity upon the ruin of a magnificent house, when he is driven out of it by sin, for that is of small value with him. With what little concern doth he say, <hi type="italic">Not one stone shall be left on another!</hi> Much of the strength of the temple lay in the largeness of the stones, and if these be thrown down, no footstep, no remembrance, of it will remain. While any part remained standing, there might be some hopes of the repair of it; but what hope is there, when not one stone is <hi type="italic">left upon another?</hi> <div eID="gen24871" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24872" type="x-p"/> III. How natural it is to us to desire to know things to come, and the times of them; more inquisitive we are apt to be about that than about our duty. His disciples knew not how to <hi type="italic">digest</hi> this doctrine of the ruin of the temple, which they thought must be their Master's royal palace, and in which they expected their preferment, and to have the posts of honour; and therefore they were in pain till they got him alone, and got more out of him concerning this matter. As he was returning to Bethany therefore, he <hi type="italic">sat upon the mount of Olives, over against the temple,</hi> where he had a full view of it; and there four of them agreed to <hi type="italic">ask him privately,</hi> what he meant by the destroying of the temple, which they understood no more than they did the predictions of his own death, so inconsistent was it with their scheme. Probably, though these four proposed the question, yet Christ's discourse, in answer to it, was in the hearing of the rest of the disciples, yet <hi type="italic">privately,</hi> that is, apart from the multitude. Their enquiry is, <hi type="italic">When shall these things be?</hi> They will not question, at least not seem to question, whether they shall be or no (for their Master has said that they shall), but are willing to hope it is a great way off. Yet they ask not precisely the day and year (therein they were modest), but say, "Tell us <hi type="italic">what shall be the sign, when all these things shall be fulfilled?</hi> What presages shall there be of them, and how may we prognosticate their approach?"

<div eID="gen24872" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Great Afflictions Foretold.</title> <div sID="gen24873" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">5</hi> And Jesus answering them began to say, Take heed lest any <hi type="italic">man</hi> deceive you: <hi type="super">6</hi> For many shall come in my name, saying, I am <hi type="italic">Christ;</hi> and shall deceive many. 7 And when ye shall hear of wars and rumours of wars, be ye not troubled: for <hi type="italic">such things</hi> must needs be; but the end <hi type="italic">shall</hi> not <hi type="italic">be</hi> yet. <hi type="super">8</hi> For nation shall rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom: and there shall be earthquakes in divers places, and there shall be famines and troubles: these <hi type="italic">are</hi> the beginnings of sorrows. <hi type="super">9</hi> But take heed to yourselves: for they shall deliver you up to councils; and in the synagogues ye shall be beaten: and ye shall be brought before rulers and kings for my sake, for a testimony against them. 10 And the gospel must first be published among all nations. 11 But when they shall lead <hi type="italic">you,</hi> and deliver you up, take no thought beforehand what ye shall speak, neither do ye premeditate: but whatsoever shall be given you in that hour, that speak ye: for it is not ye that speak, but the Holy Ghost. <hi type="super">12</hi> Now the brother shall betray the brother to death, and the father the son; and children shall rise up against <hi type="italic">their</hi> parents, and shall cause them to be put to death. <hi type="super">13</hi> And ye shall be hated of all <hi type="italic">men</hi> for my name's sake: but he that shall endure unto the end, the same shall be saved. <div eID="gen24873" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24874" type="x-p"/> Our Lord Jesus, in reply to their question, sets himself, not so much to satisfy their curiosity as to direct their consciences; leaves them still in the dark concerning the <hi type="italic">times</hi> and <hi type="italic">seasons,</hi> which the father has <hi type="italic">kept in his own power,</hi> and which <hi type="italic">it was not for them to know;</hi> but gives them the cautions which were needful, with reference to the events that should now shortly come to pass. <div eID="gen24874" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24875" type="x-p"/> I. They must take heed that they be not <hi type="italic">deceived</hi> by the <hi type="italic">seducers</hi> and <hi type="italic">imposters</hi> that should now shortly arise (<reference osisRef="Mark.13.5-Mark.13.6">v. 5, 6</reference>); "<hi type="italic">Take heed lest any man deceive you,</hi> lest, having found the <hi type="italic">true Messiah,</hi> you lose him again in the crowd of <hi type="italic">pretenders,</hi> or be inveigled to embrace others in rivalship with him. Many shall come <hi type="italic">in my name</hi> (not in the name of <hi type="italic">Jesus</hi>), but saying, <hi type="italic">I am the Christ,</hi> and so claiming the dignities which I only an entitled to." After the Jews had rejected the true Christ, they were imposed upon, and so <hi type="italic">ex</hi>posed by many false Christs, but never before; those false Christs <hi type="italic">deceived many;</hi> Therefore <hi type="italic">take heed lest they deceive you.</hi> Note, When many are deceived, we should thereby be awakened to look to ourselves. <div eID="gen24875" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24876" type="x-p"/> II. They must take heed that they be not <hi type="italic">disturbed</hi> at the noise of wars, which they should be alarmed with, <reference osisRef="Mark.13.7-Mark.13.8">v. 7, 8</reference>. Sin introduced <hi type="italic">wars,</hi> and they come <hi type="italic">from men's lusts.</hi> But at some times the nations are more distracted and wasted with wars than at other times; so it shall be now; Christ was born into the world when there was a general peace, but soon after he went out of the world there were general wars; <hi type="italic">Nation shall rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom.</hi> And what will become of them then who are to preach the gospel to every nation? <hi type="italic">Inter arma silent leges—Amidst the clash of arms, the voice of law is not heard.</hi> "But <hi type="italic">be not troubled at it.</hi>" 1. "Let it be no <hi type="italic">surprise</hi> to you; you are bid to expect it, and <hi type="italic">such things must needs be,</hi> for God has appointed them, in order to further accomplishment of his purposes, and by the <hi type="italic">wars of the Jews</hi>" (which Josephus has given us a large account of) "God will punish the <hi type="italic">wickedness of the Jews.</hi>" 2. "Let it be no <hi type="italic">terror</hi> to you, as if your interest were in danger of being overthrown, or your work obstructed by these wars; you have no concern in them, and therefore need not be apprehensive of any damage by them." Note, Those that despise the smiles of the world, and do not court and covet them, may despise the frowns of the world, and need not fear them. If we seek not to rise with them that <hi type="italic">rise in the world,</hi> why should we dread falling with them that fall in the world? 3. "Let it not be looked upon as an omen of the approaching period of the world, for the <hi type="italic">end is not yet,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.13.7">v. 7</reference>. Think not that these <hi type="italic">wars</hi> will bring the world to a period; no, there are other intermediate counsels to be fulfilled betwixt that end and the end of all things, which are designed to prepare you for the end, but not to hasten it out of due time." 4. "Let it not be looked upon as if in them God has done his worst; no, he has more arrows in his quiver, and they are <hi type="italic">ordained against the persecutors;</hi> be not troubled at the wars you shall hear of, for they are but <hi type="italic">the beginnings of sorrows,</hi> and therefore, instead of being disturbed at <hi type="italic">them,</hi> you ought to <hi type="italic">prepare for worse;</hi> for there shall also be <hi type="italic">earthquakes in divers places,</hi> which shall bury multitudes in the ruins of their own houses, and there <hi type="italic">shall be famines,</hi> by which many of the poor shall perish for want of bread, and <hi type="italic">troubles</hi> and commotions; so that there shall be no peace to him that <hi type="italic">goes out</hi> or <hi type="italic">comes in.</hi> The world shall be full of <hi type="italic">troubles,</hi> but <hi type="italic">be not ye troubled;</hi> without are <hi type="italic">fightings,</hi> within are <hi type="italic">fears,</hi> but <hi type="italic">fear not ye their fear.</hi>" Note, The disciples of Christ, if it be not their own fault, may enjoy a holy security and serenity of mind, when all about them is in the greatest disorder. <div eID="gen24876" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24877" type="x-p"/> III. They must take heed that they be not <hi type="italic">drawn away</hi> from Christ, and from their duty to him, by the sufferings they should meet with for Christ's sake. Again, he saith, "<hi type="italic">Take heed to yourselves,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.13.9">v. 9</reference>. Though you may escape the <hi type="italic">sword of war,</hi> better than some of your neighbours, because you interest not yourselves in the public quarrels, yet be not secure; you will be exposed to the <hi type="italic">sword of justice</hi> more than others, and the parties that contend with one another, will unite against you. <hi type="italic">Take heed</hi> therefore lest you <hi type="italic">deceive</hi> yourselves with the hopes of outward prosperity, and such a temporal kingdom as you have been dreaming of, when it is <hi type="italic">through many tribulations</hi> that <hi type="italic">you must enter into the kingdom of God.</hi> Take heed lest you needlessly expose yourselves to trouble, and pull it upon your own head. <hi type="italic">Take heed</hi> what you say and do, for you will have many eyes upon you." Observe, <div eID="gen24877" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24878" type="x-p"/> 1. What the trouble is which they must expect. <div eID="gen24878" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24879" type="x-p"/> (1.) They shall be <hi type="italic">hated of all men;</hi> trouble enough! The thoughts of <hi type="italic">being hated</hi> are grievous to a tender spirit, and the fruits of that hatred must needs be a constant vexation; those that are <hi type="italic">malicious,</hi> will be <hi type="italic">mischievous.</hi> It was not for any thing amiss in them, or done amiss by them, that they were <hi type="italic">hated,</hi> but for Christ's name sake, because they were called by his name, called upon his name, preached his name, and wrought miracles in his name. The world hated them because he loved them. <div eID="gen24879" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24880" type="x-p"/> (2.) Their own <hi type="italic">relations</hi> shall <hi type="italic">betray them,</hi> those to whom they were most nearly allied, and on whom therefore they depended for protection; "They <hi type="italic">shall betray you,</hi> shall inform against you, and be your prosecutors." If a father has a child that is a Christian, he shall become void of natural affection, it shall be swallowed up in bigotry, and he shall betray his own child to the persecutors, as if he were a worshipper of other gods, <reference osisRef="Deut.13.6-Deut.13.10">Deut. xiii. 6-10</reference>. <div eID="gen24880" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24881" type="x-p"/> (3.) Their <hi type="italic">church-rulers</hi> shall inflict <hi type="italic">their censures</hi> upon them; "You shall be <hi type="italic">delivered up</hi> to the great Sanhedrim at Jerusalem, and to the inferior courts and consistories in other cities, and shall be <hi type="italic">beaten in the synagogues</hi> with forty stripes at a time, as offenders against the law which was read in the synagogue." It is no new thing for the church's artillery, through the treachery of its officers, to be turned against some of its best friends. <div eID="gen24881" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24882" type="x-p"/> (4.) <hi type="italic">Governors</hi> and <hi type="italic">kings</hi> shall use their power against them. Because the Jews have not power to put them to death, they shall incense the Roman powers against them, as they did Herod against James and Peter; and they shall <hi type="italic">cause you to be put to death,</hi> as enemies to the empire. They must resist unto blood, and still resist. <div eID="gen24882" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24883" type="x-p"/> 2. What they shall have to comfort themselves with, in the midst of these great and sore troubles. <div eID="gen24883" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24884" type="x-p"/> (1.) That the work they were called to should be carried on and prosper, notwithstanding all this opposition which they should meet with in it (<reference osisRef="Mark.13.10">v. 10</reference>); "<hi type="italic">The gospel</hi> shall, for all this, be <hi type="italic">published among all nations,</hi> and before the destruction of Jerusalem the <hi type="italic">sound</hi> of it shall <hi type="italic">go forth into all the earth;</hi> not only through all the nation of the Jews, but to all the nations of the earth." It is comfort to those who suffer for the gospel, that, though they may be crushed and borne down, the gospel cannot; it shall keep its ground, and carry the day. <div eID="gen24884" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24885" type="x-p"/> (2.) That their sufferings, instead of obstructing their work, should forward it; "Your being <hi type="italic">brought before governors and kings</hi> shall be for <hi type="italic">a testimony of them</hi> (so some read it, <reference osisRef="Mark.13.9">v. 9</reference>); it shall give you an opportunity of preaching the gospel to those before whom you are brought as criminals, to whom otherwise you could not have access." Thus St. Paul's being brought before Felix, and Festus, and Agrippa, and Nero, was a testimony to them concerning Christ and his gospel. Or, as we read it, It shall be for a testimony <hi type="italic">against them,</hi> against both the judges and the prosecutors, who pursue those with the utmost rage that appear, upon examination, to be not only innocent but excellent persons. The gospel is a testimony to us concerning Christ and heaven. If we receive it, it will be a testimony for us: it will justify and save us; if not, it will be a testimony <hi type="italic">against</hi> us in the great day. <div eID="gen24885" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24886" type="x-p"/> (3.) That, when they were brought before kings and governors for Christ's sake, they should have special assistance from heaven, to plead Christ's cause and their own (<reference osisRef="Mark.13.11">v. 11</reference>); "<hi type="italic">Take no thought before-hand what he shall speak,</hi> be not solicitous how to address yourselves to great men, so as to obtain their favour; your cause is just and glorious, and needs not be supported by premeditated speeches and harangues; but <hi type="italic">whatsoever shall be given you in that hour,</hi> whatsoever shall be suggested to you, and put into your minds, and into your mouths" (<hi type="italic">pro re nat&#226;—on the spur of the occasion</hi>), "that <hi type="italic">speak ye,</hi> and fear not the success of it, because it is <hi type="italic">off-hand,</hi> for <hi type="italic">it is not ye that speak,</hi> purely by the strength of your own wisdom, consideration, and resolution, but it is <hi type="italic">the Holy Ghost.</hi>" Note, Those whom Christ calls out to be advocates for him, shall be furnished with full instructions: and when we are engaged in the service of Christ, we may depend upon the aids of the Spirit of Christ. <div eID="gen24886" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24887" type="x-p"/> (4.) That heaven at last would <hi type="italic">make amends for all;</hi> "You will meet with a great deal of hardship in your way, but have a good heart on it, your warfare will be accomplished, and your testimony finished, and <hi type="italic">he that shall endure to the end, the same shall be saved,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Mark.13.13">v. 13</reference>. Perseverance gains the crown. The salvation here promised is more than a deliverance from evil, it is an everlasting blessedness, which shall be an abundant recompence for all their services and sufferings. All this we have, <reference osisRef="Matt.10.17">Matt. x. 17</reference>, &c.

<div eID="gen24887" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Destruction of the Temple Foretold.</title> <div sID="gen24888" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">14</hi> But when ye shall see the abomination of desolation, spoken of by Daniel the prophet, standing where it ought not, (let him that readeth understand,) then let them that be in Judæa flee to the mountains: <hi type="super">15</hi> And let him that is on the housetop not go down into the house, neither enter <hi type="italic">therein,</hi> to take any thing out of his house: <hi type="super">16</hi> And let him that is in the field not turn back again for to take up his garment. <hi type="super">17</hi> But woe to them that are with child, and to them that give suck in those days! <hi type="super">18</hi> And pray ye that your flight be not in the winter. <hi type="super">19</hi> For <hi type="italic">in</hi> those days shall be affliction, such as was not from the beginning of the creation which God created unto this time, neither shall be. <hi type="super">20</hi> And except that the Lord had shortened those days, no flesh should be saved: but for the elect's sake, whom he hath chosen, he hath shortened the days. <hi type="super">21</hi> And then if any man shall say to you, Lo, here <hi type="italic">is</hi> Christ; or, lo, <hi type="italic">he is</hi> there; believe <hi type="italic">him</hi> not: <hi type="super">22</hi> For false Christs and false prophets shall rise, and shall show signs and wonders, to seduce, if <hi type="italic">it were</hi> possible, even the elect. <hi type="super">23</hi> But take ye heed: behold, I have foretold you all things. <div eID="gen24888" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24889" type="x-p"/> The Jews, in rebelling against the Romans, and in persecuting the Christians, were hastening to their own ruin apace, both efficiently and meritoriously, were setting both God and man against them; see <reference osisRef="1Thess.2.15">1 Thess. ii. 15</reference>. Now here we have a prediction of that ruin which came upon them within less than forty years after this: we had it before, <reference osisRef="Matt.24.15">Matt. xxiv. 15</reference>, &c. Observe, <div eID="gen24889" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24890" type="x-p"/> I. What is here foretold concerning it. <div eID="gen24890" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24891" type="x-p"/> 1. That the Roman <hi type="italic">armies</hi> should make a descent upon Judea, and invest Jerusalem, the holy city. These were the <hi type="italic">abomination</hi> of <hi type="italic">desolation,</hi> which the Jews did <hi type="italic">abominate,</hi> and by which they should be made <hi type="italic">desolate.</hi> The country of thine enemy is called <hi type="italic">the land which thou abhorrest,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.7.16">Isa. vii. 16</reference>. <hi type="italic">Therefore</hi> it was an abomination, because it brought with it nothing but desolation. They had rejected Christ as an <hi type="italic">abomination,</hi> who would have been their <hi type="italic">salvation;</hi> and now God brought upon them an abomination that would be their <hi type="italic">desolation,</hi> thus spoken of by Daniel <hi type="italic">the prophet</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mark.9.27">ch. ix. 27</reference>), as that by which this sacrifice and offering should be made to cease. This army stood <hi type="italic">where it ought not,</hi> in and about the <hi type="italic">holy city,</hi> which the heathen ought not to have approached, nor would have been suffered to approach, if Jerusalem had not first profaned the crown of their holiness. This the church complains of, <reference osisRef="Lam.1.10">Lam. i. 10</reference>, The <hi type="italic">heathen entered into her sanctuary, whom thou didst command that they should not enter into the congregation;</hi> but sin made the breach, at which the glory went out, and the abomination of desolation broke in, <hi type="italic">and stood where it ought not.</hi> Now, let <hi type="italic">him that readeth</hi> this, <hi type="italic">understand it,</hi> and endeavor to take it right. Prophecies should not be too plain, and yet intelligible to those that search them; and they are best understood by comparing them first with one another, and at last with the event. <div eID="gen24891" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24892" type="x-p"/> 2. That when the Roman <hi type="italic">army</hi> should come into the country, there would be no safety any where but by quitting the country, and that with all possible expedition. It will be in vain to <hi type="italic">fight,</hi> the enemies will be too hard for them; in vain to <hi type="italic">abscond,</hi> the enemies will find them out; and in vain to <hi type="italic">capitulate,</hi> the enemies will give them no quarter; a man cannot have so much as his life given him for a prey, but by <hi type="italic">fleeing to the mountains</hi> out of Judea; and let him take the first alarm, and make the best of his way. If he be <hi type="italic">on the house-top,</hi> trying from thence to discover the motions of the enemy, and spies them coming, let him not <hi type="italic">go down, to take any thing out of the house,</hi> for it will occasion his losing of time, which is more precious than his best goods, and will but encumber him, and embarrass his flight. If he be in the field, and there discover the approach of the enemy, let him get away as he is, and not <hi type="italic">turn back again, to take up his garment,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.13.16">v. 16</reference>. If he can save his life, let him reckon it is a good bargain, though he can save nothing else, and be thankful to God, that, though he is cut short, he is not cut off. <div eID="gen24892" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24893" type="x-p"/> 3. That it would go very hard at that time with poor mothers and nurses (<reference osisRef="Mark.13.17">v. 17</reference>); "<hi type="italic">Woe to them that are with child,</hi> that dare not go into strange places, that cannot shift for themselves, nor make haste as others can. And <hi type="italic">woe to them that give suck,</hi> that know not how either to leave the tender infants behind them, or to carry them along with them." Such is the vanity of the creature, that the time may often be, when the greatest comforts may prove the greatest burthens. It would likewise be very uncomfortable, if they should be forced to flee <hi type="italic">in the winter</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mark.13.18">v. 18</reference>), when the <hi type="italic">weather</hi> and <hi type="italic">ways</hi> were bad, when the roads would be scarcely passable, especially in the mountains to which they must flee. If there be no remedy but that trouble must come, yet we may desire and pray that, if it be God's will, the circumstances of it may be so ordered as to be a mitigation of the trouble; and when things are bad, we ought to consider they might have been worse. It is bad to be forced to flee, but it would have been worse if it had been <hi type="italic">in the winter.</hi> <div eID="gen24893" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24894" type="x-p"/> 4. That throughout all the country of the Jews, there should be such destruction and desolation made, as could not be paralleled in any history (<reference osisRef="Mark.13.19">v. 19</reference>); <hi type="italic">In those days shall be affliction, such as was not from the beginning</hi> of time; that is, <hi type="italic">of the creation which God created,</hi> for time and the creation are of equal date, <hi type="italic">unto this day, neither shall be</hi> to the end of time; such a complication of miseries, and of such continuance. The destruction of Jerusalem by the Chaldeans was very terrible, but this exceeded it. It threatened a universal slaughter of all the people of the Jews; so barbarously did they devour one another, and the Romans devour them all, that, if their wars had continued a little longer, <hi type="italic">no flesh could have been saved,</hi> not one Jew could have been left alive; but in the midst of wrath God remembered mercy; and, (1.) He <hi type="italic">shortened the days;</hi> he let fall his controversy before he had <hi type="italic">made a full end.</hi> As a church and nation the ruin was complete, but many particular persons had their lives given them for a prey, by the storm's subsiding when it did. 2. It was <hi type="italic">for the elects' sake</hi> that those days were shortened; <hi type="italic">many</hi> among them fared the better for the sake of the <hi type="italic">few</hi> among them that believed in Christ, and were faithful to him. There was a promise, that <hi type="italic">a remnant</hi> should be saved (<reference osisRef="Isa.10.22">Isa. x. 22</reference>), and that God would not, for his servants' sakes, <hi type="italic">destroy them all</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.65.8">Isa. lxvi. 8</reference>); and these promises must be fulfilled. God's own <hi type="italic">elect cry day and night to him,</hi> and their prayers must be answered, <reference osisRef="Luke.18.7">Luke xviii. 7</reference>. <div eID="gen24894" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24895" type="x-p"/> II. What directions are given to the disciples with reference to it. <div eID="gen24895" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24896" type="x-p"/> 1. They must shift for the safety of <hi type="italic">their lives;</hi> "When you see the country invaded, and the city invested, flatter not yourselves with thoughts that the enemy will retire, or that you may be able to make your part good with them; but, without further deliberation or delay, <hi type="italic">let them that are in Judea, flee to the mountains,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.13.14">v. 14</reference>. Meddle not with the strife that <hi type="italic">belongs not to you; let the potsherds strive with the potsherds of the earth,</hi> but do you go out of the ship when you see it sinking, that you die not the <hi type="italic">death of the uncircumcised</hi> in heart." <div eID="gen24896" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24897" type="x-p"/> 2. They must provide for the safety of <hi type="italic">their souls;</hi> "<hi type="italic">Seducers</hi> will be busy at that time, for they love to fish in troubled waters, and therefore then you must double your guard; <hi type="italic">then, if any man shall</hi> say unto you, <hi type="italic">Lo, here is Christ,</hi> or, <hi type="italic">Lo, he is there,</hi> you know he is in heaven, and will come again at the end of time, to judge the world, and therefore <hi type="italic">believe them not;</hi> having received <hi type="italic">Christ,</hi> be not drawn into the snares of any <hi type="italic">antichrist;</hi> for <hi type="italic">false Christs,</hi> and <hi type="italic">false prophets, shall arise,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Mark.13.22">v. 22</reference>. When the gospel kingdom was in the setting up, Satan mustered all his force, to oppose it, and made use of all his wiles; and God permitted it, for the trial of sincerity of some, and the discovery of the hypocrisy of others, and the confusion of those who rejected Christ, when he was offered to them. <hi type="italic">False Christs</hi> shall <hi type="italic">rise,</hi> and false prophets that shall preach them up; or such, as, though they pretend not to be Christs, set up for <hi type="italic">prophets,</hi> and undertake to foretel things to come, and they shall <hi type="italic">show signs</hi> and lying <hi type="italic">wonders;</hi> so early did the <hi type="italic">mystery of iniquity</hi> begin to <hi type="italic">work,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Thess.2.7">2 Thess. ii. 7</reference>. They <hi type="italic">shall seduce, if it were possible, the very elect;</hi> so plausible shall their pretences be, and so industrious shall they be to impose upon people, that they shall drawn away many that were forward and zealous professors of religion, many that were very likely to have persevered; for nothing will be effectual to secure men but that foundation of God which stands immovably sure, <hi type="italic">The Lord knoweth them that are his,</hi> who shall be preserved when the faith of some is overthrown, <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.18-2Tim.2.19">2 Tim. ii. 18, 19</reference>. They <hi type="italic">shall seduce, if it were possible, the very elect;</hi> but it is not possible to seduce them; the <hi type="italic">election shall obtain,</hi> whoever are <hi type="italic">blinded,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.11.7">Rom. xi. 7</reference>. But, in consideration hereof, let the disciples be cautious whom they give credit to (<reference osisRef="Mark.13.23">v. 23</reference>); But <hi type="italic">take ye heed.</hi> Christ knew that they were of the <hi type="italic">elect,</hi> who could not possibly be <hi type="italic">seduced,</hi> and yet he said to them, <hi type="italic">Take heed.</hi> An assurance of persevering, and cautions against apostasy, will very well consist with each other. Though Christ said to them, <hi type="italic">Take heed,</hi> it doth not therefore follow, that their perseverance was doubtful, for they were kept by the power of God; and though their perseverance was secured, yet it doth not therefore follow, that this caution was needless, because they must be kept in the use of proper means. God will keep them, but they must keep themselves. "<hi type="italic">I have foretold you all things;</hi> have foretold you of this danger, that, being <hi type="italic">fore-warned,</hi> you may be <hi type="italic">fore-armed;</hi> I have foretold <hi type="italic">all things</hi> which you needed to have foretold to you, and therefore take heed of hearkening to such as pretend to be prophets, and to foretel more than I have foretold." The sufficiency of the scripture is good argument against listening to such as pretend to inspiration.

<div eID="gen24897" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Afflictions of the Jews Foretold.</title> <div sID="gen24898" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">24</hi> But in those days, after that tribulation, the sun shall be darkened, and the moon shall not give her light, 25 And the stars of heaven shall fall, and the powers that are in heaven shall be shaken. <hi type="super">26</hi> And then shall they see the Son of man coming in the clouds with great power and glory. 27 And then shall he send his angels, and shall gather together his elect from the four winds, from the uttermost part of the earth to the uttermost part of heaven. <div eID="gen24898" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24899" type="x-p"/> These verses seem to point at Christ's second coming, to judge the world; the disciples, in their question, had confounded the <hi type="italic">destruction</hi> of Jerusalem and the <hi type="italic">end of the world</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.24.3">Matt. xxiv. 3</reference>), which was built upon a mistake, as if the temple must needs stand as long as the world stands; this mistake Christ rectifies, and shows that the <hi type="italic">end of the world in those days,</hi> those other days you enquire about, the day of Christ's coming, and the day of judgment, shall be <hi type="italic">after that tribulation,</hi> and not coincident with it. Let those who live to see the Jewish nation destroyed, take heed of thinking that, because the Son of man doth not visibly come in the clouds <hi type="italic">then,</hi> he will never <hi type="italic">so</hi> come; no, he will come <hi type="italic">after that.</hi> And here he foretels, <div eID="gen24899" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24900" type="x-p"/> 1. The final dissolution of the present frame and fabric of the world; even of that part of it which seems least liable to change, the upper part, the pure and more refined part; <hi type="italic">The sun shall be darkened,</hi> and the <hi type="italic">moon</hi> shall no more <hi type="italic">give her light;</hi> for they shall be quite outshone by the glory of the Son of man, <reference osisRef="Isa.24.23">Isa. xxiv. 23</reference>. The <hi type="italic">stars of heaven,</hi> that from the beginning had kept their place and regular motion, shall fall as leaves in autumn; and the <hi type="italic">powers that are in heaven,</hi> the heavenly bodies, the fixed stars, <hi type="italic">shall be shaken.</hi> <div eID="gen24900" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24901" type="x-p"/> 2. The visible appearance of the Lord Jesus, to whom the judgment of that day shall be committed (<reference osisRef="Mark.13.26">v. 26</reference>); <hi type="italic">Then shall they see the Son of man coming in the clouds.</hi> Probably he will come over that very place where he sat when he said this; for the clouds are in the lower region of the air. He shall come with <hi type="italic">great power and glory,</hi> such as will be suited to the errand on which he comes. <hi type="italic">Every eye shall then see him.</hi> <div eID="gen24901" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24902" type="x-p"/> 3. The gathering together of all the elect to him (<reference osisRef="Mark.13.27">v. 27</reference>); He shall <hi type="italic">send his angels,</hi> and <hi type="italic">gather together his elect</hi> to him, to <hi type="italic">meet him in the air,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Thess.4.17">1 Thess. iv. 17</reference>. They shall be fetched from one end of the world to the other, so that none shall be missing from that <hi type="italic">general</hi> assembly; they shall be fetched <hi type="italic">from the uttermost part of the earth,</hi> most remote from the places where Christ's tribunal shall be set, and shall be brought to the <hi type="italic">uttermost part of heaven;</hi> so sure, so swift, so easy, shall their conveyance be, that there shall none of them miscarry, though they were to be brought from the uttermost part of the earth one way, to the uttermost part of the heaven another way. A faithful Israelite shall be carried safely, though it were from the utmost border of the land of bondage to the utmost border of the land of promise.

<div eID="gen24902" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Watchfulness Inculcated.</title> <div sID="gen24903" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">28</hi> Now learn a parable of the fig tree; When her branch is yet tender, and putteth forth leaves, ye know that summer is near: <hi type="super">29</hi> So ye in like manner, when ye shall see these things come to pass, know that it is nigh, <hi type="italic">even</hi> at the doors. <hi type="super">30</hi> Verily I say unto you, that this generation shall not pass, till all these things be done. <hi type="super">31</hi> Heaven and earth shall pass away: but my words shall not pass away. <hi type="super">32</hi> But of that day and <hi type="italic">that</hi> hour knoweth no man, no, not the angels which are in heaven, neither the Son, but the Father. <hi type="super">33</hi> Take ye heed, watch and pray: for ye know not when the time is. 34 <hi type="italic">For the Son of man is</hi> as a man taking a far journey, who left his house, and gave authority to his servants, and to every man his work, and commanded the porter to watch. 35 Watch ye therefore: for ye know not when the master of the house cometh, at even, or at midnight, or at the cockcrowing, or in the morning: <hi type="super">36</hi> Lest coming suddenly he find you sleeping. <hi type="super">37</hi> And what I say unto you I say unto all, Watch. <div eID="gen24903" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24904" type="x-p"/> We have here the application of this prophetical sermon; <hi type="italic">now learn</hi> to look forward in a right manner. <div eID="gen24904" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24905" type="x-p"/> I. "As to the <hi type="italic">destruction</hi> of Jerusalem, <hi type="italic">expect</hi> it to come very <hi type="italic">shortly;</hi> as when the <hi type="italic">branch of the fig-tree becomes soft,</hi> and the <hi type="italic">leaves sprout forth,</hi> ye expect that summer will come shortly, <reference osisRef="Mark.13.28">v. 28</reference>. When second causes begin to work, ye expect their effects in their proper order and time. So when <hi type="italic">ye see these things come to pass,</hi> when ye see the Jewish nation embroiled in wars, distracted by false Christs and prophets, and drawing upon them the displeasure of the Romans, especially when ye see them persecuting you for your Master's sake, and thereby standing to what they did when they put him to death, and repeating it, and so filling up the measure of their iniquity, then say that their <hi type="italic">ruin is nigh, even at the door,</hi> and provide for yourselves accordingly." The disciples themselves were indeed all of them, except John, taken away from the evil to come, but the next generation whom they were to train up, would live to see it; and by these instructions which Christ left behind him would be kept from sharing in it; "<hi type="italic">This generation</hi> that is now rising up, shall not all be worn off before <hi type="italic">all these things</hi> come to pass, which I have told you of, relating to Jerusalem, and they shall begin to take effect now shortly. And as this destruction is near and within ken, so it is sure. The decree is gone forth, it is a <hi type="italic">consummation determined,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Dan.9.27">Dan. ix. 27</reference>. Christ doth not speak these things, merely to frighten them; no, they are declarations of God's fixed purpose; "<hi type="italic">Heaven and earth shall pass away,</hi> at the end of time; but <hi type="italic">my words shall not pass away</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mark.13.31">v. 31</reference>), not one of these predictions shall fail of a punctual accomplishment." <div eID="gen24905" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24906" type="x-p"/> II. "As to the <hi type="italic">end of the world,</hi> do not enquire when it will come, for it is not a question fit to be asked, for of <hi type="italic">that day,</hi> and <hi type="italic">that hour, knoweth no man;</hi> it is a thing at a great distance; the exact time is fixed in the counsel of God, but is not revealed by any word of God, either to <hi type="italic">men</hi> on earth, or to <hi type="italic">angels in heaven;</hi> the angels shall have timely notice to prepare to attend in that day, and it shall be published, when it comes to the children of men, with sound of trumpet; but, at present, <hi type="italic">men</hi> and <hi type="italic">angels</hi> are kept in the dark concerning the precise time of it, that they may both attend to their proper services in the present day." But it follows, <hi type="italic">neither the Son;</hi> but is there any thing which the Son is ignorant of? We read indeed of a book which was sealed, till the Lamb opened the seals; but did not he know what was in it, before the seals were opened? Was not he privy to the writing of it? There were those in the primitive times, who taught from this text, that there were some things that Christ, as man, was <hi type="italic">ignorant</hi> of; and from these were called <hi type="italic">Agnoetæ;</hi> they said, "It was no more absurd to say so, than to say that his human soul suffered grief and fear;" and many of the orthodox fathers approved of this. Some would evade it, by saying that Christ spoke this in a way of prudential economy, to divert the disciples from further enquiry: but to this one of the ancients answers, <hi type="italic">It is not fit to speak too nicely in this matter</hi>—<hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">ou dei pany akribologein</hi></hi>, so Leontius in Dr. Hammond, "It is certain (says Archbishop Tillotson) that Christ, as God, could not be ignorant of any thing; but the divine wisdom which dwelt in our Saviour, did communicate itself to his human soul, according to the divine pleasure, so that his human nature might sometimes not know some things; therefore Christ is said to grow in wisdom (<reference osisRef="Luke.2.52">Luke ii. 52</reference>), which he could not be said to do, if the human nature of Christ did necessarily know all things by virtue of its union with the divinity." Dr. Lightfoot explains it thus; Christ calls himself the Son, as Messiah. Now the Messiah, as such, was the father's servant (<reference osisRef="Isa.42.1">Isa. xlii. 1</reference>), sent and deputed by him, and as such a one he refers himself often to his Father's will and command, and owns he <hi type="italic">did nothing of himself</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.5.19">John v. 19</reference>); in like manner he might be said to <hi type="italic">know nothing of himself.</hi> The revelation of Jesus Christ was what <hi type="italic">God gave unto him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.1.1">Rev. i. 1</reference>. He thinks, therefore, that we are to distinguish between those excellencies and perfections of his, which resulted from the personal union between the divine and human nature, and those which flowed from the anointing of the Spirit; from the former flowed the infinite dignity of his perfect freedom from all sin; but from the latter flowed his power of working miracles, and his foreknowledge of things to come. What therefore (saith he) was to be revealed by him to his church, he was pleased to take, not from the union of the human nature with the divine, but from the revelation of the Spirit, by which he yet knew not this, but <hi type="italic">the Father</hi> only knows it; that is, God only, the Deity; for (as Archbishop Tillotson explains it) it is not used here <hi type="italic">personally,</hi> in distinction from the Son and the Holy Ghost, but as the Father is, <hi type="italic">Fons et Principium Deitatis</hi>—<hi type="italic">The Fountain of Deity.</hi> <div eID="gen24906" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24907" type="x-p"/> III. "As to both, your duty is to <hi type="italic">watch and pray.</hi> Therefore the time is kept a secret, that you may be engaged to stand always upon your guard (<reference osisRef="Mark.13.33">v. 33</reference>); <hi type="italic">Take ye heed</hi> of every thing that would indispose you for your Master's coming, and would render your accounts <hi type="italic">perplexed,</hi> and your spirits so too; <hi type="italic">watch</hi> for his coming, that it may not at any time be a surprise to you, and <hi type="italic">pray</hi> for that grace which is necessary to qualify you for it, for <hi type="italic">ye know not when the time is;</hi> and you are concerned to be ready for that <hi type="italic">every day,</hi> which may come <hi type="italic">any day.</hi>" This he illustrates, in the close, by a parable. <div eID="gen24907" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24908" type="x-p"/> 1. Our Master is gone away, and left us something in trust, in charge, which we must give account of, <reference osisRef="Mark.13.34">v. 34</reference>. He is <hi type="italic">as a man taking a far journey;</hi> for he is gone to be away a great while, he has <hi type="italic">left his house</hi> on earth, and left his servants in their offices, given <hi type="italic">authority</hi> to some, who are to be overseers, and <hi type="italic">work</hi> to others, who are to be labourers. They that have <hi type="italic">authority</hi> given them, in that had <hi type="italic">work</hi> assigned them, for those that have the greatest <hi type="italic">power</hi> have the most <hi type="italic">business;</hi> and to them to whom he gave <hi type="italic">work,</hi> he gave some sort of <hi type="italic">authority,</hi> to do that work. And when he took his last leave, he <hi type="italic">appointed the porter to watch,</hi> to be sure to be ready to open to him at his return; and in the mean time to take care to whom he opened his gates, not to thieves and robbers, but only to his Master's friends and servants. Thus our Lord Jesus, when he <hi type="italic">ascended on high,</hi> left something for all his servants to do, expecting they should all do him service in his absence, and be ready to receive him at his return. <hi type="italic">All</hi> are appointed to work, and some authorized to rule. <div eID="gen24908" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24909" type="x-p"/> 2. We ought to be always upon our watch, in expectation of his return, <reference osisRef="Mark.13.35-Mark.13.37">v. 35-37</reference>. (1.) Our Lord <hi type="italic">will come,</hi> and will come as the <hi type="italic">Master of the house,</hi> to take account of his servants, of their work, and of the improvement they have made. (2.) We know not <hi type="italic">when he will come;</hi> and he has very wisely kept us at uncertainty, that we might all be always ready. We know not <hi type="italic">when he will come,</hi> just at what precise time; the <hi type="italic">Master of the house</hi> perhaps will come <hi type="italic">at even,</hi> at nine at night; or it may be <hi type="italic">at midnight,</hi> or a <hi type="italic">cock-crowing,</hi> at three in the morning, or perhaps not until six. This is applicable to his coming to us in particular, at our death, as well as to the general judgment. Our present life is a <hi type="italic">night,</hi> a dark night, compared with the other life; we know not in which watch of the night our Master will come, whether in the days of youth, or middle age, or old age; but, as soon as we are born, we begin to die, and therefore, as soon as we are capable of expecting any thing, we must expect death. (3.) Our great care must be, that, whenever our Lord comes, he do not <hi type="italic">find us sleeping,</hi> secure in ourselves, off our guard, indulging ourselves in ease and sloth, mindless of our work and duty, and thoughtless of our Lord's coming; <hi type="italic">ready</hi> to say, He will not come, and <hi type="italic">unready</hi> to meet him. (4.) His coming will indeed be <hi type="italic">coming suddenly;</hi> it will be a great <hi type="italic">surprise</hi> and <hi type="italic">terror</hi> to those that are careless, and asleep, it will come upon them as a thief in the night. (5.) It is therefore the indispensable duty of all Christ's disciples, to <hi type="italic">watch,</hi> to be awake, and keep awake; "<hi type="italic">What I say unto you</hi> four (<reference osisRef="Mark.13.37">v. 37</reference>), I <hi type="italic">say unto all</hi> the twelve, or rather to <hi type="italic">you</hi> twelve, I say unto all my disciples and followers; what I say to you of this generation, I say to all that shall believe in men, through your word, in every age, <hi type="italic">Watch, watch,</hi> expect my second coming, prepare for it, that you may be found in peace, without spot, and blameless."  <chapter eID="Mark.13"/> <div eID="gen24909" type="x-p"/>

<div eID="gen24912" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen24911" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Christ Anointed at Bethany; Judas Engages to Betray Christ.</title> <div sID="gen24913" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> After two days was <hi type="italic">the feast of</hi> the passover, and of unleavened bread: and the chief priests and the scribes sought how they might take him by craft, and put <hi type="italic">him</hi> to death. <hi type="super">2</hi> But they said, Not on the feast <hi type="italic">day,</hi> lest there be an uproar of the people. <hi type="super">3</hi> And being in Bethany in the house of Simon the leper, as he sat at meat, there came a woman having an alabaster box of ointment of spikenard very precious; and she brake the box, and poured <hi type="italic">it</hi> on his head. <hi type="super">4</hi> And there were some that had indignation within themselves, and said, Why was this waste of the ointment made? <hi type="super">5</hi> For it might have been sold for more than three hundred pence, and have been given to the poor. And they murmured against her. <hi type="super">6</hi> And Jesus said, Let her alone; why trouble ye her? she hath wrought a good work on me. <hi type="super">7</hi> For ye have the poor with you always, and whensoever ye will ye may do them good: but me ye have not always. <hi type="super">8</hi> She hath done what she could: she is come aforehand to anoint my body to the burying. <hi type="super">9</hi> Verily I say unto you, Wheresoever this gospel shall be preached throughout the whole world, <hi type="italic">this</hi> also that she hath done shall be spoken of for a memorial of her. <hi type="super">10</hi> And Judas Iscariot, one of the twelve, went unto the chief priests, to betray him unto them. <hi type="super">11</hi> And when they heard <hi type="italic">it,</hi> they were glad, and promised to give him money. And he sought how he might conveniently betray him. <div eID="gen24913" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24914" type="x-p"/> We have here instances, <div eID="gen24914" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24915" type="x-p"/> I. Of the <hi type="italic">kindness of Christ's friends,</hi> and the provision made of respect and honour for him. Some friends he had, even in and about Jerusalem, that loved him, and never thought they could do enough for him, among whom, though Israel be not gathered, he is, and will be, glorious. <div eID="gen24915" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24916" type="x-p"/> 1. Here was <hi type="italic">one friend,</hi> that was so kind as to <hi type="italic">invite him to sup with him;</hi> and he was so kind as to accept the invitation, <reference osisRef="Mark.14.3">v. 3</reference>. Though he had a prospect of his death approaching, yet he did not abandon himself to a melancholy retirement from all company, but conversed as freely with his friends as usual. <div eID="gen24916" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24917" type="x-p"/> 2. Here was <hi type="italic">another friend,</hi> that was so kind as to <hi type="italic">anoint his head</hi> with very precious ointment as he <hi type="italic">sat at meat.</hi> This was an extraordinary piece of respect paid him by a good woman that thought nothing too good to bestow upon Christ, and to do him honour. Now the scripture was fulfilled, <hi type="italic">When the king sitteth at his table, my spikenard sendeth forth the smell thereof,</hi> <reference osisRef="Song.1.12">Cant. i. 12</reference>. Let us <hi type="italic">anoint</hi> Christ as our <hi type="italic">Beloved,</hi> kiss him with a kiss of <hi type="italic">affection;</hi> and anoint him as our <hi type="italic">Sovereign,</hi> kiss him with a kiss of <hi type="italic">allegiance.</hi> Did he pour out his soul unto death for us, and shall we think any box of ointment too precious to pour out upon him? It is observable that she took care to pour it all out upon Christ's head; she <hi type="italic">broke the box</hi> (so we read it); but because it was an <hi type="italic">alabaster box,</hi> not easily broken, nor was it necessary that it should be broken, to get out the ointment, some read it, she <hi type="italic">shook</hi> the box, or <hi type="italic">knocked it to the ground,</hi> to loosen what was in it, that it might be got out the better; or, she <hi type="italic">rubbed</hi> and <hi type="italic">scraped</hi> out all that stuck tot he sides of it. Christ must have been honoured with <hi type="italic">all we</hi> have, and we must not think to keep back any part of the price. Do we give him the <hi type="italic">precious ointment</hi> of our best affections? Let him have them <hi type="italic">all;</hi> love him <hi type="italic">with all the heart.</hi> <div eID="gen24917" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24918" type="x-p"/> Now, (1.) There were those that put a <hi type="italic">worse construction</hi> upon this than it <hi type="italic">deserved.</hi> They called it a <hi type="italic">waste of the ointment,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.14.4">v. 4</reference>. Because they could not have found their hearts to put themselves to such an expense for the honouring of Christ, they thought that she was <hi type="italic">prodigal,</hi> who did. Note, As the <hi type="italic">vile person</hi> ought to be <hi type="italic">called liberal,</hi> nor the <hi type="italic">churl</hi> said to be <hi type="italic">bountiful</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.32.5">Isa. xxxii. 5</reference>); so the <hi type="italic">liberal</hi> and <hi type="italic">bountiful</hi> ought not to be called <hi type="italic">wasteful.</hi> They pretend it might have been <hi type="italic">sold,</hi> and <hi type="italic">given to the poor,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.14.5">v. 5</reference>. But as a <hi type="italic">common piety</hi> to the <hi type="italic">corban</hi> will not excuse from a <hi type="italic">particular charity</hi> to a poor parent (<reference osisRef="Mark.7.11">ch. vii. 11</reference>), so a common charity to the poor will not excuse from a particular act of piety to the Lord Jesus. What thy hand finds to do, that is good, <hi type="italic">do it with thy might.</hi> <div eID="gen24918" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24919" type="x-p"/> (2.) Our Lord Jesus put a <hi type="italic">better construction</hi> upon it than, for aught that appears, was <hi type="italic">designed.</hi> Probably, she intended no more, than to show the great honour she had for him, before all the company, and to complete his entertainment. But Christ makes it to be an act of <hi type="italic">great faith,</hi> as well as <hi type="italic">great love</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mark.14.8">v. 8</reference>); "<hi type="italic">She is come aforehand, to anoint my body to the burying,</hi> as if she foresaw that my resurrection would prevent her doing it afterward." This funeral rite was a kind of presage of, or prelude to, his death approaching. See how Christ's heart was filled with the thoughts of his death, how every thing was construed with a reference to that, and how familiarly he spoke of it upon all occasions. It is usual for those who are <hi type="italic">condemned to die,</hi> to have their coffins prepared, and other provision made for their funerals, while they are yet alive; and <hi type="italic">so</hi> Christ accepted <hi type="italic">this.</hi> Christ's death and burial were the lowest steps of his humiliation, and therefore, though he cheerfully submitted to them, yet he would have some marks of honour to attend them, which might help to take off the <hi type="italic">offence of the cross,</hi> and be an intimation how <hi type="italic">precious in the sight of the Lord the death of his saints is.</hi> Christ never rode in triumph into Jerusalem, but when he came thither to suffer; nor had ever his head anointed, but for <hi type="italic">his burial.</hi> <div eID="gen24919" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24920" type="x-p"/> (3.) He recommended this piece of heroic piety to the applause of the church in all ages; <hi type="italic">Wherever this gospel shall be preached, it shall be spoken of, for a memorial of her,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.14.9">v. 9</reference>. Note, The honour which attends well-doing, even in this world, is sufficient to balance the reproach and contempt that are cast upon it. <hi type="italic">The memory of the just is blessed,</hi> and they that had <hi type="italic">trial of cruel mockings,</hi> yet <hi type="italic">obtained a good report,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.11.6">Heb. xi. 6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.11.39">39</reference>. Thus was this good woman repaid for her box of ointment, <hi type="italic">Nec oleum perdidit nec operam—She lost neither her oil nor her labour.</hi> She got by it that good name which is <hi type="italic">better than precious ointment.</hi> Those that <hi type="italic">honour</hi> Christ <hi type="italic">he will honour.</hi> <div eID="gen24920" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24921" type="x-p"/> II. Of the <hi type="italic">malice of Christ's enemies,</hi> and the preparation made by them to do him mischief. <div eID="gen24921" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24922" type="x-p"/> 1. The chief priests, his <hi type="italic">open enemies,</hi> consulted how they might <hi type="italic">put him to death,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.14.1-Mark.14.2">v. 1, 2</reference>. The feast of the <hi type="italic">passover</hi> was now at hand, and at <hi type="italic">that</hi> feast he must be crucified, (1.) That his death and suffering might be the more public, and that all <hi type="italic">Israel,</hi> even those <hi type="italic">of the dispersion,</hi> who came from all parts to the feast, might be witnesses of it, and of the wonders that attended it. (2.) That the Anti-type might answer to the type. Christ, our Passover, was sacrificed for us, and brought us out of the house of bondage, at the same time that the paschal lamb was sacrificed, and Israel's deliverance out of Egypt was <hi type="italic">commemorated.</hi> <div eID="gen24922" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24923" type="x-p"/> Now see, [1.] How <hi type="italic">spiteful</hi> Christ's enemies were; they did not think it enough to banish or imprison him, for they aimed not only to <hi type="italic">silence</hi> him, and <hi type="italic">stop</hi> his progress for the future, but to be revenged on him for all the good he had done. [2.] How <hi type="italic">subtle</hi> they were; <hi type="italic">Not on the feast-day,</hi> when the people are together; they do not say, Lest they should be disturbed in their devotions, and diverted from them, but, <hi type="italic">Lest there should be an uproar</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mark.14.2">v. 2</reference>); lest they should rise, and rescue him, and <hi type="italic">fall foul</hi> upon those that <hi type="italic">attempt</hi> any thing against him. They who <hi type="italic">desired</hi> nothing more than the <hi type="italic">praise</hi> of men, dreaded nothing more than the rage and displeasure of men. <div eID="gen24923" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24924" type="x-p"/> 2. Judas, his <hi type="italic">disguised enemy,</hi> contracted with them for the betraying of him, <reference osisRef="Mark.14.10-Mark.14.11">v. 10, 11</reference>. He is said to be <hi type="italic">one of the twelve</hi> that were Christ's family, intimate with him, trained up for the service of the kingdom; and he <hi type="italic">went to the chief priests,</hi> to tender his service in this affair. <div eID="gen24924" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24925" type="x-p"/> (1.) That which he proposed to them, was, to <hi type="italic">betray Christ</hi> to them, and to give them notice when and where they might find him, and seize him, without making an <hi type="italic">uproar among the people,</hi> which they were afraid of, if they should seize him when he appeared <hi type="italic">in public,</hi> in the midst of his admirers. Did he know then what help it was they wanted, and where they were run aground in their counsels? It is probable that he did not, for the debate was held in their close <hi type="italic">cabal.</hi> Did they know that he had a mind to serve them, and make court to him? No, they could not imagine that any of his intimates should be so base; but Satan, who was entered into Judas, knew what occasion they had for him, and could guide him to be <hi type="italic">guide to them,</hi> who were contriving to <hi type="italic">take Jesus.</hi> Note, The spirit that works in all the children of disobedience, knows how to bring them in to the assistance one of another in a wicked project, and then to harden them in it, with the fancy that Providence favours them. <div eID="gen24925" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24926" type="x-p"/> (2.) That which he proposed to himself, was, to <hi type="italic">get money</hi> by the bargain; he had what he aimed at, when <hi type="italic">they promised to give him money.</hi> Covetousness was Judas's master-lust, <hi type="italic">his own iniquity,</hi> and that betrayed him to the sin of betraying his Master; the devil suited his temptation to <hi type="italic">that,</hi> and so conquered him. It is not said, They promised him <hi type="italic">preferment</hi> (he was not ambitious of that), but, they promised him <hi type="italic">money.</hi> See what need we have to double our guard against the sin that <hi type="italic">most easily besets us.</hi> Perhaps it was Judas's covetousness that brought him at first to <hi type="italic">follow Christ,</hi> having a promise that he should be cash-keeper, or purser, to the society, and he loved in his heart to be fingering money; and now that there was money to be got on the other side, he was as ready to betray him as ever he had been to follow him. Note, Where the principle of men's profession of religion is carnal and worldly, and the serving of a secular interest, the very same principle, whenever the wind turns, will be the bitter root of a vile and scandalous apostasy. <div eID="gen24926" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24927" type="x-p"/> (3.) Having secured the money, he set himself to make good his bargain; he sought <hi type="italic">how he might conveniently betray him,</hi> how he might <hi type="italic">seasonably deliver him up,</hi> so as to answer the intention of those who had hired him. See what need we have to be careful that we do not ensnare ourselves in sinful engagements. If at any time we be so ensnared in the words of our mouths, we are concerned to deliver ourselves by a speedy retreat, <reference osisRef="Prov.6.1-Prov.6.5">Prov. vi. 1-5</reference>. It is a rule in our law, as well as in our religion, that an <hi type="italic">obligation</hi> to do an <hi type="italic">evil thing</hi> is <hi type="italic">null</hi> and <hi type="italic">void;</hi> it binds to repentance, not to performance. See how the way of sin is down-hill—when men are <hi type="italic">in,</hi> they must be <hi type="italic">on;</hi> and what <hi type="italic">wicked</hi> contrivances many have in their sinful pursuits, to compass their designs <hi type="italic">conveniently;</hi> but such conveniences will prove mischiefs in the end.

<div eID="gen24927" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Institution of the Lord's Supper.</title> <div sID="gen24928" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">12</hi> And the first day of unleavened bread, when they killed the passover, his disciples said unto him, Where wilt thou that we go and prepare that thou mayest eat the passover? 13 And he sendeth forth two of his disciples, and saith unto them, Go ye into the city, and there shall meet you a man bearing a pitcher of water: follow him. <hi type="super">14</hi> And wheresoever he shall go in, say ye to the goodman of the house, The Master saith, Where is the guest chamber, where I shall eat the passover with my disciples? <hi type="super">15</hi> And he will show you a large upper room furnished <hi type="italic">and</hi> prepared: there make ready for us. <hi type="super">16</hi> And his disciples went forth, and came into the city, and found as he had said unto them: and they made ready the passover. <hi type="super">17</hi> And in the evening he cometh with the twelve. <hi type="super">18</hi> And as they sat and did eat, Jesus said, Verily I say unto you, One of you which eateth with me shall betray me. <hi type="super">19</hi> And they began to be sorrowful, and to say unto him one by one, <hi type="italic">Is</hi> it I? and another <hi type="italic">said, Is</hi> it I? <hi type="super">20</hi> And he answered and said unto them, <hi type="italic">It is</hi> one of the twelve, that dippeth with me in the dish. <hi type="super">21</hi> The Son of man indeed goeth, as it is written of him: but woe to that man by whom the Son of man is betrayed! good were it for that man if he had never been born. <hi type="super">22</hi> And as they did eat, Jesus took bread, and blessed, and brake <hi type="italic">it,</hi> and gave to them, and said, Take, eat: this is my body. 23 And he took the cup, and when he had given thanks, he gave <hi type="italic">it</hi> to them: and they all drank of it. <hi type="super">24</hi> And he said unto them, This is my blood of the new testament, which is shed for many. <hi type="super">25</hi> Verily I say unto you, I will drink no more of the fruit of the vine, until that day that I drink it new in the kingdom of God. <hi type="super">26</hi> And when they had sung a hymn, they went out into the mount of Olives. <hi type="super">27</hi> And Jesus saith unto them, All ye shall be offended because of me this night: for it is written, I will smite the shepherd, and the sheep shall be scattered. <hi type="super">28</hi> But after that I am risen, I will go before you into Galilee. <hi type="super">29</hi> But Peter said unto him, Although all shall be offended, yet <hi type="italic">will</hi> not I. <hi type="super">30</hi> And Jesus saith unto him, Verily I say unto thee, That this day, <hi type="italic">even</hi> in this night, before the cock crow twice, thou shalt deny me thrice. 31 But he spake the more vehemently, If I should die with thee, I will not deny thee in any wise. Likewise also said they all. <div eID="gen24928" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24929" type="x-p"/> In these verses we have, <div eID="gen24929" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24930" type="x-p"/> I. Christ's eating the passover with his disciples, the night before he died, with the joys and comforts of which ordinance he prepared himself for his approaching sorrows, the full prospect of which did not indispose him for that solemnity. Note, No apprehension of trouble, come or coming, should put us by, or put us out of frame for, our attendance on holy ordinances, as we have opportunity for it. <div eID="gen24930" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24931" type="x-p"/> 1. Christ ate the passover at the <hi type="italic">usual time</hi> when the other Jews did, as Dr. Whitby had fully made out, and not, as Dr. Hammond would have it, the night before. It was on the first day of that feast, which (taking in all the eight days of the feast) was called, <hi type="italic">The feast of unleavened bread,</hi> even that day when they <hi type="italic">killed the passover,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.14.12">v. 12</reference>. <div eID="gen24931" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24932" type="x-p"/> 2. He directed his disciples how to find the place where he intended to eat the passover; and hereby gave such another proof of his infallible knowledge of things distant and future (which to us seem altogether <hi type="italic">contingent</hi>), as he had given when he sent them for the ass on which he rode in triumph (<reference osisRef="Mark.11.6">ch. xi. 6</reference>); "<hi type="italic">Go into the city</hi> (for the <hi type="italic">passover</hi> must be <hi type="italic">eaten</hi> in Jerusalem), and <hi type="italic">there shall meet you a man bearing a pitcher of water</hi> (a servant sent for water to clean the rooms in his master's house); <hi type="italic">follow him, go in</hi> where he <hi type="italic">goes,</hi> enquire for his master, <hi type="italic">the good man of the house</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mark.14.14">v. 14</reference>), and desire him to show you a room." No doubt, the inhabitants of Jerusalem had rooms fitted up to be <hi type="italic">let out,</hi> for this occasion, to those that came out of the country to keep the passover, and one of those Christ made use of; not any friend's house, nor any house he had formerly frequented, for then he would have said, "Go to such a friend," or, "You know where we used to be, go thither and prepare." Probably he went where he was not known, that he might be <hi type="italic">undisturbed</hi> with his disciples. Perhaps he notified it by <hi type="italic">a sign,</hi> to conceal it from Judas, that he might not know till he came to the place; and by <hi type="italic">such a sign</hi> to intimate that he will dwell in the <hi type="italic">clean heart,</hi> that is, <hi type="italic">washed</hi> as with <hi type="italic">pure water.</hi> Where he designs to come, a pitcher of water must go before him; see <reference osisRef="Isa.1.16-Isa.1.18">Isa. i. 16-18</reference>. <div eID="gen24932" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24933" type="x-p"/> 3. He ate the passover in an <hi type="italic">upper room furnished,</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">estromenon</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">laid with carpets</hi> (so Dr. Hammond); it would seem to have been a very handsome <hi type="italic">dining-room.</hi> Christ was far from affecting any thing that looked stately in eating his common meals; on the contrary, he chose that which was homely, sat down on the grass: but, when he was to keep a sacred feast, in honour of that he would be at the expense of as good a room as he could get. God looks not at <hi type="italic">outward pomp,</hi> but he looks at the tokens and expressions of <hi type="italic">inward reverence</hi> for a divine institution, which, it is to be feared, those want, who, to save charges, deny themselves decencies in the worship of God. <div eID="gen24933" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24934" type="x-p"/> 4. He ate it <hi type="italic">with the twelve,</hi> who were his family, to teach those who have the charge of families, not only families of <hi type="italic">children,</hi> but families of <hi type="italic">servants,</hi> or families of <hi type="italic">scholars,</hi> or <hi type="italic">pupils,</hi> to keep up religion among them, and worship God with them. If Christ came <hi type="italic">with the twelve,</hi> then Judas was with them, though he was at this time contriving to betray his Master; and it is plain by what follows (<reference osisRef="Mark.14.20">v. 20</reference>), that he was there: he did not absent himself, lest he could have been suspected; had his <hi type="italic">seat</hi> been <hi type="italic">empty</hi> at this feast, they would have said, as Saul of David, <hi type="italic">He is not clean, surely he is not clean,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.20.26">1 Sam. xx. 26</reference>. Hypocrites, though they know it is at their peril, yet crowd into special ordinances, to keep up their repute, and palliate their secret wickedness. Christ did not <hi type="italic">exclude</hi> him from the feast, though he <hi type="italic">knew</hi> his wickedness, for it was not as yet become public and scandalous. Christ, designing to put the <hi type="italic">keys of the kingdom of heaven</hi> into the hands of men, who can judge only according to outward appearance, would hereby both direct and encourage them in their admissions to his table, to be satisfied with a justifiable profession, because they cannot discern the <hi type="italic">root of bitterness</hi> till it <hi type="italic">springs up.</hi> <div eID="gen24934" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24935" type="x-p"/> II. Christ's discourse with his disciples, as they were <hi type="italic">eating</hi> the passover. It is probable that they had discourse, according to the custom of the feast, of the deliverance of Israel out of Egypt, and the preservation of the first-born, and were as pleasant as they used to be together on this occasion, till Christ told them that which would mix <hi type="italic">trembling</hi> with their <hi type="italic">joys.</hi> <div eID="gen24935" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24936" type="x-p"/> 1. They were <hi type="italic">pleasing</hi> themselves with the society of <hi type="italic">their Master;</hi> but he tells them that they must now presently lose him; <hi type="italic">The Son of man is betrayed;</hi> and they knew, for he had often told them, what followed—If he be <hi type="italic">betrayed,</hi> the next news you will hear of him, is, that he is <hi type="italic">crucified</hi> and <hi type="italic">slain;</hi> God hath determined it concerning him, and he agrees to it; <hi type="italic">The Son of man goes, as it is written of him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.14.21">v. 21</reference>. It was <hi type="italic">written</hi> in the counsels of God, and <hi type="italic">written</hi> in the prophecies of the Old Testament, not one jot or tittle of either of which can <hi type="italic">fall to the ground.</hi> <div eID="gen24936" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24937" type="x-p"/> 2. They were <hi type="italic">pleasing</hi> themselves with the society <hi type="italic">one of another,</hi> but Christ casts a damp upon the joy of that, by telling them, <hi type="italic">One of you that eateth with me shall betray me,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.14.18">v. 18</reference>. Christ said this, if it might be, to startle the conscience of Judas, and to awaken him to repent of his wickedness, and to draw back (for it was not too late) from the brink of the pit. But for aught that appears, he who was <hi type="italic">most concerned in</hi> the warning, was <hi type="italic">least concerned at</hi> it. All the rest were affected with it. (1.) They began to be <hi type="italic">sorrowful.</hi> As the remembrance of our former falls into sin, so the fear of the like again, doth often much embitter the comfort of our spiritual feasts, and damp our joy. Here were the <hi type="italic">bitter herbs,</hi> with which this <hi type="italic">passover-feast</hi> was taken. (2.) They began to be <hi type="italic">suspicious</hi> of themselves; they said <hi type="italic">one by one, Is it I?</hi> <hi type="italic">And another said, Is it I?</hi> They are to be commended for their <hi type="italic">charity,</hi> that they were more jealous of themselves than of <hi type="italic">one another.</hi> It is the law of charity, to <hi type="italic">hope the best</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Cor.13.5-1Cor.13.7">1 Cor. xiii. 5-7</reference>), because we assuredly <hi type="italic">know,</hi> therefore we may justly <hi type="italic">suspect,</hi> more evil by ourselves than by our brethren. They are also to be commended for their acquiescence in what Christ said; they trusted more to <hi type="italic">his words</hi> than to <hi type="italic">their own hearts;</hi> and therefore do not say, "I am sure <hi type="italic">it is not I,</hi>" but, "<hi type="italic">Lord, is it I?</hi> see if there be such a <hi type="italic">way of wickedness in us,</hi> such a <hi type="italic">root of bitterness,</hi> and discover it to us, that we may pluck up that <hi type="italic">root,</hi> and stop up that <hi type="italic">way.</hi>" <div eID="gen24937" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24938" type="x-p"/> Now, in answer to their enquiry, Christ saith that, [1.] Which would make them easy; "It is not <hi type="italic">you,</hi> or <hi type="italic">you;</hi> it is this that now <hi type="italic">dips with me in the dish;</hi> the adversary and enemy is this wicked Judas."
