[2.] Which, one would think, should make Judas very <hi type="italic">uneasy.</hi> If he go on in his undertaking, it is upon the sword's point, for <hi type="italic">woe to that many by whom the Son of man is betrayed;</hi> he is undone, for every undone; his sin will soon <hi type="italic">find him out;</hi> and it were <hi type="italic">better for him that he had never been born,</hi> and had never had a being than such a miserable one as he must have. It is very probable that Judas encouraged himself in it with <hi type="italic">this</hi> thought, that his Master had often said he must be betrayed; "And if it must be done, surely God <hi type="italic">will not find fault</hi> with him that doth it, for who <hi type="italic">hath resisted his will?</hi>" As that objector argues, <reference osisRef="Rom.9.19">Rom. ix. 19</reference>. But Christ tells him that this will be no shelter or excuse to him; <hi type="italic">The Son of man indeed goes; as it is written of him,</hi> as a lamb to the slaughter; but <hi type="italic">woe to that man by whom he is betrayed.</hi> God's decree to permit the sins of men, and bring glory to himself out of them, do neither necessitate their sins, nor determine to them, nor will they be any <hi type="italic">excuse</hi> of the sin, or <hi type="italic">mitigation</hi> of the punishment. Christ was delivered indeed by <hi type="italic">the determinate counsel and fore-knowledge of God;</hi> but, notwithstanding that, it is <hi type="italic">with wicked hands that he is crucified and slain,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.2.23">Acts ii. 23</reference>. <div eID="gen24938" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24939" type="x-p"/> III. The institution of the Lord's supper. <div eID="gen24939" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24940" type="x-p"/> 1. It was instituted in the close of a <hi type="italic">supper,</hi> when they were sufficiently fed with the <hi type="italic">paschal lamb,</hi> to show that in the Lord's supper there is no <hi type="italic">bodily repast</hi> intended; to preface it with such a thing, is to revive Moses again. But it is food for <hi type="italic">the soul</hi> only, and therefore a very little of that which is for the body, as much as will serve for a <hi type="italic">sign,</hi> is enough. It was at the close of the <hi type="italic">passover-supper,</hi> which by this was evangelized, and then superseded and set aside. Much of the doctrine and duty of the eucharist is illustrated to us by the law of the passover (<reference osisRef="Exod.12.1-Exod.12.36">Exod. xii.</reference>); for the Old-Testament institutions, though they do not <hi type="italic">bind us,</hi> yet <hi type="italic">instruct</hi> us, by the help of a gospel-key to them. And these two ordinances lying here so near together, it may be good to compare them, and observe how much shorter and plainer the institution of the Lord's supper is, than that of the passover was. Christ's yoke is easy in comparison with that of the ceremonial law, and his ordinances are more spiritual. <div eID="gen24940" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24941" type="x-p"/> 2. It was instituted by the <hi type="italic">example</hi> of Christ himself; not with the ceremony and solemnity of a law, as the ordinance of baptism was, after Christ's resurrection (<reference osisRef="Matt.28.19">Matt. xxviii. 19</reference>), with, <hi type="italic">Be it enacted by the authority aforesaid,</hi> by a power given to Christ <hi type="italic">in heaven and on earth</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mark.14.18">v. 18</reference>); but by the practice of our Master himself, because intended for those who are already his disciples, and taken into covenant with him: but it has the obligation of the law, and was intended to remain in full force, power, and virtue, till his second coming. <div eID="gen24941" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24942" type="x-p"/> 3. It was instituted with <hi type="italic">blessing</hi> and <hi type="italic">giving of thanks;</hi> the gifts of common providence are to be so received (<reference osisRef="1Tim.4.4-1Tim.4.5">1 Tim. iv. 4, 5</reference>), much more than the gifts of special grace. He <hi type="italic">blessed</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mark.14.22">v. 22</reference>), and <hi type="italic">gave thanks,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.14.23">v. 23</reference>. At his other meals, he was wont to <hi type="italic">bless,</hi> and <hi type="italic">give thanks</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mark.6.41">ch. vi. 41</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mark.8.7">viii. 7</reference>) so remarkably, that he was known by it, <reference osisRef="Luke.24.30-Luke.24.31">Luke xxiv. 30, 31</reference>. And he did the same at this meal. <div eID="gen24942" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24943" type="x-p"/> 4. It was instituted to be a <hi type="italic">memorial</hi> of his <hi type="italic">death;</hi> and therefore he <hi type="italic">broke</hi> the bread, to show how it pleased the Lord to <hi type="italic">bruise him;</hi> and he called the <hi type="italic">wine,</hi> which is the blood of the grape, the <hi type="italic">blood of the New Testament.</hi> The death Christ died was a <hi type="italic">bloody death,</hi> and frequent mention is made of the <hi type="italic">blood,</hi> the <hi type="italic">precious</hi> blood, as the pride of our redemption; for the blood is <hi type="italic">the life,</hi> and made <hi type="italic">atonement for the soul,</hi> <reference osisRef="Lev.17.11-Lev.17.14">Lev. xvii. 11-14</reference>. The pouring out of the blood was the most sensible indication of the <hi type="italic">pouring out of his soul,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.53.12">Isa. liii. 12</reference>. Blood has a <hi type="italic">voice</hi> (<reference osisRef="Gen.4.10">Gen. iv. 10</reference>); and <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> blood is so often mentioned, because it was to <hi type="italic">speak,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.12.24">Heb. xii. 24</reference>. It is called the <hi type="italic">blood of the New Testament;</hi> for the covenant of grace became a <hi type="italic">testament,</hi> and of force by the death of Christ, the testator, <reference osisRef="Heb.9.16">Heb. ix. 16</reference>. It is said to be <hi type="italic">shed for many,</hi> to justify <hi type="italic">many</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.53.11">Isa. liii. 11</reference>), to bring <hi type="italic">many</hi> sons to glory, <reference osisRef="Heb.2.10">Heb. ii. 10</reference>. It was sufficient for <hi type="italic">many,</hi> being of infinite value; it has been of use to <hi type="italic">many;</hi> we read of a great multitude which no man could number, that had all <hi type="italic">washed their robes, and made them white in the blood of the Lamb</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rev.7.9-Rev.7.14">Rev. vii. 9-14</reference>); and still it is a <hi type="italic">fountain opened.</hi> How comfortable is this to poor repenting sinners, that the blood of Christ is <hi type="italic">shed for many!</hi> And if for <hi type="italic">many,</hi> why not for <hi type="italic">me?</hi> If for sinners, sinners of the Gentiles, the chief of sinners, then <hi type="italic">why not for me?</hi> <div eID="gen24943" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24944" type="x-p"/> 5. It was instituted to be a <hi type="italic">ratification</hi> of the covenant made with us in him, and a sign of the conveyance of those benefits to us, which were purchased for us by his death; and therefore he broke the bread <hi type="italic">to them</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mark.14.22">v. 22</reference>), and said, <hi type="italic">Take, eat</hi> of it: he gave the cup <hi type="italic">to them,</hi> and ordered them to <hi type="italic">drink of it,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.14.23">v. 23</reference>. Apply the doctrine of Christ crucified to yourselves, and let it be <hi type="italic">meat</hi> and <hi type="italic">drink</hi> to your souls, strengthening, nourishing, and refreshing, to you, and the support and comfort of your spiritual life. <div eID="gen24944" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24945" type="x-p"/> 6. It was instituted with an eye to the happiness of heaven, and to be an earnest and fore-taste of that, and thereby to put our mouths out of taste for all the pleasures and delights of sense (<reference osisRef="Mark.14.25">v. 25</reference>); <hi type="italic">I will drink no more of the fruit of the vine,</hi> as it is a bodily refreshment. I have done with it. <hi type="italic">No one, having tasted spiritual</hi> delights, <hi type="italic">straightway desires</hi> sensitive ones, for he saith, The <hi type="italic">spiritual</hi> is better (<reference osisRef="Luke.5.39">Luke v. 39</reference>); but <hi type="italic">every one</hi> that hath tasted <hi type="italic">spiritual</hi> delights, straightway desires <hi type="italic">eternal</hi> ones, for he saith, Those are <hi type="italic">better still;</hi> and therefore let me <hi type="italic">drink no more of the fruit of the vine,</hi> it is dead and flat to those that have been made to <hi type="italic">drink</hi> of the <hi type="italic">river</hi> of God's pleasures; but, Lord, hasten the day, when I shall <hi type="italic">drink</hi> it new and fresh <hi type="italic">in the kingdom of God,</hi> where it shall be for ever new, and in perfection. <div eID="gen24945" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24946" type="x-p"/> 7. It was closed with a <hi type="italic">hymn,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.14.26">v. 26</reference>. Though Christ was in the midst of his enemies, yet he did not, for fear of them, omit this sweet duty of singing psalms. Paul and Silas sang, when the <hi type="italic">prisoners heard them.</hi> This was an <hi type="italic">evangelical song,</hi> and gospel times are often spoken of in the Old Testament, as times of rejoicing, and praise is expressed by <hi type="italic">singing.</hi> This was Christ's <hi type="italic">swan-like</hi> song, which he sung just before he entered upon his agony; probably, that which is usually sung, <reference osisRef="Ps.113.1-Ps.118.29">Ps. cxiii. to cxviii</reference>. <div eID="gen24946" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24947" type="x-p"/> IV. Christ's discourse with his disciples, as they were returning to Bethany by moonlight. When the had <hi type="italic">sung the hymn,</hi> presently they <hi type="italic">went out.</hi> It was now near bedtime, but our Lord Jesus had his heart so much upon his suffering, that he would not <hi type="italic">come into the tabernacle of his house,</hi> nor<hi type="italic">go up into his bed,</hi> nor <hi type="italic">give sleep to his eyes,</hi> when that work was to be done, <reference osisRef="Ps.132.3-Ps.132.4">Ps. cxxxii. 3, 4</reference>. The Israelites were forbidden to go out of their houses the night that they ate the passover, for fear of the sword of the destroying angel, <reference osisRef="Exod.12.22-Exod.12.23">Exod. xii. 22, 23</reference>. But because Christ, the <hi type="italic">great shepherd,</hi> was to be <hi type="italic">smitten,</hi> he <hi type="italic">went out</hi> purposely to expose himself to the sword, as a champion; they <hi type="italic">evaded</hi> the destroyer, but Christ <hi type="italic">conquered</hi> him, and brought <hi type="italic">destructions to a perpetual end.</hi> <div eID="gen24947" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24948" type="x-p"/> 1. Christ here foretels that in his sufferings he should be <hi type="italic">deserted</hi> by all his disciples; "<hi type="italic">You will all be offended because of me, this night.</hi> I know you will (<reference osisRef="Mark.14.27">v. 27</reference>), and what I tell you now, is no other than what the scripture has told you before; <hi type="italic">I will smite the shepherd,</hi> and then <hi type="italic">the sheep will be scattered.</hi>" Christ knew this before, and yet welcomed them at his table; he sees the falls and miscarriages of his disciples, and yet doth not refuse them. Nor should we be discouraged from coming to the Lord's supper, by the fear of relapsing into sin afterward; but, the greater of our danger is, the more need we have to fortify ourselves by the diligent conscientious use of holy ordinances. Christ tells them that they would be <hi type="italic">offended in him,</hi> would begin to question whether he were the Messiah or no, when they saw him <hi type="italic">overpowered</hi> by his enemies. Hitherto, they had <hi type="italic">continued with him in his temptations;</hi> though they had sometimes offended him, yet they had not been <hi type="italic">offended in him,</hi> nor turned the back upon him; but now the storm would be so great, that they would all <hi type="italic">slip their anchors,</hi> and be in danger of <hi type="italic">shipwreck.</hi> Some trials are more particular (as <reference osisRef="Rev.2.10">Rev. ii. 10</reference>, <hi type="italic">The devil shall cast some of you into prison</hi>); but others are more general, an <hi type="italic">hour of temptation, which shall come upon all the world,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.3.10">Rev. iii. 10</reference>. The <hi type="italic">smiting</hi> of the shepherd is often the <hi type="italic">scattering</hi> of the sheep: magistrates, ministers, masters of families, if these are, as they should be, <hi type="italic">shepherds</hi> to those under their charge, when any thing comes amiss to them, the whole flock suffers for it, and is endangered by it. <div eID="gen24948" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24949" type="x-p"/> But Christ encourages them with a promise that they shall rally again, shall return both to their duty and to their comfort (<reference osisRef="Mark.14.28">v. 28</reference>); "<hi type="italic">After I am risen,</hi> I will <hi type="italic">gather you in</hi> from all the places <hi type="italic">wither you are scattered,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.34.12">Ezek. xxxiv. 12</reference>. I will <hi type="italic">go before you into Galilee,</hi> will see our friends, and enjoy one another there." <div eID="gen24949" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24950" type="x-p"/> 2. He foretels that he should be <hi type="italic">denied</hi> particularly by Peter. When they <hi type="italic">went out</hi> to go to the mount of Olives, we may suppose that they dropped Judas (he stole away from them), whereupon the rest began to think <hi type="italic">highly</hi> of themselves, that they <hi type="italic">stuck</hi> to their Master, when Judas quitted him. But Christ tells them, that though they should be kept by his grace from Judas's apostasy, yet they would have no reason to boast of their constancy. Note, Though God keeps us from being as bad as the worst, yet we may well be ashamed to think that we are not better than we are. <div eID="gen24950" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24951" type="x-p"/> (1.) Peter is confident that he should not <hi type="italic">do so ill</hi> as the rest of his disciples (<reference osisRef="Mark.14.29">v. 29</reference>); <hi type="italic">Though all should be offended,</hi> all his brethren here present, <hi type="italic">yet will not I.</hi> He supposes himself not only stronger than others, but so much stronger, as to be able to receive the shock of a temptation, and bear up against it, <hi type="italic">all alone;</hi> to <hi type="italic">stand,</hi> though nobody stood <hi type="italic">by him.</hi> It is bred in the bone with us, to <hi type="italic">think well</hi> of ourselves, and <hi type="italic">trust</hi> to <hi type="italic">our own hearts.</hi> <div eID="gen24951" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24952" type="x-p"/> (2.) Christ tells him that he will <hi type="italic">do worse</hi> than any of them. They will all <hi type="italic">desert</hi> him, but he will <hi type="italic">deny</hi> him; not once, but <hi type="italic">thrice;</hi> and that presently; "<hi type="italic">This day, even this night before the cock crow twice,</hi> thou wilt <hi type="italic">deny</hi> that ever thou hadst any knowledge of me, or acquaintance with me, as one ashamed and afraid to own me." <div eID="gen24952" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24953" type="x-p"/> (3.) He stands to his promise; "<hi type="italic">If I should die with thee, I will not deny thee;</hi> I will adhere to thee, though it cost me my life:" and, no doubt, he thought as he said. Judas said nothing like this, when Christ told him he would betray him. He sinned by contrivance, Peter by surprise; he <hi type="italic">devised the wickedness</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mic.2.1">Mic. ii. 1</reference>), Peter was <hi type="italic">overtaken in this fault,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gal.6.1">Gal. vi. 1</reference>. It was ill done of Peter, to contradict his Master. If he had said, with fear and trembling, "Lord, give me grace to keep me from denying thee, lead me not into this temptation, deliver me from this evil," it might have been prevented: but they were all thus confident; they who said, <hi type="italic">Lord, is it I?</hi> now said, <hi type="italic">It shall never be me.</hi> Being acquitted from their fear of betraying Christ, they were now secure. But he that thinks he stands, must learn to take heed lest he fall; and he that <hi type="italic">girdeth on the harness,</hi> not boast <hi type="italic">as though he had put it off.</hi>

<div eID="gen24953" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Agony in the Garden.</title> <div sID="gen24954" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">32</hi> And they came to a place which was named Gethsemane: and he saith to his disciples, Sit ye here, while I shall pray. <hi type="super">33</hi> And he taketh with him Peter and James and John, and began to be sore amazed, and to be very heavy; <hi type="super">34</hi> And saith unto them, My soul is exceeding sorrowful unto death: tarry ye here, and watch. <hi type="super">35</hi> And he went forward a little, and fell on the ground, and prayed that, if it were possible, the hour might pass from him. <hi type="super">36</hi> And he said, Abba, Father, all things <hi type="italic">are</hi> possible unto thee; take away this cup from me: nevertheless not what I will, but what thou wilt. <hi type="super">37</hi> And he cometh, and findeth them sleeping, and saith unto Peter, Simon, sleepest thou? couldest not thou watch one hour? <hi type="super">38</hi> Watch ye and pray, lest ye enter into temptation. The spirit truly <hi type="italic">is</hi> ready, but the flesh <hi type="italic">is</hi> weak. <hi type="super">39</hi> And again he went away, and prayed, and spake the same words. <hi type="super">40</hi> And when he returned, he found them asleep again, (for their eyes were heavy,) neither wist they what to answer him. <hi type="super">41</hi> And he cometh the third time, and saith unto them, Sleep on now, and take <hi type="italic">your</hi> rest: it is enough, the hour is come; behold, the Son of man is betrayed into the hands of sinners. <hi type="super">42</hi> Rise up, let us go; lo, he that betrayeth me is at hand. <div eID="gen24954" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24955" type="x-p"/> Christ is here entering upon his sufferings, and begins with those which were the sorest of all his sufferings, those in his <hi type="italic">soul.</hi> Here we have him in his <hi type="italic">agony;</hi> this melancholy story we had in Matthew; this <hi type="italic">agony</hi> in soul was the <hi type="italic">wormwood and the gall</hi> in the <hi type="italic">affliction and misery;</hi> and thereby it appeared that no sorrow was <hi type="italic">forced upon him,</hi> but that it was what he <hi type="italic">freely</hi> admitted. <div eID="gen24955" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24956" type="x-p"/> I. He retired for prayer; <hi type="italic">Sit ye here</hi> (saith he to his disciples), while I go a little further, and <hi type="italic">pray.</hi> He had lately prayed <hi type="italic">with them</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.17.1-John.17.26">John xvii.</reference>); and now he appoints them to withdraw while he goes to his Father upon an errand peculiar to himself. Note, Our praying with our families will not excuse our neglect of secret worship. When Jacob entered into his agony, he first <hi type="italic">sent over all that he had,</hi> and was <hi type="italic">left alone,</hi> and then <hi type="italic">there wrestled a man with him</hi> (<reference osisRef="Gen.32.23-Gen.32.24">Gen. xxxii. 23, 24</reference>), though he had been at prayer before (<reference osisRef="Mark.14.9">v. 9</reference>), it is likely, with his family. <div eID="gen24956" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24957" type="x-p"/> II. Even into that retirement he took with him <hi type="italic">Peter, and James, and John</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mark.14.33">v. 33</reference>), three competent witnesses of this part of his humiliation; and though great spirits care not how few know any thing of their agonies, he was not ashamed that they should see. These three had boasted most of their ability and willingness to suffer with him; Peter here, in this chapter, and James and John (<reference osisRef="Mark.10.39">ch. x. 39</reference>); and therefore Christ takes them to stand by, and see what a struggle he had with the <hi type="italic">bloody baptism</hi> and the <hi type="italic">bitter cup,</hi> to convince them that they knew not what they said. It is fit that they who are most confident, should be <hi type="italic">first</hi> tried, that they may be made sensible of their folly and weakness. <div eID="gen24957" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24958" type="x-p"/> III. There he was in a tremendous agitation (<reference osisRef="Mark.14.33">v. 33</reference>); <hi type="italic">He began to be sore amazed</hi>—<hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">ekthambeisthai</hi></hi>, a word not used in Matthew, but very significant; it bespeaks something like that <hi type="italic">horror of great darkness,</hi> which <hi type="italic">fell upon Abraham</hi> (<reference osisRef="Gen.15.12">Gen. xv. 12</reference>), or, rather, something much worse, and more frightful. The <hi type="italic">terrors of God set themselves in array against him,</hi> and he allowed himself the actual and intense contemplation of them. Never was <hi type="italic">sorrow</hi> like unto <hi type="italic">his</hi> at that time; never any had such experience as he had from eternity of divine favours, and therefore never any had, or could have, such a sense as he had of divine favours. Yet there was not the least disorder or irregularity in this commotion of his spirits; his affections rose not tumultuously, but under direction, and as they were called up, for he had no corrupt nature to mix with them, as we have. If water have a sediment at the bottom, though it may be clear while it stands still, yet, when shaken, it grows muddy; so it is with our affections: but pure water in a clean glass, though ever so much stirred, continues clear; and so it was with Christ. Dr. Lightfoot thinks it very probable that the devil did now appear to our Saviour in a visible shape, in his <hi type="italic">own shape</hi> and <hi type="italic">proper colour,</hi> to terrify and affright him, and to drive him from his hope in God (which he aimed at in persecuting Job, a type of Christ, to make him <hi type="italic">curse God, and die</hi>), and to deter him from the further prosecution of his undertaking; whatever hindered him from that, he looked upon as coming from Satan, <reference osisRef="Matt.16.23">Matt. xvi. 23</reference>. When the devil had tempted him in the wilderness, it is said, He departed <hi type="italic">from him for a season</hi> (<reference osisRef="Luke.4.13">Luke iv. 13</reference>), intending another grapple with him, and in another way; finding that he could not by his flatteries <hi type="italic">allure</hi> him into sin, he would try by his terrors to <hi type="italic">affright</hi> him into it, and so <hi type="italic">make void</hi> his design. <div eID="gen24958" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24959" type="x-p"/> IV. He made a sad complaint of this agitation. He said, <hi type="italic">My soul is exceeding sorrowful.</hi> 1. He was <hi type="italic">made sin for us,</hi> and therefore was thus <hi type="italic">sorrowful;</hi> he fully knew the <hi type="italic">malignity</hi> of the <hi type="italic">sins</hi> he was to <hi type="italic">suffer for;</hi> and having the highest degree of love to God, who was <hi type="italic">offended</hi> by them, and of love to <hi type="italic">man,</hi> who was damaged and endangered by them, now that those were set in order before him, no marvel that <hi type="italic">his soul</hi> was <hi type="italic">exceeding sorrowful.</hi> Now was he made to <hi type="italic">serve with our sins,</hi> and was thus <hi type="italic">wearied with our iniquities.</hi> 2. He <hi type="italic">was made a curse</hi> for us; the curses of the law were transferred to him as our surety and representative, not as originally <hi type="italic">bound with us,</hi> but a <hi type="italic">bail to the action.</hi> And when his soul was thus exceeding sorrowful, he did, as it were, yield to them, and lie down under the load, until by his death he had satisfied for sin, and so for ever abolished the curse. He now <hi type="italic">tasted death</hi> (as he is said to do, <reference osisRef="Heb.2.9">Heb. ii. 9</reference>), which is not an extenuating expression, as if he did <hi type="italic">but</hi> taste it; no, he <hi type="italic">drank up</hi> even the dregs of the cup; but it is rather <hi type="italic">aggravating;</hi> it did not go down by wholesale, but he <hi type="italic">tasted</hi> all the bitterness of it. This was that <hi type="italic">fear</hi> which the apostle speaks of (<reference osisRef="Heb.5.7">Heb. v. 7</reference>), a natural fear of pain and death, which it is natural to human nature to startle at. <div eID="gen24959" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24960" type="x-p"/> Now the consideration of Christ's sufferings in <hi type="italic">his soul,</hi> and his <hi type="italic">sorrows</hi> for us, should be of use to us, <div eID="gen24960" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24961" type="x-p"/> (1.) To <hi type="italic">embitter our sins.</hi> Can we ever entertain a <hi type="italic">favourable</hi> or so much as a <hi type="italic">slight</hi> thought of sin, when we see what impression sin (though but imputed) made upon the Lord Jesus? Shall that <hi type="italic">sit light</hi> upon our souls, which sat <hi type="italic">so heavy</hi> upon his? Was Christ in such an agony for our sins, and shall we never be in an agony about them? How should we look upon him whom we have <hi type="italic">pressed,</hi> whom we have <hi type="italic">pierced,</hi> and <hi type="italic">mourn,</hi> and be <hi type="italic">in bitterness!</hi> It becomes us to be <hi type="italic">exceeding sorrowful</hi> for sin, because Christ was so, and never to <hi type="italic">make a mock</hi> at it. If Christ thus suffered for sin, let us <hi type="italic">arm ourselves with the same mind.</hi> <div eID="gen24961" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24962" type="x-p"/> (2.) To <hi type="italic">sweeten our sorrows;</hi> if our souls be at any time <hi type="italic">exceeding sorrowful,</hi> through the afflictions of this present time, let us remember that our Master was so before us, and the <hi type="italic">disciple is not greater than his Lord.</hi> Why should we affect to <hi type="italic">drive away</hi> sorrow, when Christ for our sakes courted it, and submitted to it, and thereby not only took out the <hi type="italic">sting</hi> of it, and made it <hi type="italic">tolerable,</hi> but put <hi type="italic">virtue</hi> into it, and made it <hi type="italic">profitable</hi> (for <hi type="italic">by the sadness of the countenance the heart is made better</hi>), nay, and put <hi type="italic">sweetness</hi> into it, and made it comfortable. Blessed Paul was <hi type="italic">sorrowful,</hi> and yet <hi type="italic">always rejoicing.</hi> If we be <hi type="italic">exceeding sorrowful,</hi> it is but <hi type="italic">unto death;</hi> that will be the period of all our sorrows, if Christ be <hi type="italic">ours;</hi> when the <hi type="italic">eyes</hi> are closed, all tears are <hi type="italic">wiped away</hi> from them. <div eID="gen24962" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24963" type="x-p"/> V. He ordered his disciples to keep with him, not because he needed their help, but because he would have them to <hi type="italic">look upon him and receive instruction;</hi> he said to them, <hi type="italic">Tarry ye here and watch.</hi> He had said to the other disciples nothing but, Sit ye here (<reference osisRef="Mark.14.32">v. 32</reference>); but these three he bids to tarry <hi type="italic">and watch,</hi> as expecting more from them than from the rest. <div eID="gen24963" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24964" type="x-p"/> VI. He addressed himself to God by prayer (<reference osisRef="Mark.14.35">v. 35</reference>); He <hi type="italic">fell on the ground, and prayed.</hi> It was but a little before this, that in prayer he <hi type="italic">lifted up his eyes</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.17.1">John xvii. 1</reference>); but here, being in an agony, he <hi type="italic">fell upon his face,</hi> accommodating himself to his present humiliation, and teaching us thus to abase ourselves before God; it becomes us to <hi type="italic">be low,</hi> when we come into the presence of the <hi type="italic">Most High.</hi> 1. As <hi type="italic">Man,</hi> he <hi type="italic">deprecated</hi> his sufferings, that, <hi type="italic">if it were possible, the hour might pass from him</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mark.14.35">v. 35</reference>); "This <hi type="italic">short,</hi> but <hi type="italic">sharp</hi> affliction, that which I am now <hi type="italic">this hour</hi> to enter upon, let man's salvation be, <hi type="italic">if possible,</hi> accomplished without it." We have his very words (<reference osisRef="Mark.14.36">v. 36</reference>), <hi type="italic">Abba, Father.</hi> The Syriac word is here retained, which Christ used, and which signifies <hi type="italic">Father,</hi> to intimate what an emphasis our Lord Jesus, in his <hi type="italic">sorrows,</hi> laid upon it, and would have us to lay. It is with an eye to this, that St. Paul retains this word, putting it into the mouths of all that have the <hi type="italic">Spirit of adoption;</hi> they are taught to cry, <hi type="italic">Abba, Father,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.8.15">Rom. viii. 15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gal.4.6">Gal. iv. 6</reference>. Father, <hi type="italic">all things are possible to thee.</hi> Note, Even that which we cannot expect to be done for us, we ought yet to believe that God is <hi type="italic">able to do:</hi> and when we submit to his will, and refer ourselves to his wisdom and mercy, it must be with a believing acknowledgment of his power, that <hi type="italic">all things are possible to him.</hi> 2. As <hi type="italic">Mediator,</hi> he <hi type="italic">acquiesced</hi> in the will of God concerning them; "<hi type="italic">Nevertheless, not what I will, but what thou wilt.</hi> I know the matter is settled, and cannot be altered, <hi type="italic">I must suffer</hi> and die, and I bid it welcome." <div eID="gen24964" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24965" type="x-p"/> VII. He roused his disciples, who were dropped asleep while he was at prayer, <reference osisRef="Mark.14.37-Mark.14.38">v. 37, 38</reference>. He comes to look after them, since they did not look after him; and he <hi type="italic">finds them asleep,</hi> so little affected were they with his sorrows, his complaints, and prayers. This carelessness of theirs was a presage of their further offence in deserting him; and it was an aggravation of it, that he had so lately commended them for <hi type="italic">continuing with him in his temptations,</hi> though they had not been without their faults. Was he so willing to make the best of them, and were they so indifferent in approving themselves to him? They had lately promised not to be <hi type="italic">offended in him;</hi> what! and yet mind him so little? He particularly upbraided Peter with his drowsiness; <hi type="italic">Simon, sleepest thou?</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">Kai sy teknon</hi></hi>;—"<hi type="italic">What thou, my son?</hi> Thou that didst so positively promise thou wouldest not deny me, dost thou slight me thus? From thee I expected better things. <hi type="italic">Couldest thou not watch one hour?</hi>" He did not require him to watch <hi type="italic">all night</hi> with him, only for <hi type="italic">one hour.</hi> It aggravates our faintness and short continuance in Christ's service, that he doth not over-task us, nor weary us with it, <reference osisRef="Isa.43.23">Isa. xliii. 23</reference>. He puts upon us <hi type="italic">no other burthen</hi> than to <hi type="italic">hold fast till he comes</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rev.2.24-Rev.2.25">Rev. ii. 24, 25</reference>); and behold, <hi type="italic">he comes quickly,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.3.11">Rev. iii. 11</reference>. <div eID="gen24965" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24966" type="x-p"/> As those whom Christ <hi type="italic">loves</hi> he <hi type="italic">rebukes</hi> when they do amiss, so those whom he <hi type="italic">rebukes</hi> he counsels and comforts. 1. It was a very wise and faithful word of advice which Christ here gave to his disciples; <hi type="italic">Watch and pray, lest ye enter into temptation,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.14.38">v. 38</reference>. It was bad to <hi type="italic">sleep</hi> when Christ was in his agony, but they were entering into further temptation, and if they did not stir up themselves, and fetch in grace and strength from God by prayer, they would <hi type="italic">do worse;</hi> and so they did, when they all forsook him, and fled. 2. It was a very kind and tender excuse that Christ made for them; "<hi type="italic">The spirit truly is willing;</hi> I know it is, it is <hi type="italic">ready,</hi> it is <hi type="italic">forward;</hi> you would willingly <hi type="italic">keep awake,</hi> but you cannot." This may be taken as a reason for that exhortation, "<hi type="italic">Watch and pray;</hi> because, though <hi type="italic">the spirit is willing,</hi> I grant it is (you have sincerely resolved never to be <hi type="italic">offended in me</hi>), yet <hi type="italic">the flesh is weak,</hi> and if you do not <hi type="italic">watch</hi> and <hi type="italic">pray,</hi> and use the means of perseverance, you may be overcome, notwithstanding." The consideration of the <hi type="italic">weakness</hi> and infirmity of <hi type="italic">our flesh</hi> should engage and quicken us to <hi type="italic">prayer</hi> and <hi type="italic">watchfulness,</hi> when we are entering into temptation. <div eID="gen24966" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24967" type="x-p"/> VIII. He <hi type="italic">repeated</hi> his address to his Father (<reference osisRef="Mark.14.39">v. 39</reference>); <hi type="italic">He went again, and prayed,</hi> saying, <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">ton auton logon</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">the same word,</hi> or matter, or business; he spoke to the same purport, and again <hi type="italic">the third time.</hi> This teaches us, that <hi type="italic">men ought to pray, and not to faint,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.18.1">Luke xviii. 1</reference>. Though the answers to our prayers do not come quickly, yet we must renew our requests, and <hi type="italic">continue instant in prayer;</hi> for <hi type="italic">the vision is for an appointed time, and at the end it shall speak, and not lie,</hi> <reference osisRef="Hab.2.3">Hab. ii. 3</reference>. Paul, when he was <hi type="italic">buffeted by a messenger of Satan, besought the Lord thrice,</hi> as Christ did here, before he obtained an answer of peace, <reference osisRef="2Cor.12.7-2Cor.12.8">2 Cor. xii. 7, 8</reference>. A little before this, when Christ, in the <hi type="italic">trouble of his soul,</hi> prayed, <hi type="italic">Father, glorify thy name,</hi> he had an immediate answer by a voice from heaven, <hi type="italic">I have both glorified it, and I will glorify it yet again;</hi> but now he must come a second and third time, for the visits of God's grace, in answer to prayer, come sooner or later, according to the pleasure of his will, that we may be kept depending. <div eID="gen24967" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24968" type="x-p"/> IX. He <hi type="italic">repeated</hi> his visits to his disciples. Thus he gave a specimen of his continued care for his church on earth, even when it is <hi type="italic">half asleep,</hi> and not duly concerned for itself, while he ever lives making intercession with his Father <hi type="italic">in heaven.</hi> See how, as became a <hi type="italic">Mediator,</hi> he passes and repasses between both. He came the <hi type="italic">second time</hi> to his disciples, and <hi type="italic">found them asleep again,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.14.40">v. 40</reference>. See how the infirmities of Christ's disciples <hi type="italic">return</hi> upon them, notwithstanding their resolutions, and <hi type="italic">overpower</hi> them, notwithstanding their resistance; and what clogs those bodies of ours are to our souls, which should make us long for that blessed state in which they shall be no more our encumbrance. This second time he spoke to them as before, but <hi type="italic">they wist not what to answer him;</hi> they were ashamed of their drowsiness, and had nothing to say in excuse for it. Or, They were so overpowered with it, that, like men between sleeping and waking, they knew not where they were, or what they said. But, the <hi type="italic">third time,</hi> they were bid to <hi type="italic">sleep</hi> if they would (<reference osisRef="Mark.14.41">v. 41</reference>); "<hi type="italic">Sleep on now, and take your rest.</hi> I have now no more occasion for your watching, you may sleep, if you will, for me." <hi type="italic">It is enough;</hi> we had not that word in Matthew. "You have had warning enough to keep awake, and would not take it; and now you shall see what little reason you have to be secure." <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">Apekei</hi></hi>, <hi type="italic">I discharge you</hi> from any <hi type="italic">further attendance;</hi> so some understand it; "Now <hi type="italic">the hour is come,</hi> in which I knew you would all forsake me, even take your course;" as he said to Judas, <hi type="italic">What thou doest, do quickly.</hi> The <hi type="italic">Son of man</hi> is now <hi type="italic">betrayed into the hands of sinners,</hi> the chief priests and elders; those <hi type="italic">worst</hi> of sinners, because they made a profession of sanctity. "Come, <hi type="italic">rise up,</hi> do not lie dozing there. <hi type="italic">Let us go</hi> and meet the enemy, for <hi type="italic">lo, he that betrayeth me is at hand,</hi> and I must not now think of making an escape." When we see trouble at the door, we are concerned to stir up ourselves to get ready for it.

<div eID="gen24968" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Treachery of Judas.</title> <div sID="gen24969" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">43</hi> And immediately, while he yet spake, cometh Judas, one of the twelve, and with him a great multitude with swords and staves, from the chief priests and the scribes and the elders. <hi type="super">44</hi> And he that betrayed him had given them a token, saying, Whomsoever I shall kiss, that same is he; take him, and lead <hi type="italic">him</hi> away safely. <hi type="super">45</hi> And as soon as he was come, he goeth straightway to him, and saith, Master, master; and kissed him. <hi type="super">46</hi> And they laid their hands on him, and took him. 47 And one of them that stood by drew a sword, and smote a servant of the high priest, and cut off his ear. <hi type="super">48</hi> And Jesus answered and said unto them, Are ye come out, as against a thief, with swords and <hi type="italic">with</hi> staves to take me? <hi type="super">49</hi> I was daily with you in the temple teaching, and ye took me not: but the scriptures must be fulfilled. <hi type="super">50</hi> And they all forsook him, and fled. <hi type="super">51</hi> And there followed him a certain young man, having a linen cloth cast about <hi type="italic">his</hi> naked <hi type="italic">body;</hi> and the young men laid hold on him: <hi type="super">52</hi> And he left the linen cloth, and fled from them naked. <div eID="gen24969" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24970" type="x-p"/> We have here the <hi type="italic">seizing</hi> of our Lord Jesus by the officers of the chief priests. This was what his enemies had long aimed at, they had often sent to <hi type="italic">take him;</hi> but he had escaped out of their hands, because <hi type="italic">his hour was not come,</hi> nor could they now have taken him, had he not freely surrendered himself. He began first to suffer <hi type="italic">in his soul,</hi> but afterward suffered in his body, that he might satisfy for sin, which begins in the heart, but afterwards makes the members of the body <hi type="italic">instruments of unrighteousness.</hi> <div eID="gen24970" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24971" type="x-p"/> I. Here is a band of rude miscreants employed to <hi type="italic">take</hi> our Lord Jesus and make him a prisoner; <hi type="italic">a great multitude with swords and staves.</hi> There is no wickedness so black, no villany so horrid, but there may be found among the children of men fit tools to be made use of, that will not scruple to be employed; so miserably depraved and vitiated is mankind. At the head of this rabble is Judas, <hi type="italic">one of the twelve,</hi> one of those that had been many years intimately conversant with our Lord Jesus, had prophesied in his name, and in his name cast out devils, and yet <hi type="italic">betrayed</hi> him. It is no new thing for a very fair and plausible profession to end in a shameful and fatal apostasy. <hi type="italic">How art thou fallen, O Lucifer!</hi> <div eID="gen24971" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24972" type="x-p"/> II. Men of no less figure than the <hi type="italic">chief priests, and the scribes,</hi> and <hi type="italic">the elders,</hi> sent them, and set them on work, who pretended to expect the Messiah, and to be ready to welcome him; and yet, when he <hi type="italic">is come,</hi> and has given undeniable proofs that it is he that <hi type="italic">should come,</hi> because he doth not make court to them, nor countenance and support their pomp and grandeur, because he appears not as a temporal prince, but sets up a spiritual kingdom, and preaches repentance, reformation, and a holy life, and directs men's thoughts, and affections, and aims, to another world, they set themselves against him, and, without giving the credentials he produces an impartial examination, resolve to run him down. <div eID="gen24972" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24973" type="x-p"/> III. Judas betrayed him <hi type="italic">with a kiss;</hi> abusing the freedom Christ used to allow his disciples of kissing his cheek at their return when they had been any time absent. He called him, <hi type="italic">Master, Master, and kissed him;</hi> he said, <hi type="italic">Rabbi, Rabbi,</hi> as if he had been now more respectful to him than ever. It is enough to put one for ever out of conceit with being called of men <hi type="italic">Rabbi, Rabbi</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.23.7">Matt. xxiii. 7</reference>), since it was with this compliment that Christ was betrayed. He bid them take him, and <hi type="italic">lead him away safely.</hi> Some think that he spoke this <hi type="italic">ironically,</hi> knowing that they could not secure him unless he pleased, that this Samson could break their bonds asunder as threads of tow, and make is escape, and then he should get the money, and Christ the honour, and no harm done; and I should think so too, but that Satan was <hi type="italic">entered into him,</hi> so that the worst and most malicious intention of this action is not too black to be supposed. Nay, he had often heard his Master say, that, being <hi type="italic">betrayed,</hi> he should be <hi type="italic">crucified,</hi> and had no reason to think otherwise. <div eID="gen24973" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24974" type="x-p"/> IV. They arrested him, and made him their prisoner (<reference osisRef="Mark.14.46">v. 46</reference>); <hi type="italic">They laid their hands on him,</hi> rude and violent hands, and <hi type="italic">took him</hi> into custody; triumphing, it is likely, that they had done that which has been often before attempted in vain. <div eID="gen24974" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24975" type="x-p"/> V. Peter laid about him in defence of his Master, and wounded one of the assailants, being for the present mindful of his promise, to venture his life with his Master. He was <hi type="italic">one of them that stood by,</hi> of them that <hi type="italic">were with him</hi> (so the word signifies), of <hi type="italic">those three</hi> disciples that were <hi type="italic">with him</hi> in the garden; he <hi type="italic">drew a sword,</hi> and aimed, it is likely, to cut off the head, but missed his blow, and only <hi type="italic">cut off the ear,</hi> of a servant of the high priest, <reference osisRef="Mark.14.47">v. 47</reference>. It is easier to <hi type="italic">fight</hi> for Christ, than to <hi type="italic">die</hi> for him; but Christ's good soldiers overcome, not by taking other people's lives, but by laying down their own, <reference osisRef="Rev.12.11">Rev. xii. 11</reference>. <div eID="gen24975" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24976" type="x-p"/> VI. Christ argues with them that had seized him, and shows them the absurdity of their proceedings against him. 1. That they came out <hi type="italic">against him,</hi> as against a <hi type="italic">thief,</hi> whereas he was <hi type="italic">innocent</hi> of any crime; he <hi type="italic">taught daily in the temple,</hi> and if he had any wicked design, there it would some time or other have been discovered; nay, these officers of the <hi type="italic">chief priests,</hi> being <hi type="italic">retainers</hi> to the temple, may be supposed to have heard his sermons there (I was <hi type="italic">with you</hi> in the temple); and had he not taught them excellent doctrine, even his enemies themselves being judges? Were not <hi type="italic">all the words of his mouth in righteousness?</hi> Was there any thing <hi type="italic">froward or perverse in them?</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.8.8">Prov. viii. 8</reference>. By his fruits he was known to be a good tree; why then did they come out against him <hi type="italic">as a thief?</hi> 2. That they came to take him thus <hi type="italic">privately,</hi> whereas he was neither <hi type="italic">ashamed</hi> nor <hi type="italic">afraid</hi> to appear <hi type="italic">publicly</hi> in the temple. He was none of those <hi type="italic">evil-doers</hi> that <hi type="italic">hate the light,</hi> neither come <hi type="italic">to the light,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.3.20">John iii. 20</reference>. If their masters had any thing to say to him, they might meet him any day in the temple, where he was ready to answer all challenges, all charges; and there they might do as they pleased with him, for the priests had the custody of the temple, and the command of the guards about it: but to come upon him thus at midnight, and in the place of his retirement, was base and cowardly. This was to do as David's enemy, that <hi type="italic">sat in the lurking places of the villages, to murder the innocent,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.10.8">Ps. x. 8</reference>. But this was not all. 3. They came <hi type="italic">with swords and staves,</hi> as if he had been in arms against the government, and must have the <hi type="italic">posse comitatus</hi> raised to reduce him. There was no occasion for those weapons; but they made this ado, (1.) To secure themselves from the rage of some; they came armed, because they <hi type="italic">feared the people;</hi> but thus <hi type="italic">were they in great fear, where no fear was,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.53.5">Ps. liii. 5</reference>. (2.) To expose him to the rage of others. By coming <hi type="italic">with swords and staves to take him,</hi> they represented him to the people (who are apt to take impressions this way) as a dangerous turbulent man, and so endeavored to incense them against him, and make them cry out, <hi type="italic">Crucify him, crucify him,</hi> having no other way to gain their point. <div eID="gen24976" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24977" type="x-p"/> VII. He reconciled himself to all this injurious, ignominious treatment, by referring himself to the Old-Testament predictions of the Messiah. I am hardly used, <hi type="italic">but</hi> I submit, for <hi type="italic">the scriptures must be fulfilled,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.14.49">v. 49</reference>. 1. See here what a regard Christ had to the <hi type="italic">scriptures;</hi> he would bear any thing rather than that the least jot or tittle of the word of God should fall to the ground; and as he had an eye to them in his sufferings, so he has in his glory; for what is Christ doing in the government of the world, but <hi type="italic">fulfilling the scriptures?</hi> 2. See what use we are to make of the Old Testament; we must search for Christ, the true <hi type="italic">treasure hid in that field:</hi> as the history of the New Testament expounds the prophecies of Old, so the prophecies of the Old Testament illustrate the history of the New. <div eID="gen24977" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24978" type="x-p"/> VIII. All Christ's disciples, hereupon, deserted him (<reference osisRef="Mark.14.50">v. 50</reference>); <hi type="italic">They all forsook him, and fled.</hi> They were very confident that they should adhere to him; but even good men know not what they will do, till they are tried. If it was such a comfort to him as he had lately intimated, that they had hitherto <hi type="italic">continued with him</hi> in his lesser trials (<reference osisRef="Luke.22.28">Luke xxii. 28</reference>), we may well imagine what a grief it was to him, that they deserted him now in the greatest, when they might have done him some service—when he was abused, to protect him, and when accused, to witness for him. Let not those that suffer for Christ, think it strange, if they be thus deserted, and if all the herd shun the wounded deer; they are not better than their Master, nor can expect to be better used either by their enemies or by their friends. When St. Paul was in peril, none <hi type="italic">stood by him,</hi> but <hi type="italic">all men forsook him,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Tim.4.16">2 Tim. iv. 16</reference>. <div eID="gen24978" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24979" type="x-p"/> IX. The noise disturbed the neighbourhood, and some of the neighbours were brought into danger by the riot, <reference osisRef="Mark.14.51-Mark.14.52">v. 51, 52</reference>. This passage of story we have not in any other of the evangelists. Here is an account of a <hi type="italic">certain young man,</hi> who, as it should seem, was no disciple of Christ, nor, as some have imagined, a servant of the house wherein Christ had eaten the passover, who <hi type="italic">followed him</hi> to see what would become of him (as the <hi type="italic">sons of the prophets,</hi> when they understood that Elijah was to be <hi type="italic">taken up,</hi> went to <hi type="italic">view afar off,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Kgs.2.7">2 Kings ii. 7</reference>), but some young man that lived near the garden, perhaps in the house to which the garden belonged. Now observe concerning him, <div eID="gen24979" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24980" type="x-p"/> 1. How he was <hi type="italic">frightened out of his bed,</hi> to be a <hi type="italic">spectator</hi> of Christ's sufferings. Such a <hi type="italic">multitude,</hi> so armed, and coming with so much fury, and in the dead of night, and in a quiet village, could not but produce a great stir; this alarmed our <hi type="italic">young man,</hi> who perhaps thought they was some tumult or rising in the city, some <hi type="italic">uproar among the people,</hi> and had the curiosity to go, and see what the matter was, and was in such haste to inform himself, that he could not stay to dress himself, but threw a sheet about him, as if he would appear like a walking ghost, in grave clothes, to frighten those who had frightened him, and ran among the thickest of them with this question, <hi type="italic">What is to do here?</hi> Being told, he had a mind to see the issue, having, no doubt, heard much of the fame of this Jesus; and therefore, when all his disciples had quitted him, he continued to <hi type="italic">follow him,</hi> desirous to <hi type="italic">hear</hi> what he would say, and <hi type="italic">see</hi> what he would do. Some think that his having no other garment than this <hi type="italic">linen cloth</hi> upon his naked body, intimates that he was one of those Jews who made a great profession of piety that their neighbours, in token of which, among other instances of austerity and mortification of the body, they used no clothes but one linen garment, which, though contrived to be modest enough, was thin and cold. But I rather think that this was not his constant wear. <div eID="gen24980" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24981" type="x-p"/> 2. See how he was <hi type="italic">frightened into his bed</hi> again, when he was in danger of being made a <hi type="italic">sharer</hi> in Christ's sufferings. His own disciples had run away from him; but this young man, having no concern for him, thought he might securely attend him, especially being so far from being armed, that he was not so much as clothed; but <hi type="italic">the young men,</hi> the Roman soldiers, who were called to assist, <hi type="italic">laid hold of him,</hi> for all was fish that came to their net. Perhaps they were now vexed at themselves, that they had suffered the disciples to <hi type="italic">run away,</hi> and they being got out of their reach they resolved to seize the first they could <hi type="italic">lay their hands on;</hi> though this young man was perhaps one of the <hi type="italic">strictest sect</hi> of the Jewish church, yet the Roman soldiers made no conscience of abusing him upon this occasion. Finding himself in danger, he <hi type="italic">left the linen cloth</hi> by which they had <hi type="italic">caught hold of him,</hi> and <hi type="italic">fled away naked.</hi> This passage is recorded to show what a barbarous crew this was, that was sent to seize Christ, and what a narrow escape the disciples had of falling into their hands, out of which nothing could have kept them but their Master's care of them; <hi type="italic">If ye seek me, let these go their way,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.18.8">John xviii. 8</reference>. It also intimates that there is <hi type="italic">no hold</hi> of those who are led by curiosity only, and not by faith and conscience, to follow Christ.

<div eID="gen24981" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Christ Brought before the High Priest.</title> <div sID="gen24982" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">53</hi> And they led Jesus away to the high priest: and with him were assembled all the chief priests and the elders and the scribes. <hi type="super">54</hi> And Peter followed him afar off, even into the palace of the high priest: and he sat with the servants, and warmed himself at the fire. <hi type="super">55</hi> And the chief priests and all the council sought for witness against Jesus to put him to death; and found none. <hi type="super">56</hi> For many bare false witness against him, but their witness agreed not together. <hi type="super">57</hi> And there arose certain, and bare false witness against him, saying, 58 We heard him say, I will destroy this temple that is made with hands, and within three days I will build another made without hands. <hi type="super">59</hi> But neither so did their witness agree together. 60 And the high priest stood up in the midst, and asked Jesus, saying, Answerest thou nothing? what <hi type="italic">is it which</hi> these witness against thee? <hi type="super">61</hi> But he held his peace, and answered nothing. Again the high priest asked him, and said unto him, Art thou the Christ, the Son of the Blessed? <hi type="super">62</hi> And Jesus said, I am: and ye shall see the Son of man sitting on the right hand of power, and coming in the clouds of heaven. <hi type="super">63</hi> Then the high priest rent his clothes, and saith, What need we any further witnesses? <hi type="super">64</hi> Ye have heard the blasphemy: what think ye? And they all condemned him to be guilty of death. <hi type="super">65</hi> And some began to spit on him, and to cover his face, and to buffet him, and to say unto him, Prophesy: and the servants did strike him with the palms of their hands. <div eID="gen24982" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24983" type="x-p"/> We have here Christ's arraignment, trial, conviction, and condemnation, in the <hi type="italic">ecclesiastical</hi> court, before the great sanhedrim, of which the <hi type="italic">high priest</hi> was president, or judge of the court; the same Caiaphas that had lately adjudged it expedient he should be put to death, guilty or not guilty (<reference osisRef="John.11.50">John xi. 50</reference>), and who therefore might justly be excepted against as partial. <div eID="gen24983" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24984" type="x-p"/> I. Christ is hurried away to his <hi type="italic">house,</hi> his <hi type="italic">palace</hi> it is called, such state did he live in. And there, though, in the dead of the night, <hi type="italic">all the chief priests, and elders, and scribes,</hi> that were in the secret, were <hi type="italic">assembled,</hi> ready to receive the prey; so sure were they of it. <div eID="gen24984" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24985" type="x-p"/> II. <hi type="italic">Peter followed</hi> at a distance, such a degree of cowardice was his late courage dwindled into, <reference osisRef="Mark.14.54">v. 54</reference>. But when he came to the high priest's palace, he <hi type="italic">sneakingly</hi> went, and <hi type="italic">sat with the servants,</hi> that he might not be suspected to belong to Christ. The high priest's fire side was no proper place, nor his servants proper company, for Peter, but it was his <hi type="italic">entrance into a temptation.</hi> <div eID="gen24985" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24986" type="x-p"/> III. Great diligence was used to procure, for love or money, false witnesses against Christ. They had seized him as a malefactor, and now they had him they had no indictment to prefer against him, no crime to lay to his charge, but they <hi type="italic">sought for witnesses against him;</hi> pumped some with ensnaring questions, offered bribes to others, if they <hi type="italic">would accuse him,</hi> and endeavored to frighten others, if they <hi type="italic">would not,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.14.55-Mark.14.56">v. 55, 56</reference>. The chief priests and elders were by the law entrusted with the prosecuting and punishing of <hi type="italic">false witnesses</hi> (<reference osisRef="Deut.19.16-Deut.19.17">Deut. xix. 16, 17</reference>); yet those were now ringleaders in a crime that tends to overthrow of all justice. It is time to cry, <hi type="italic">Help, Lord,</hi> when the physicians of a land are its troublers, and those that should be the conservators of peace and equity, are the corrupters of both. <div eID="gen24986" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24987" type="x-p"/> IV. He was at length charged with words spoken some years ago, which, as they were represented, seemed to threaten <hi type="italic">the temple,</hi> which they had made no better than an idol of (<reference osisRef="Mark.14.57-Mark.14.58">v. 57, 58</reference>); but the witnesses to this matter did not agree (<reference osisRef="Mark.14.59">v. 59</reference>), for one swore that he said, <hi type="italic">I am able to destroy the temple of God, and to build it in three days</hi> (so it is in Matthew); the other swore that he said, <hi type="italic">I will destroy this temple, that is made with hands,</hi> and <hi type="italic">within three days, I will build</hi> not it, but <hi type="italic">another made without hands;</hi> now these two differ much from each other; <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">oude ise en he martyria</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">their testimony was not sufficient,</hi> nor equal to the charge of a capital crime; so Dr. Hammond: they did not accuse him of that upon which a <hi type="italic">sentence of death</hi> might be founded, no not by the utmost stretch of their law. <div eID="gen24987" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24988" type="x-p"/> V. He was urged to be his own accuser (<reference osisRef="Mark.14.60">v. 60</reference>); The <hi type="italic">high priest stood up</hi> in a heat, and said, <hi type="italic">Answerest thou nothing?</hi> This he said under pretence of justice and fair dealing, but really with a design to ensnare him, that they might <hi type="italic">accuse him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.11.53-Luke.11.54">Luke xi. 53, 54</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.20.20">xx. 20</reference>. We may well imagine with what an air of haughtiness and disdain this proud high priest brought our Lord Jesus to this question; "Come you, the prisoner at the bar, you hear what is sworn against you; what have you now to say for yourself?" Pleased to think that <hi type="italic">he</hi> seemed silent, who had so often silenced those that picked quarrels with him. Still Christ <hi type="italic">answered nothing,</hi> that he might set us an example, 1. Of <hi type="italic">patience</hi> under calumnies and false accusations; when we are <hi type="italic">reviled,</hi> let us not <hi type="italic">revile again,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Pet.2.23">1 Pet. ii. 23</reference>. And, 2. Of <hi type="italic">prudence,</hi> when a man shall be made an <hi type="italic">offender for a word</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.29.21">Isa. xxix. 21</reference>), and our <hi type="italic">de</hi>fence made our <hi type="italic">of</hi>fence; it is an evil time indeed when the prudent shall <hi type="italic">keep silence</hi> (lest they make bad worse), <hi type="italic">and commit their cause to him that judgeth righteously.</hi> But, <div eID="gen24988" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24989" type="x-p"/> VI. When he was asked <hi type="italic">whether he was the Christ,</hi> he confessed, and denied not, that <hi type="italic">he was,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.14.61-Mark.14.62">v. 61, 62</reference>. He asked, <hi type="italic">Art thou the Son of the Blessed?</hi> that is the Son of <hi type="italic">God?</hi> for, as Dr. Hammond observes, the Jews, when they named <hi type="italic">God,</hi> generally added, <hi type="italic">blessed for ever;</hi> and thence <hi type="italic">the Blessed</hi> is the title of <hi type="italic">God,</hi> a peculiar title, and applied to Christ, <reference osisRef="Rom.9.5">Rom. ix. 5</reference>. And for the proof of his being the <hi type="italic">Son of God,</hi> he binds them over to his second coming; "<hi type="italic">Ye shall see the Son of man sitting on the right hand of power;</hi> that <hi type="italic">Son of man</hi> that now appears so mean and despicable, whom ye <hi type="italic">see</hi> and trample upon (<reference osisRef="Isa.53.2-Isa.53.3">Isa. liii. 2, 3</reference>), you shall shortly see and <hi type="italic">tremble before.</hi>" Now, one would think that such a word as this which our Lord Jesus seems to have spoken with a grandeur and majesty not agreeable to his present appearance (for through the thickest cloud of his humiliation some rays of glory were still darted forth), should have startled the court, and at least, in the opinion of some of them, should have amounted to a <hi type="italic">demurrer,</hi> or <hi type="italic">arrest of judgment,</hi> and that they should have stayed process till they had considered further of it; when Paul at the bar reasoned of the <hi type="italic">judgment to come,</hi> the judge <hi type="italic">trembled,</hi> and adjourned the trial, <reference osisRef="Acts.24.25">Acts xxiv. 25</reference>. But these chief priests were so miserably blinded with malice and rage, that, like the horse rushing into the battle, they <hi type="italic">mocked at fear, and were not affrighted,</hi> neither <hi type="italic">believed they that it was the sound of the trumpet,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.39.22">Job xxxix. 22</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.39.24">24</reference>. And see <reference osisRef="Job.15.25-Job.15.26">Job xv. 25, 26</reference>. <div eID="gen24989" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24990" type="x-p"/> VII. The high priest, upon this confession of his, convicted him as a <hi type="italic">blasphemer</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mark.14.63">v. 63</reference>); He <hi type="italic">rent his clothes</hi>—<hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">chitonas autou</hi></hi>. Some think the word signifies his pontifical vestments, which, for the greater state, he had put on, though in the night, upon this occasion. As before, in his enmity to Christ, he said he knew not what (<reference osisRef="John.11.51-John.11.52">John xi. 51, 52</reference>), so now he did he knew not what. If Saul's rending Samuel's mantle was made to signify the rending of the kingdom from him (<reference osisRef="1Sam.15.27-1Sam.15.28">1 Sam. xv. 27, 28</reference>), much more did Caiaphas's rending his own clothes signify the rending of the priesthood from him, as the rending of the veil, at Christ's death, signified the throwing of all open. Christ's clothes, even when he was crucified, were kept entire, and not rent: for when the Levitical priesthood was rent in pieces and done away, <hi type="italic">This Man, because he continues ever, has an unchangeable priesthood.</hi> <div eID="gen24990" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24991" type="x-p"/> VIII. They agreed that he was a blasphemer, and, as such, was guilty of a capital crime, <reference osisRef="Mark.14.64">v. 64</reference>. The question <hi type="italic">seemed</hi> to be put fairly, <hi type="italic">What think ye?</hi> But it was really <hi type="italic">prejudged,</hi> for the high priest had said, <hi type="italic">Ye have heard the blasphemy;</hi> he gave judgment first, who, as president of the court, ought to have voted last. So they <hi type="italic">all condemned him</hi> to be <hi type="italic">guilty of death;</hi> what friends he had in the great sanhedrim, did not appear, it is probable that they had not notice. <div eID="gen24991" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24992" type="x-p"/> IX. They set themselves to abuse him, and, as the Philistines with Samson, to make sport with him, <reference osisRef="Mark.14.65">v. 65</reference>. It should seem that some of the priests themselves that had condemned him, so far forgot the dignity, as well as duty, of their place, and the gravity which became them, that they helped their servants in playing the fool with a condemned prisoner. This they made their diversion, while they <hi type="italic">waited for the morning,</hi> to complete their villany. That <hi type="italic">night of observations</hi> (as the passover-night was called) they <hi type="italic">made a merry night of.</hi> If they did not think it below them to abuse Christ, shall we think any thing below us, by which we may do him honour?

<div eID="gen24992" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Peter's Fall.</title> <div sID="gen24993" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">66</hi> And as Peter was beneath in the palace, there cometh one of the maids of the high priest: <hi type="super">67</hi> And when she saw Peter warming himself, she looked upon him, and said, And thou also wast with Jesus of Nazareth. <hi type="super">68</hi> But he denied, saying, I know not, neither understand I what thou sayest. And he went out into the porch; and the cock crew. <hi type="super">69</hi> And a maid saw him again, and began to say to them that stood by, This is <hi type="italic">one</hi> of them. <hi type="super">70</hi> And he denied it again. And a little after, they that stood by said again to Peter, Surely thou art <hi type="italic">one</hi> of them: for thou art a Galilæan, and thy speech agreeth <hi type="italic">thereto.</hi> <hi type="super">71</hi> But he began to curse and to swear, <hi type="italic">saying,</hi> I know not this man of whom ye speak. <hi type="super">72</hi> And the second time the cock crew. And Peter called to mind the word that Jesus said unto him, Before the cock crow twice, thou shalt deny me thrice. And when he thought thereon, he wept. <div eID="gen24993" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24994" type="x-p"/> We have here the story of Peter's denying Christ. <div eID="gen24994" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24995" type="x-p"/> 1. It began in <hi type="italic">keeping at a distance</hi> from him. Peter had followed <hi type="italic">afar off</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mark.14.54">v. 54</reference>), and now was <hi type="italic">beneath in the palace,</hi> at the lower end of the hall. Those that are <hi type="italic">shy</hi> of Christ, are in a fair way to <hi type="italic">deny</hi> him, that are shy of attending on holy ordinances, shy of the communion of the faithful, and loth to be seen on the side of despised godliness. <div eID="gen24995" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24996" type="x-p"/> 2. It was occasioned by his associating with the high priest's servants, and sitting among them. They that think it dangerous to be in company with Christ's disciples, because thence they may be drawn in to <hi type="italic">suffer for him,</hi> will find it much more dangerous to be in company with his enemies, because there they may be drawn in to <hi type="italic">sin against him.</hi> <div eID="gen24996" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24997" type="x-p"/> 3. The temptation was, his being charged as a disciple of Christ; <hi type="italic">Thou also wert with Jesus of Nazareth,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.14.67">v. 67</reference>. <hi type="italic">This is one of them</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mark.14.69">v. 69</reference>), <hi type="italic">for thou art a Galilean,</hi> one may know that by thy speaking broad, <reference osisRef="Mark.14.70">v. 70</reference>. It doth not appear that he was <hi type="italic">challenged</hi> upon it, or in danger of being <hi type="italic">prosecuted</hi> as a criminal for it, but only <hi type="italic">bantered</hi> upon it, and in danger of being ridiculed as a fool for it. While the chief priests were abusing the Master, the servants were abusing the disciples. Sometimes the cause of Christ seems to fall so much on the losing side, that every body has a stone to throw at it, and even the <hi type="italic">abjects gather themselves together against</hi> it. When Job was on the dunghill, he was had in derision of those that were the <hi type="italic">children of base men,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.30.8">Job xxx. 8</reference>. Yet, all things considered, the temptation could not be called <hi type="italic">formidable;</hi> it was only a <hi type="italic">maid</hi> that casually cast her eye upon him, and, for aught that appears, without design of giving him any trouble, said, <hi type="italic">Thou art one of them,</hi> to which he needed not to have made any reply, or might have said, "And if I be, I hope that is no treason." <div eID="gen24997" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24998" type="x-p"/> 4. The sin was very great; he <hi type="italic">denied Christ before men,</hi> at a time when he ought to have confessed and owned him, and to have appeared in court a witness for him. Christ had often given notice to his disciples of his own sufferings; yet, when they came, they were to Peter as great a surprise and terror as if he had never heard of them before. He had often told them that they must <hi type="italic">suffer</hi> for him, must <hi type="italic">take up their cross,</hi> and follow him; and yet Peter is so terribly afraid of suffering, upon the very first alarm of it, that he will lie and swear, and do any thing, to avoid it. When Christ was admired and flocked after, he could readily own him; but now that he is deserted, and despised, and run down, he is ashamed of him, and will own no relation to him. <div eID="gen24998" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24999" type="x-p"/> 5. His repentance was very speedy. He repeated his denial thrice, and the third was worst of all, for then he <hi type="italic">cursed</hi> and <hi type="italic">swore,</hi> to confirm his denial; and that the third blow, which, one would think, should have <hi type="italic">stunned him,</hi> and knocked him down, <hi type="italic">startled him,</hi> and roused him up. Then the <hi type="italic">cock crew</hi> the second time, which put him in mind of his Master's words, the warning he had given him, with that particular circumstance of the <hi type="italic">cock crowing twice;</hi> by recollecting that, he was made sensible of his sin and the aggravations of it; and when he thought thereon, he wept. Some observe that this evangelist, who wrote, as some have thought, by St. Peter's direction, speaks as fully of Peter's sin as any of them, but more briefly of his <hi type="italic">sorrow,</hi> which Peter, in modesty, would not have to be magnified, and because he thought he could never sorrow enough for great a sin. His repentance here is thus expressed, <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">epibalon eklaie</hi></hi>, where something must be supplied. He <hi type="italic">added to weep,</hi> so some; making it a Hebraism; he wept, and the more he thought of it, the more he wept; he continued weeping; he <hi type="italic">flung out,</hi> and wept; <hi type="italic">burst out</hi> into tears; <hi type="italic">threw himself down,</hi> and wept; he <hi type="italic">covered his face,</hi> and wept, so some; cast his garment about his head, that he might not be seen to weep; he <hi type="italic">cast his eyes</hi> upon his Master, who turned, and looked upon him; so Dr. Hammond supplies it, and it is a probable conjecture. Or, as we understand it, <hi type="italic">fixing his mind upon it,</hi> he wept. It is not a transient thought of that which is humbling, that will suffice, but we must dwell upon it. Or, what if this word should mean his <hi type="italic">laying a load</hi> upon himself, throwing a confusion into his own face? he did as the <hi type="italic">publican</hi> that smote his breast, in sorrow for sin; and this amounts to his weeping bitterly.  <chapter eID="Mark.14"/> <div eID="gen24999" type="x-p"/>

<div eID="gen25002" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen25001" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Christ Brought before Pilate.</title> <div sID="gen25003" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> And straightway in the morning the chief priests held a consultation with the elders and scribes and the whole council, and bound Jesus, and carried <hi type="italic">him</hi> away, and delivered <hi type="italic">him</hi> to Pilate. <hi type="super">2</hi> And Pilate asked him, Art thou the King of the Jews? And he answering said unto him, Thou sayest <hi type="italic">it.</hi> <hi type="super">3</hi> And the chief priests accused him of many things: but he answered nothing. <hi type="super">4</hi> And Pilate asked him again, saying, Answerest thou nothing? behold how many things they witness against thee. <hi type="super">5</hi> But Jesus yet answered nothing; so that Pilate marvelled. <hi type="super">6</hi> Now at <hi type="italic">that</hi> feast he released unto them one prisoner, whomsoever they desired. <hi type="super">7</hi> And there was <hi type="italic">one</hi> named Barabbas, <hi type="italic">which lay</hi> bound with them that had made insurrection with him, who had committed murder in the insurrection. <hi type="super">8</hi> And the multitude crying aloud began to desire <hi type="italic">him to do</hi> as he had ever done unto them. 9 But Pilate answered them, saying, Will ye that I release unto you the King of the Jews? <hi type="super">10</hi> For he knew that the chief priests had delivered him for envy. <hi type="super">11</hi> But the chief priests moved the people, that he should rather release Barabbas unto them. 12 And Pilate answered and said again unto them, What will ye then that I shall do <hi type="italic">unto him</hi> whom ye call the King of the Jews? <hi type="super">13</hi> And they cried out again, Crucify him. <hi type="super">14</hi> Then Pilate said unto them, Why, what evil hath he done? And they cried out the more exceedingly, Crucify him. <div eID="gen25003" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25004" type="x-p"/> Here we have, I. A <hi type="italic">consultation</hi> held by the great Sanhedrim for the effectual prosecution of our Lord Jesus. They met <hi type="italic">early in the morning</hi> about it, and went into a grand committee, to find out <hi type="italic">ways and means</hi> to get him put to death; they lost no time, but followed their blow in good earnest, lest there should be an <hi type="italic">uproar among the people.</hi> The unwearied industry of wicked people in doing that which is evil, should shame us for our backwardness and slothfulness in that which is good. They that <hi type="italic">war</hi> against Christ and thy soul, are up early; <hi type="italic">How long then wilt thou sleep, O sluggard?</hi> <div eID="gen25004" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25005" type="x-p"/> II. The delivering of him up a prisoner to Pilate; they <hi type="italic">bound him.</hi> He was to be the great sacrifice, and sacrifices must be bound with cords, <reference osisRef="Ps.118.27">Ps. cxviii. 27</reference>. Christ was bound, to make bonds easy to us, and enable us, as Paul and Silas, to sing in bonds. It is good for us often to <hi type="italic">remember the bonds</hi> of the Lord Jesus, as bound with him who was <hi type="italic">bound for us.</hi> They led him through the streets of Jerusalem, to expose <hi type="italic">him</hi> to contempt, who, while he taught in the temple, but a day or two before, was had in veneration; and we may well imagine how miserably he looked after such a night's usage as he had had; so buffeted, spit upon, and abused. Their delivering him to the Roman power was a type of ruin of their church, which hereby they merited, and brought upon themselves; it signified that the promise, the covenant, and the oracles, of God, and the visible state church, which were the glory of Israel, and had been so long in their possession, should now be delivered up to the Gentiles. By delivering up the <hi type="italic">king</hi> they do, in effect, deliver up the <hi type="italic">kingdom of God,</hi> which is therefore, as it were, by their own consent, taken from them, and given to another nation. If they had delivered up Christ, to gratify the desires of the Romans, or to satisfy and jealousies of theirs concerning him, it had been another matter; but they voluntarily betrayed him that was <hi type="italic">Israel's crown,</hi> to them that were <hi type="italic">Israel's yoke.</hi> <div eID="gen25005" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25006" type="x-p"/> III. The examining of him by Pilate upon interrogatories (<reference osisRef="Mark.15.2">v. 2</reference>); "<hi type="italic">Art thou the king of the Jews?</hi> Dost thou pretend to be so, to be that Messiah whom the Jews expect as a temporal prince?"—"Yea," saith Christ, "it is as <hi type="italic">thou sayest,</hi> I am that Messiah, but not such a one as they expect."
